book.about: Carter Alexander Nolasco was born at twenty-seven weeks, weighing two pounds, six ounces. His nursery was finished, his name chosen, and then an ordinary Sunday unraveled in minutes. In Hallelujah Even Here, Meredith P. Nolasco walks through the emergency that brought him into the world, the NICU days of monitors and prayers, the first time she held him on Day 12, and the night he slipped into eternity. She writes about the silent morning after, the ache of mothering a toddler while mourning an infant, and the questions friends and strangers ask without knowing what they cost. She had known the grief of a miscarriage and believed that if she did everything right things would unfold as planned; Carter's story showed how fragile that expectation is. This is not a guide on how to grieve, a roadmap or a promise that everything will feel reconciled. It is a telling, in twenty-six short chapters with dated journal entries written to her son, and an honest wrestling with God, including the hardest question: why a child?

sections.h2: For mothers who have known this kind of loss
paras: If you are searching for language, this book may lend you some. The author describes the silent morning after, the milk that came in with no baby to feed, and the way she woke each day and thought of the same Friday. She writes that she did not soften it: "So I don't soften it." She also writes that she no longer needs to make people comfortable in her grief.

sections.h2: For fathers and the people who love them
paras: The author writes about her husband with respect. Their grief is the same loss from different places. She names it in a line that returns through the chapter: "Same loss. Different heart journey." The book does not instruct a father. It shows two people choosing, again and again, to stay beside each other.

sections.h2: For friends, family and caregivers who want to know what helps
paras: A chapter called I Can't Imagine turns a familiar sentence around, and a chapter called How Are You Doing? asks what that question costs. She writes that people who "sit in the valley" with her are doing "holy work without knowing it." A reader who wants to sit with someone grieving will find what that can look like.

sections.h2: For anyone wrestling with why a child
paras: The book gives space to anger, numbness and the question itself. It does not say that a child's death makes sense. It says that Scripture rarely explains and often shows. The author asks her questions of God in the open and also writes of moments when she felt "undeniably held."

audience.headline: A mother tells the story of her son, who lived twelve days, and finds a place for her grief to breathe.
audience.body: For mothers who have known the loss of a baby and are searching for language for the pain, for the fathers who stand beside them, and for anyone who has lost a child or loves someone who has. Meredith P. Nolasco writes in twenty-six short chapters, with dated entries addressed to her son, about a birth at twenty-seven weeks, the NICU, the night he died and the long months after. It offers companionship rather than answers. A note on subjects: this is a memoir of the death of a baby. It describes an emergency birth, intensive care, the moments of the baby's death, cremation, and the physical and emotional weight of grief, told honestly and without graphic detail. It is a mother's telling, not medical, counseling or mental health advice. If grief or trauma is overwhelming you, please contact a physician or licensed professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

quote.text: I write for the mothers who have known this kind of loss, who are searching for language for a pain that feels unspeakable.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people carrying the loss of a baby
paras: This is the story of Carter Alexander Nolasco, born at twenty-seven weeks and weighing two pounds, six ounces. His nursery was finished and his name was chosen. Then an ordinary Sunday came apart in minutes. The author does not hand the reader a method. She tells what happened, what she asked God, and what she learned about holding sorrow and love in the same hands.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a telling, not a guide. The Introduction says so in plain words: "This is not a guide on how to grieve."
It stays close to one family and one baby. The chapters follow the emergency, the NICU days, the one hour of holding him on Day 12, the night he died, and the months after.

It speaks to fathers and to the people around a grieving family. A chapter on what people say, a chapter on a marriage under strain and a chapter on mothering a toddler while mourning an infant sit beside the hospital chapters.
It brings the hardest question to God and does not tidy the answer. One chapter is titled Why a Child?, another Wrestling, another A Stubborn Hope.
Hope is present but not loud. The author writes that hope here "exists right alongside the pain" and is "sometimes steady, sometimes barely there, but real."

paras: Chapter 2 begins with a normal Sunday: church in the morning, waffles after, a soccer ball in the backyard. Then pain, then the floor, then sirens. At twenty-seven weeks, her water broke, and she writes that "What had been a normal Sunday unraveled in minutes." A nurse held the baby in until the surgical team could take her in for an emergency C-section. She whispered prayers, asking God to go where she could not. Then, she writes, "He was here. Tiny. Fighting. Alive."

Chapter 4 begins with a gift. The lead physician asked whether she would like to hold him, and for the first time she did, with him resting on her chest. "I felt my whole body exhale," she writes. She went home planning to spend the whole next day with him. She had no way to know, she writes, that "it would be the only time I would ever hold him full of life." That evening came three calls from the hospital. Chapter 4 ends in the NICU, in her arms, with the beeps fading and the words "Carter was gone."

In Chapter 7, the author looks at a photograph and thinks that she should have kept a small piece of his hair. Days later, sitting in his room with his hospital blanket in her lap, she peels back a fold and finds "two small pieces of his hair, intertwined, caught in the fabric." She does not claim to understand why a child died. She does write that "He knows every hair on Carter's head" and that God "left a couple for his mom." It is one of the book's smallest and most tender chapters.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author asks the question herself in the first paragraph and answers it plainly: "Because I have to." She says there is "a weight to Carter's story that will not let me stay silent," and calls it "a sacred urgency" that does not lift until the words are out.
She says who the book is for and what it will not do. "This book is simply a telling," she writes, "Of our baby who lived." And her last sentence to the reader is the title: "Hallelujah even here."

faq.q: What is Hallelujah Even Here about?
faq.a: It is Meredith P. Nolasco's honest telling of her son Carter, born at twenty-seven weeks, who lived twelve days in the NICU, and of grief, faith and the hardest question: why a child? It is told in twenty-six short chapters with dated entries written to her son.

faq.q: Is it a book about pregnancy and infant loss?
faq.a: Yes, in the sense that it follows one family through the birth and death of a baby who lived twelve days. The phrase pregnancy and infant loss does not appear in the interior, and the book does not claim to cover the subject broadly. The author also mentions an earlier miscarriage in one line. It is one mother's story, not a reference book.

faq.q: Is it about a premature baby?
faq.a: Yes. The baby was born at twenty-seven weeks after a sudden emergency, spent twelve days in the NICU and died there. The word premature does not appear in the book. It speaks of twenty-seven weeks, the NICU, monitors and a two pound, six ounce baby.

faq.q: Is it a guide on how to grieve?
faq.a: No. The Introduction says it is "not a roadmap, or a list of steps." It offers companionship and does not tie itself up neatly: "It's not a story that ties itself up neatly in the end."

faq.q: What does the book say about surrender to God?
faq.a: She describes surrender as "a posture. A choice," not giving up but "loosening my grip." Looking back, she would tell her earlier self to "Loosen your grip" and to cling more to God's sovereignty than to statistics. She also writes that surrender "doesn't feel like peace" at first.

faq.q: Does it speak to healing after loss?
faq.a: It does not promise a cure or a timeline. It describes a slow, uneven mercy: shock that shelters, sorrow that arrives later, joy and grief that "stand side by side," and a purpose that grows quieter. The author writes that the hope she found "doesn't erase sorrow or rush healing."

faq.q: Is it for grieving parents, including fathers?
faq.a: Yes. The Introduction names mothers and fathers, and a chapter is given to what grief looks like inside a marriage. It is also written for anyone who has lost a child or loves someone who has.

book.about: In Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, a single pint of stem cells flown in from Germany dripped into John Vallely's bloodstream while his blood count stood at zero. The Pyramid Principle is the true story of a former UCLA basketball player, NBA first-round pick and Houston Rocket who faced opponents tougher than any he met on the court. It begins on Balboa Island in Newport Beach, where a boy too small and too slow shot a thousand shots a night in the alley behind his house, and follows him through high school and Orange Coast College to his dream of playing for Coach John Wooden. Then life moves past the hardwood: his nine-year-old daughter's cancer and the family's loss of her at twelve, a courtroom battle with a bank, and Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma, and then a rematch with it. Through every struggle he turned to the guidance he had relied on since college, the words and teachings of John Wooden, the coach he considers the greatest teacher of his time. It is a story of love, loss, faith and perseverance, and of a family that kept saying, We are still a family.

sections.h2: For sports fans who want the story behind the jersey
paras: If you love basketball memoir, this is the view from inside Coach Wooden's program. John was named captain of a UCLA team the press wrote off as "The Team Without," after key players left for the NBA. He writes about the Bruins' routines, Wooden's lessons, teammates such as Kareem, and the road from Orange Coast College to Westwood. It ends with his induction into the UCLA Hall of Fame.

sections.h2: For families walking through childhood cancer
paras: Erin was nine when she was diagnosed and twelve when she died. John writes about the treatments, the hospital, the wig that floated off in a hotel pool, and her determination to go to a Father and Daughter Valentine's Dance. It is told as one father's testimony, not a manual. If you are in that hospital hallway now, you will find company in these pages, and you should also know it does not hide how much it hurts.

sections.h2: For survivors, and anyone fighting a battle they did not choose
paras: John fought Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma twice, and the book carries you through the diagnosis, the transplant and the rematch. Along the way he fought a long lawsuit against a bank with only a small legal team beside him. Whatever your battle is, the question he keeps returning to is the same: what does it mean to have done your best?

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who need hope in a hard season
paras: A basketball memoir that does not stay on the court. The Pyramid Principle is the true story of John Vallely, a former UCLA basketball player, NBA first-round pick and Houston Rocket. It moves from a boy shooting in an alley to the hardest opponents of his life.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts in a stem cell transplant room. The book opens at Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, where a pint of stem cells flown in from Germany drips into his bloodstream while his blood count stands at zero, then goes back to the beginning to show how he got there.

It is built on a teacher's wisdom. John calls Coach John Wooden the greatest teacher of his time, and the book returns to Wooden's Pyramid of Success, with a quotation from Wooden opening several chapters.

It tells the loss honestly. His daughter Erin was diagnosed with cancer at nine and the family lost her at twelve. John writes that the earthly pain of loss is as great as ever, and he writes of the comfort of heaven in the same pages.
It refuses a shallow idea of winning. Success, he says in his Hall of Fame speech, is not wealth, power or position as the world defines it, but the peace of mind of knowing you did your best.
It is a family story. His son Eric told him, "Dad, we are still a family," and the book is dedicated to Eric.

blocks.text: Every copy opens with a dedication to the author's son Eric, an introduction, and a table of contents of 22 chapters. Chapter 1, "The Journey Begins," opens like this:

paras: This incredible journey all started with a dream, a ball, and the sweet sound of a one-dribble pull-up and a basketball swishing through a hoop. It is a sound that is so pure, so soothing, a satisfying reward for executing the perfect shot: no rim, no backboard, nothing but net. The ultimate dream would be executing the ideal shot for the legendary Coach John Wooden and the Blue and Gold of UCLA.

In 1935, my father bought a bayfront property for $7,000 in the Southern California town of Newport Beach. He built bedrooms for my sister and me then hung a backboard up on the garage. Initially, my family complained about the constant sound of the ball bouncing off the basket. After years of dedication, my shot was so smooth that the noise could only be described as calming. Even my dribbling sounded rhythmic. Whether it was on the alleyway asphalt or the hardwood floor, that sound would change my life and one day lead to hope. During those years, I would spend hours upon hours in the alley shooting baskets, intoxicated by the sound and relentless in my efforts to hear it again and again.

stories.h2: The boy who was too slow
paras: At Corona del Mar High School John was 5 feet 3 inches and 104 pounds, undersized even for a guard. Years of shooting in the alley made him a great shooter, and he grew six inches in his sophomore year. By his senior year he was 6 feet 2 inches and leading his team in scoring. His own mom, he says, told him he was too slow. A letter of interest from UCLA, signed by Coach Wooden, then arrived, with a catch: he needed a 3.0 GPA, and his was 2.9. Karen, who would become his wife, told him, "You can do this, John."

stories.h2: Nine hundred people for one little girl
paras: After Erin died, nine hundred people came to her memorial service at Saint Andrews Presbyterian Church in Newport Beach: nurses, doctors, teachers, friends and children from the community. John knew he had to speak and did not know if he could hold it together. He writes that as the choir sang "Amazing Grace," it felt like heaven came down to the church. Years later, the family joined the "Dribble for Victory Over Cancer" event, where Erin was the honorary captain and every athlete pinned the name of someone they loved to their shirt.

stories.h2: A fight in a downtown tower
paras: John's legal case against a bank was, in his words, "going uphill and sideways." He found a one-man law office in Costa Mesa and a lawyer who greeted him with, "I was a big fan of your days at UCLA." The chapter is named for the question Coach Wooden asked: "Are you right?"

author.bio: John Vallely grew up on Balboa Island in Newport Beach, California. Undersized at Corona del Mar High School, he began his college career at Orange Coast College before playing basketball for Coach John Wooden at UCLA. He went on to the NBA as a first-round pick and a Houston Rocket, and is a UCLA Hall of Famer. He has battled Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma twice. The book was written with Paul Weissenstein.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: John writes that while he lay in that transplant room, in despair, he needed a way to hold on to hope in the face of uncertainty. "As I wrestled to find God's strength for my weakness in this battle, my only recourse was to turn to the same source of guidance and wisdom I have used for every critical struggle in my own life: the words and teachings of John Wooden, my UCLA basketball coach and a man I consider the greatest teacher of his time."

So the book is a record of what he learned and where it led. In the final chapter he writes, "I know in my head and from my experience that heaven is real," and "I still struggle and question. I'm still learning and growing." It is honest about faith in the way the best testimonies are: no tidy answers, only a man still choosing joy each day.

faq.q: What is The Pyramid Principle about?
faq.a: The true story of John Vallely, a former UCLA basketball player and NBA first-round pick, and how he drew on Coach John Wooden's teaching to face his daughter's cancer, a courtroom battle and his own lymphoma.

faq.q: Is it a basketball memoir?
faq.a: It starts there. The book follows him from a small boy shooting in an alley to playing for Coach Wooden at UCLA and in the NBA, then moves past the court to loss and illness.

faq.q: Is it an underdog story?
faq.a: Yes. John was undersized, a junior college player who was overlooked and still picked to start for Coach Wooden, and later he took on a bank with a small legal team.

faq.q: Is it the same as Minto's The Pyramid Principle?
faq.a: No. That is a different book on business writing. This is a sports memoir named for Coach Wooden's Pyramid of Success.

faq.q: Does the book describe a stem cell transplant?
faq.a: Yes. It opens in the transplant room at MD Anderson Cancer Center and returns to the treatment later as John's lymphoma comes back.

faq.q: Does it talk about heaven?
faq.a: Yes. The final chapter, "Faith," is John's personal testimony about heaven, grief and joy.

faq.q: Is it a good book for a Christian athlete?
faq.a: It is a faith memoir by a former college and NBA player. It shows a believer carrying Coach Wooden's teaching and his trust in God through loss and illness.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Sports fans, families walking through childhood cancer, cancer survivors, and anyone who has leaned on a mentor's wisdom in a hard season.

book.short: A memoir-play hybrid about a best friend nicknamed Beetle and how God used one man's humor to shape the lives around him.
book.about: The Beetle Experience is the story of Stephen Michael Bailey, known to nearly everyone as Beetle, told by his best friend, Dana Morrison. It is not a traditional memoir, and it is not a conventional stage play either. It is a memoir-play hybrid: prose memories, dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues and vignettes that can be read, remembered, performed or passed along. Beetle was a laughter-generating, treasure-hunting, car-rebuilding, churchgoing, movie-quoting, sasquatch-hunting, model rocket-making bundle of joy, plump, freckled, kind and gentle, with a Rubik's cube in hand. The book unfolds in six acts, from the pre-Beetle days and a run of pranks through the campfire years where he got his name, a turning point of change and hardship, years of breaking and mending, and Beetle's final days and homecoming. Rooted in Proverbs 17:22, A cheerful heart is good medicine, it shows how God used one man's humor to shape the lives around him, and how laughter and faith can walk together all the way to the end.

sections.h2: For anyone who knew Beetle, and anyone who did not
paras: If you knew him, you will hear his voice: the movie quotes, the Rubik's cube in his hand, the "Saweet!" he said when something went his way. If you never met him, you will feel as if you did. Dana writes him as warm, humble and quick, with a smile that said "I'll do anything for you" without a word. Friends, family and coworkers add their own stories at the end, from a school bus left in a ditch to a hardware store where every total was "a Thoooousand dollars."

sections.h2: For readers who love funny true stories about friendship and practical jokes
paras: Act I is all pranks. A teenage Stephen and Dana move a youth leader's car to the wrong side of a church driveway while a conference is under way, then wait to hear what happens. Later chapters go treasure hunting with a metal detector, fish for metal with magnets and set out on a bigfoot hunt. The humor is gentle, the friendship is the point, and the faith is never bolted on.

sections.h2: For readers who want to finish well, and anyone losing a friend
paras: Dana's closing hope for you is to "finish well in the race in which you find yourself." The last third follows Beetle through a hospital stay in Maine, a solved Rubik's cube, hard news from a physician, and a homecoming to his own house and his dog, Max. It does not hide the loss. It also does not let sorrow have the last word. This is one friend's story, not a grief manual, and you will find company in it.

audience.headline: A best friend who made everyone laugh, and finished well.
audience.body: For anyone who knew Beetle, and anyone who did not. Dana Morrison tells the true story of Stephen Michael Bailey, a plump, freckled, kind and gentle man from Danforth, Maine, who turned every hard job into a punchline and carried his faith into his final days. It is a memoir written to be read, remembered, performed or passed along.

quote.text: A cheerful heart is good medicine.
quote.cite: Proverbs 17:22, the verse printed on the epigraph page, followed by the line "Beetle is living proof."

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want laughter and faith in the same story
paras: The Beetle Experience is a funny memoir that is not shy about the hard parts. Dana calls it "not a traditional memoir" and "not a conventional stage play either." It is something in between, and it welcomes you into the front row.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a memoir-play hybrid. Prose memories sit beside dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues, vignettes and short Reader's Notes that give the time and place, so the book can be read quietly or staged with friends.
It is told by the best friend. Dana was there for the pranks, the summers at camp and the hospital room, and he narrates as himself, turning to the audience to give you the backstory.
It keeps its promise to tell the truth. "The stories you will see are true," Dana writes. "The names haven't been changed to protect the innocent as there were likely none that were innocent."
It lets you laugh and grieve in the same breath. In Beetle's last days, a room full of visitors is telling funny stories when he says, "I'm dyin' over here… and you guys are tellin' jokes!"

It ends with an invitation and a chorus of voices. After the epilogue come simple next steps for anyone who wants to start following Jesus, then "Last Words" from family, camp friends, coworkers and neighbors who knew him.

paras: In the summer of 1988, Dana, Stephen and a friend named Scott arrive as volunteers at Living Waters Bible Camp. A loud, laughing staff member named Ty Hutchins hands out nicknames to everyone standing in the dinner line. Dana is "Crash." Scott is "Pee Wee," to his fury. Stephen becomes "Beetle," because his last name is Bailey. Then the camp's assistant director, Roger Black, insists that he gave the name first. Dana settles it by asking the audience to vote and concludes, "I guess Beetle just… named himself." The same scene gives us the day Beetle tells a camper he is 45, and keeps saying it for years.

stories.h2: Captain Kidd's treasure, or what is left of it
paras: Every summer Dana and Beetle plan the fun they will have when he is back in Maine. One year Beetle has heard a rumor that Captain Kidd buried treasure near Wiscasset, so they take an old metal detector to the water behind his parents' house. They find spent .22 casings, a shotgun shell and a bottle cap. Dana admits that historians doubt Kidd ever reached the Maine coast, but says that without the rumor "he and I might have had some great memories stolen from us." The next summer they research a real abandoned gold prospect near Danforth.

In the hospital in June 2023, Beetle reaches for the Rubik's cube on his bedside table. His hands tremble, but he works it click by click until the colors line up, and Dana sees a verse come alive: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." (2 Timothy 4:7) A few scenes later, the room explodes into laughter at Beetle's line about dying, and the laughter dissolves into tears. Dana writes that in one line Beetle gave them permission to hold both, "the comedy and the tragedy — side by side."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Dana says the book began as a collection of memories, "funny, raw, sacred, and real," about a man God used to shape his life. Every time he tried to write it as a plain memoir, it felt "too small." Beetle, he explains, "isn't a man who speaks in paragraphs. He speaks in stories. Scenes. Punchlines. Pranks." So he started staging the memories, and the book became a hybrid.

"Some stories are too full of laughter to be told quietly. Some lives are too bright to be dimmed by paragraphs alone." It is an honest tribute, built on Proverbs 17:22 and on the belief that Beetle's joy pointed past himself to Christ. The epilogue says it plainly: "He ran his race, and he finished with joy."

book.meta: Clowning From The Heart by Cindy Love: a true story of 35 years as Sparkle the gospel clown, spreading a message of love in hospitals and beyond.
book.short: The true story of Cindy Love and Sparkle, the gospel clown she became: thirty-five years of clown ministry, one smile and one hug at a time.
book.about: In 1965 a seven-year-old girl in the Mojave Desert town of California City lined up with her sisters for her town's first-ever clown contest. Nearly twenty years later the seed planted that night would grow into a calling. Clowning From the Heart is the true story of Cindy Love and Sparkle, the gospel clown she became. While working in the billing department of a hospital in Walla Walla, Washington, Cindy and a friend put on greasepaint and red noses to visit patients, and she realized that clowning could be more than a hobby: it could be her ministry. Across twenty-seven short chapters she tells how she found her mentors, learned makeup, balloon animals and sleight of hand magic, chose her name, and handed out her trademark I Hugged A Clown Today stickers. The book carries readers through parades, fairgrounds, a rehab center, a graduation, a clown communion, a conversation about bullying, and the founding of Smiles For Life, to the hard goodbyes of her last parade. It closes with Sparkle's Tool Box and a reference page on the types of clowns, for readers who feel called to bring joy to others.

faq.q: What is Clowning From The Heart about?

faq.q: Is it a book about a message of love?
faq.a: One conviction runs through it: everyone needs to be heard and to know how loved and valued they are. Sparkle listens to the lonely, the sick, the frightened and the grieving and points them to the love of the Lord.

sections.h2: For readers who love warm, funny and moving true stories
paras: If you like Christian memoir that makes you smile first and tear up second, this one is for you. There is a pastor who needs convincing, a congregation that gasps, a friend who offers to help with the sign language, and a man in a nursing home who never forgets his clown. Cindy writes with the same gentleness she showed in the room, and she does not pretend that every day was easy.

sections.h2: For readers who feel called to bring joy to others
paras: You do not need greasepaint to be touched by this book. Cindy writes, "you don't have to dress up as a clown to touch someone's life in a positive way, just be YOU." If you are thinking about clown ministry, hospital visits or simply being a kinder presence at church, you will find ideas, courage and a good sense of what the work really asks of you. It is a memoir, not a how-to manual, but the tool box at the back is generous.

paras: Clowning From The Heart is a memoir in twenty-seven short chapters, so you can read one at a bedside, on a break or over a cup of coffee. Cindy tells it plainly, with humor and tears, and with a gentle push to go and do something kind.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins in the Mojave Desert in 1965. A seven-year-old Cindy and her sisters line up in clown makeup for their town's first-ever clown contest, and her little sister wins a trip to Catalina Island.

It grows out of a hospital job. Years later, working in a hospital billing office, Cindy and a friend put on makeup and red noses to visit patients. She realizes that clowning can be more than a hobby: it can be a ministry.

It is full of the work itself. You will meet the stickers that read "I Hugged A Clown Today," the makeup, the balloon animals, the sleight-of-hand magic and the mime routines, and you will walk through parades, a rehab center, a graduation and a 12-step retreat.

paras: In her late twenties, Cindy works in a hospital billing office in Walla Walla, Washington, and visits patients in her free time dressed as a clown. One day she is asked to come see a frightened toddler named Benji, who is in a full body cast and will let no one near him. When he sees the clown, his little body relaxes and he smiles for the first time. She leaves him a Polaroid of the two of them. Later that day he does not recognize her without the makeup, until she holds up the picture and says, "Benji, look. I am the clown." For six weeks she visits on her breaks, and on the day he goes home he tells her, "I love you too."

Driving to go Christmas shopping with a friend, Cindy hears a song on the radio and cannot shake it. She tracks down the recording, adds sign language she learned partly because her mother was hard of hearing, and asks her pastor if she can stage it with children before the service. He agrees, nervously. She appears as Sparkle in the middle of a congregation that is mostly elderly. When the song ends and she kneels by the cradle, the room bursts into applause and calls of "Amen."

Asked to perform for an entire school in Adams, Oregon, a town of 389 people, Cindy dreads the high school assembly most. The older students turn out to be the best audience. She invites two strong volunteers to push a fifteen-inch needle through a balloon. Theirs pop; hers does not, because she was prepared. The trick carries a message about preparing for life, and she follows it with "The Torn Heart," a paper heart she tears apart and then shows made whole again, to talk about what love can mend.

author.bio: Cindy Love grew up in California City, a small retirement town in the Mojave Desert. In her late twenties, while working in the billing department of a hospital in Walla Walla, Washington, she first put on clown makeup to visit patients. In 1989 she began clowning in earnest, and for thirty-five years she served as Sparkle, a gospel clown, at hospitals, nursing homes, schools, churches, parks and community events. Around 2010 she founded a nonprofit called Smiles For Life so that this kind of caring could continue through other people.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Cindy says Sparkle has "touched the lives of thousands of people over the past few decades," and she writes, "I hope her story can touch you as well." The book is also an act of letting go. In the last chapter she writes a letter to Sparkle and tells her that this book "is your legacy now."

She says the most important thing she can do for anyone is to listen: "Everyone has stories to tell, whether the stories are exciting and good, or scary and bad." Sparkle was the way she was able to sit and listen, and to tell each person how loved and valued they are. This book is her way of passing that on.

faq.q: What is Clowning From The Heart about?
faq.a: It is Cindy Love's true story of becoming Sparkle, a gospel clown, and of thirty-five years of clown ministry in hospitals, nursing homes, schools, churches and parades, told in twenty-seven short chapters.

faq.q: Is it a book about a message of love?
faq.a: One conviction runs through it: everyone needs to be heard and to know how loved and valued they are. Sparkle listens to the lonely, the sick, the frightened and the grieving and points them to the love of the Lord.

faq.q: Does it teach clown makeup and balloon animals?
faq.a: It tells how Cindy learned makeup, balloon animals and sleight-of-hand magic, and it closes with Sparkle's Tool Box and a reference page on the types of clowns. It is a memoir, not a how-to manual.

faq.q: Does the book take place in hospitals?
faq.a: Many chapters do. The first came when she and a friend put on clown makeup to visit patients at the hospital where she worked; the book also covers nursing homes, a rehab center, schools, churches and parades.

faq.q: Does it say anything about Happy Birthday Jesus?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 11 tells how she found the song, built a mime-and-sign-language Christmas play with children from her church, and performed it with her pastor's trust.

faq.q: Does it carry a message that people are beautiful and valued?
faq.a: Yes. The Foreword says Cindy wants people to feel "how beautiful and special they are inside and out," and she gives a hug and a sticker to prove it, in hospital rooms, on parade routes and to strangers on the street.

faq.q: What are the types of clowns?
faq.a: A reference page near the end describes six: the rodeo clown, the tramp or hobo clown, the auguste clown, the mime clown, the classic white-faced clown and the grotesque white-faced clown.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Christian readers who enjoy warm, funny and moving true stories, readers who feel called to bring joy to others, including through clown ministry, and anyone who has visited or worked in hospitals, nursing homes or schools and wants encouragement.

paras: The book's opening scene is a one-hour delay, a rough ride at 30,000 feet, a change of altitude, a slight change of course and a holding pattern near the destination. "Yes, our flight was delayed from the original plan. Yet we arrived safely at the intended destination." The author asks what success looks like when the path is altered but the destination stays intact.

Principle 3 tells of a manager who inherited a team of technical writers. A senior member had been passed between departments with a reputation as a mediocre performer, yet believed himself a top performer. Reviewing the facts, the author found that he had a lot of knowledge and commitment but was working from assumptions, not reality. After an honest conversation he committed to clarify expectations. A year later he was seen by peer managers as one of the strongest performers in the organization. The author's reading is that "he took time to listen to the reality check and do something meaningful with it."

In Principle 7 the author remembers a flight into John Wayne Airport. Power is reduced on descent, and the quiet can feel eerie. This time the captain sang, which changed the mood. Asked why, the captain said: "I do it in the flight simulator, why not do it when it really matters." The author takes it as a reminder of how what we do in the learning space carries over to the workplace.

Invisible Wounds is the book he needed back then, written for anyone who has asked why they react so strongly. In four parts John names the enemy, shows how trauma lives in the body and rewires a child's brain for fight, flight, freeze or fawn, explores why survivors cannot simply get over it and why so many are misdiagnosed, and walks the road to healing. sections.h2: For survivors of childhood trauma, including men who were taught to push through alone

paras: John spends nearly four decades believing his pain means he is defective. He calls the sleepless nights, the startle responses and the headaches stress, anxiety and bad nerves. Then a trauma-informed therapist explains that Complex PTSD comes from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, "what happens when the people meant to protect you are the ones who cause you pain." For the first time, the chaos makes sense. He stops asking what is wrong with him and begins asking what happened to him.

At thirty-six, running a fast-growing business and traveling constantly, John wakes with his heart pounding and his chest tight. He ends up in the emergency room convinced he is dying. The physician comes back smiling. "Good news," he says. "Your heart is perfect. It's probably just stress." John writes that the physician was right, but not in the way he thought: "It was unresolved trauma that had been simmering for decades." The chapter becomes an invitation to listen to the body instead of silencing it.

Years later, volunteering at his hometown high school as a successful businessman, John sits in a small-group discussion when a mistreated teenage boy looks at him and says, "God doesn't love everyone. He plays favorites." John sees himself in that boy: the same hollow ache and quiet despair. He realizes that his success has not healed him, only distracted him. He writes, "That was the day I stopped running from my past."

author.bio: John P. Boyle grew up in a small town in the mountains of West Virginia. He went on to boarding school and Harvard and built a career as a business leader while living for nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name. Diagnosed by a trauma-informed therapist, he now writes about childhood trauma, male survivors and the role of faith in recovery. He is a husband and father and the author of Appalachian Kid.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: John says he wrote the book because he does not want you to wander as long as he did. "I don't want you to blame yourself for things that were never your fault. I don't want you to feel alone in symptoms that millions of people experience but rarely talk about."

He also gives a plain reason for writing about something so painful: "Because pain loses power when it's spoken out loud. Because healing grows when it's shared." He believes "God carried me through things I didn't understand so that I could turn back and help others," and that "none of us are meant to heal in isolation." The book ends with a letter to the boy he once was, and an invitation to write your own.

faq.q: What is Invisible Wounds about?
faq.a: It is John Boyle's account of living nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name, and a four-part guide to understanding it and walking the road to healing. The subtitle is Understanding and Healing from Complex PTSD.

faq.q: What does the book mean by complex PTSD?
faq.a: In the author's words it is "a disorder of reactions," and it "is not about what is wrong with you; it is about what happened to you." He explains that it develops from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, rather than from one event.

faq.q: What does the book say about hypervigilance and fight, flight, freeze?
faq.a: Part Two shows how trauma lives in the body and rewires a child's brain for fight, flight, freeze or fawn. Hypervigilance, startle responses and panic are among the experiences the author describes in his own life.

faq.q: Is it about childhood trauma and men's mental health?
faq.a: Yes to both. It follows the effects of a chaotic childhood into adulthood, and it speaks directly to male survivors, who are taught to push through alone.

faq.q: Does it explain emotional flashbacks and toxic shame?
faq.a: It does, in Chapter 3. John describes "gray days" that turned out to be emotional flashbacks, and he separates guilt from shame: "Guilt says, 'I did something wrong.' Shame says, 'I am something wrong.'"

faq.q: Are there exercises for calming the nervous system?
faq.a: Yes. Survivor Insight exercises help you name pain and replace self-blame with accuracy, and a 5-4-3-2-1 grounding reset helps when the body goes into panic or freeze mode. The resources section adds a five-step plan for day one.

faq.q: Is Scripture part of the healing?
faq.a: Scripture and prayer run through the book. Psalm 34:18 carried John through many dark nights, and the resources section lists verses for healing and hope. Faith appears as rescue, not doctrine.

faq.q: Is it a clinical book, and who is it for?
faq.a: No. The author explains what is happening without diagnosing and without overwhelming; it is a personal and faith-friendly account, not medical advice or a treatment guide. It is for anyone who has asked why they react so strongly, for survivors of childhood trauma, and for readers who want a faith-friendly account of recovery.

stories.h2: A boss who could not find anything
paras: In the Introduction, Andrea Anderson was working for a family preservation agency and spending days, even weeks, putting a busy boss's papers in order. Everything looked neat when she left. The boss would return from a trip and say "it looks great, but I can't find anything." After one more failed attempt she sat at the desk in tears and prayed, "God, there has got to be a better way!" Moments later she typed "filing system" into Google. The first result was Barbara Hemphill, and Barbara's numerical finding system, supported by a simple index, gave "every piece of paper" a clear place to go and "a reliable way to find it again."

Chapter 1 tells how the File Index began. In 1978 Barbara Hemphill was using alphabetical folders, and they worked "until it didn't." One person labeled a file Car while the spouse looked under Honda or Vehicle. She began writing file names on a yellow legal pad so others could see what existed, and that became her first File Index. The book compares it this way: "A File Index is to filing what a Chart of Accounts is to accounting."

Anne, a retired educator, came with six drawers of paper from two homes and no clear system. Once her Reference files had numbers and keywords such as insurance, Blue Cross and auto policy, she said "I've had these files for 20 years and could never find what I needed. Now I can find it in seconds." She printed her File Index for the front of the drawer and kept a digital copy that is searchable on her phone.

She began her career as a teacher, and her experience in education and mental health gave her deep compassion for people who feel overwhelmed. While working for a family preservation agency in 2005 she discovered Barbara Hemphill's numerical filing system, and within a year she joined Barbara's team, left her job and launched her own organizing business. Barbara Hemphill is the author of Taming the Paper Tiger and the founder of the Productive Environment Institute, and she wrote the Foreword to this book.

faq.q: What is SOAR To Success about?
faq.a: It is a guide to the Productive Environment Finding SYSTEM, a keyword-driven filing system with a File Index for paper and digital files, written by Andrea Anderson with Barbara Hemphill in ten short chapters.

faq.q: How does the filing system work?
faq.a: Paper folders are labeled with numbers, such as Ref 1 and Ref 2, and each number is logged in a File Index with keywords. Searching the index for a word like Honda or mechanic shows which numbered folder holds the paper. faq.q: Is there a way to deal with a flooded email inbox?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 teaches the ART of Organizing Email, where every message is an Action, a Reference or a Toss. It suggests triaging email by priority, and it offers the line "Today's Mail is tomorrow's pile." It does not promise inbox zero.

faq.q: What does clutter is postponed decisions mean?
faq.a: It is Barbara Hemphill's phrase, and the book repeats it in the Foreword and in Chapter 3: clutter is not caused by having too much information, it comes from decisions not yet made. The chapter on digital clutter applies it to unread mail and unsorted files too.

faq.q: What is the Magic 7?
faq.a: The seven tools the book says to have in place before you organize anything: in, out and file trays; a toss, recycle and shred setup; a calendar or planner; a contact manager; an Action system; a Reference system; and an integrated task manager, which the book names the SOAR Board.

faq.q: Is it a book about daily planning and time management?
faq.a: Part of it is. Chapter 7 teaches planning your day, week and month, and it says the breakthrough "comes from learning how to spend the time you already have." Its core, though, is the filing and decision system.

faq.q: Does the book depend on buying something else?
faq.a: The method is taught in the book, and the authors say you can use paper, a computer or both. The book also names its own digital tool, a CRM and a workshop that readers can choose for extra support.

On the twenty-first day of his life doctors found his heart was enlarged and the family hurried to Children's Hospital, where the word spoken to her years before became a source of strength. sections.h2: For parents of babies who spent time in the hospital
paras: The hospital pages are short. The baby is taken to Children's Hospital on the twenty-first day of his life, the parents stand beside his bed, and the surgeries leave him sleeping. audience.headline: A mother tells her son: every flutter, every nap, every night, I was there.
audience.body: For parents who want a gentle rhyming read-aloud about a mother's love for her son, families who have waited and prayed for a child, and parents of babies who spent time in a children's hospital. Dana House tells the true story of the promised baby she carried, the old saying about spoiling a baby with too much holding, and the frightening night his tiny heart needed help, in verse built around one refrain a child can hold on to. A note on subjects: the story includes a newborn found to have an enlarged heart, a long hospital stay and surgeries, told in simple rhyme with no graphic detail and no medical advice. It ends in the hope of home, a rainbow and a mother's steady love. Parents may want to read it first before sharing it with a child who has had hospital time of their own.

list: It is true to life. The mother speaks to her son about events from the author's own family.

paras: On the page before the promise, a praying mother asks what her family should do. A lady she does not know looks her in the eyes and boldly declares, "Your baby is on the way!" She says the child will be a gift from God, and the mother keeps those words close. Years later they carry her through the hardest pages of the book.

When the baby is weeks old, the mother keeps holding him even while he sleeps. She has heard the old saying, "You'll spoil a child if you hold a baby too much," but her mama taught her otherwise. She knows that "you just needed my touch," and that someday she will long to hold him and watch him dream, so she holds him now, sowing love into the harvest.

After six months the family goes home. It feels strange to leave, because the hospital had begun to feel like home. As they leave the ramp, "a beautiful rainbow was shining brightly in the sky," and it reminds them they are never left alone. The mother sees God's reminder through the clouds and says again, "I missed you while you were sleeping."

book.meta: The Brothers and Their Lunch Basket by Nicole Bran Clark: Jesus feeds a crowd through five loaves and two fish, retold for young readers.
book.short: Four brothers share their small lunch of five loaves and two fish and watch Jesus feed a crowd too big to count in this warm retelling for young readers.
book.about: The morning starts like any other for four brothers. Their mother is cooking pancakes, Asher is full of questions about the orange sky, Elijah is tying his shoes, Samuel is checking the weather, and David is quietly humming. On the way to school the brothers follow a commotion and find a crowd too big to count: men, women, children and even babies sitting in the grass. They overhear a question no one can answer: where can they buy bread so all these people can eat? Asher looks down at the basket. It holds only five loaves of bread and two fish. He remembers what his mother always says: when we share what we have, even if it is just a little, God can use it to bless many. So he offers their lunch, Philip takes the basket, and the man they call Jesus smiles warmly at Asher and asks the crowd to sit in smaller groups. A warm retelling for young readers about sharing and trust.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents who read aloud

sections.h2: For Sunday school teachers and children's ministry leaders
paras: A feeding-of-the-five-thousand lesson needs a way in for the youngest children, and this gives you one. The Note to Parents, Teachers, and Ministry Leaders lists values to explore, namely generosity, obedience, curiosity and faith, and it suggests reading John 6:1-14 together afterward to talk about how Jesus multiplied the loaves and fish and what that shows about faith and compassion.

sections.h2: For kids who ask big questions
paras: Asher is the boy who asks why the sky turns orange before sunrise, and he is also the boy who asks what would happen if they gave away their lunch. list: It is told through four brothers. Asher is full of questions, Elijah rushes in tying his shoes, Samuel is the careful one who checks the weather, and David hums quietly and pulls out chairs for everyone. Children often find themselves in one of them.

paras: On the way to school, the brothers hear a commotion, and Elijah decides they should look. "Oh, who cares if we're late!" he says, running toward the crowd. They find a huge gathering of men, women and children talking, laughing and playing, "and even babies were there!" David notices a smaller group of men standing aside with worried faces. stories.h2: What if we gave them our lunch?
paras: Asher looks at the basket and thinks of all those hungry faces. "I know it's not much—just five loaves of bread and two fish—but I can't stop thinking about all those hungry faces. Maybe it could help." David pushes back: "Then we will be hungry and without any food for our lunch." Asher reminds him what Ima always says, and David gives in: "You're right Asher, they do need our help. We'll be okay." Asher walks up to the man with brown eyes and says, "It's not much, but... you can have our lunch."

After the crowd has been fed, the brothers realize they are late, and school is hard. Asher stares at his lunch cubby, wondering if it still holds a miracle. David doodles loaves and fish all over his worksheet. Elijah fiddles with his pencil during read-aloud time. Samuel raises his hand to answer a math question and forgets what he was going to say. When they get home, Ima asks only, "Did you boys remember to be kind today?" and David blurts out, "We shared our lunch," and then, "And somehow... it fed everyone!"

book.about: Phil Gunn lives a simple life in a small trailer beside the river. He works the afternoon shift at the mill, eats the same breakfast at the same cafe he has visited since he was twelve, and gives what little he has to his mother, his sister in medical school and his brother, lost to the streets of Oakland. A born-again Christian, Phil reads his Bible every day. Then one ordinary morning he feels a yearning to buy a lottery ticket. His pastor preaches against gambling, and Phil knows it would be wrong. But what if he won? He tells himself he would share the wealth. After his shift he checks the numbers: he has won one hundred seventy-nine million dollars. In the middle of the night he calls his best friend, who arrives with his wife, and the three set out to celebrate. But the wife has never liked Phil, and as they drive through the dark she sees a way to take what she believes life has denied her. Of Judgement and Of Mercy is a Christian novel about what happens when a good man compromises what he believes. It explores temptation, greed and envy and the consequences of a single choice, and holds out the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

sections.h2: For readers of faith-based suspense and family drama
paras: If you like a story where the stakes are personal, this one starts at a breakfast table and stays close to the people at it. Phil, his mother, his friend George and George's wife Marge laugh together over bacon and eggs in the first chapter, and the book makes sure you know them before it begins to turn. There is a crime in this story and the book does not look away from it.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy a clear spiritual message
paras: The faith in this book is not a coat of paint. Phil listens to a Christian radio station, reads the Bible every day and prays for his brother's repentance. On the morning he buys the ticket, the passages he reads puzzle him, and the novel tells us why: he "didn't realize that by buying the lottery ticket he had compromised what he believed." Scripture, judgement and mercy run through the plot.

sections.h2: For Christian fiction readers who like a warm hero and a villain with a history
paras: Marge's resentment is not random. The book gives her an old wound, and then shows what she makes of it. George, who is easily led, is caught between his friend and his wife. If you enjoy characters who are neither all good nor all bad, and a story that is willing to ask whether anyone is beyond forgiveness, you will find them here.

audience.headline: One lottery ticket. One hundred seventy-nine million dollars. One choice that cost more than he knew.
audience.body: For readers of faith-based suspense and family drama. Phil Gunn is a born-again mill worker in the small town of Kamish, Idaho, who reads his Bible every day and gives what little he has to his family. Then he buys a lottery ticket he knows he should not buy, and wins. His best friend's wife has never liked him, and she has already begun to scheme.

quote.text: If he didn't win, it wouldn't matter. If he did, everyone would think it was a good idea. He had told himself that if he won, he would share the wealth. So the thought became a plan, and the plan became reality.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a Christian novel with a real hero and a real villain
paras: A Christian novel about what happens when a good man compromises what he believes. It runs from a trailer by the river and a breakfast café to a long night drive toward the lottery office in Boise, and it keeps asking what one small choice can set in motion.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a hero who is easy to like. Phil is six foot two, strong as a bull, sings only in the shower where nobody can hear, and orders the same breakfast at the café where the waitress knows it by heart.

It takes the temptation seriously. Phil knows his pastor preaches against gambling. The book lets him argue with himself ("Besides, what could one ticket hurt? Who would know anyway?") and shows the dread that settles in afterward.
It gives the villain a history. Marge has never liked Phil, and the book tells you why, so her scheming is not cartoonish.
It is a family story. Phil sends money to his sister Jeannie, who is away at medical school, meets his mother for breakfast and prays for a brother lost to the streets of Oakland.
It names its theme in the title. Of Judgement and Of Mercy is about temptation, greed and envy, and the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

paras: Phil feels a yearning to buy a lottery ticket and tells himself it would be wrong. He buys one anyway, with a few snacks so he will not look conspicuous. "All the time, he felt guilty but overrode it with what if?" That night he reads three Bible passages, including the story of Samson and Delilah, and cannot find the meaning he usually finds. After his shift he scribbles the numbers on a scrap of paper, races home, checks his ticket twice and whispers, "I won," and then, "I can't believe it."

stories.h2: A midnight feast and a quiet plan
paras: Phil calls his friends in the middle of the night and the three set off to celebrate. Over the long drive Marge starts to put a plan together. "Well, let's not tell anyone else about the money until after you get it," she says, and she offers to drive Phil to Boise, where he must go to the lottery headquarters to collect. "All she needed was to convince George that it was the only thing to do—and she would."

Chapter 3 begins with Phil asleep and George and Marge awake. Marge tells George a story about what happened at the restaurant, and when he starts to storm out, she asks: "What would hurt him more—your beating him up, or him losing his money?" At first, the narrator tells us, her plan did not include getting rid of Phil. "But the more she thought about it—and the more she told George about it—the more certain she became that it would be necessary."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book is a story, and it lets the story speak. It is built on two verses that Pastor Whittington's congregation heard on a hot August morning and that George remembers late in the book: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord," and "For the love of money is the root of all evil."

Those verses are the book's questions. What does one compromise cost? What do envy and greed do to a friendship? And, in the final chapters, what does mercy look like when it is offered to someone who has not earned it? The novel holds out the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

book.about: In July 2009 Dan Zebarth heard the words he had dreaded since childhood: pancreatic cancer. Days later the diagnosis changed to a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, but the surgery that followed was extremely difficult and he was given eight months to live. The book is his true account of what came next: during his hospital recovery he saw and heard Jesus; when the cancer spread to his liver and became Stage IV, he writes that the Holy Spirit promised to work on healing him; after years of chemotherapy he asked his doctor whether the cancer was still present, and the biopsy came back benign. Sixteen years after diagnosis he is cancer-free, he writes. The book opens with his early life in Augusta, Wisconsin, follows his cancer journey chapter by chapter, and in Part IV his wife tells the story from her side. Appendices offer guidance for navigating a cancer journey with faith and courage, patterns of God's interventions, family letters and supporting medical documentation. He writes plainly about the statistics and the fear, and does not promise that healing follows a formula.

sections.h2: For anyone facing a serious illness
paras: If you have just heard hard news, you may want to read one person's account before you decide what you think. Dan writes about the first diagnosis, the day it changed to a neuroendocrine tumor, the surgery, the long recovery and the years of chemotherapy. sections.h2: For the spouses, families and friends who walk beside someone who is ill
paras: Part IV may be the part you need. Kay writes about being away from home for a month, about the hospital vigil and the email updates, and about the fourteen blessings and answered prayers she and Dan listed, from a diagnosis that changed, to the fragrance of roses in the pre-op waiting room. Dan says he cannot imagine what her journey was like. If you are the one keeping watch, there is company here.

sections.h2: For readers of Christian testimony and memoir
paras: This is a first-person account of faith, prayer and trusting God through suffering, written by a man with a business, a marriage and children he adored, who says he has been "blessed throughout my life with visits from Jesus." He writes about what he saw and heard and what he believes, and he says plainly that God's work is "personal, sovereign, and often mysterious."

audience.body: For anyone facing a serious diagnosis, and for the family walking beside them. Daniel Zebarth tells, in his own words, what happened after a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in July 2009: a neuroendocrine tumor, a hard surgery at Mayo, Stage IV spread to his liver, years of chemotherapy, and what he believes God did through it all. His wife, Kay, tells the same story from her side.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who need honest hope in a hard season
paras: A true account that does not hide the fear. It began as a testimony written for his family, and friends who walked with them encouraged him to share it with others facing illness.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by two people. Dan writes Part III, his cancer journey, in eleven chapters. In Part IV, Kay tells it in her own words, drawing on the emails she sent to family during the weeks he was in the hospital.

It is plain about the numbers. The foreword notes the statistics Dan shares, "over 66,000 Americans diagnosed annually and a mortality rate hovering near 78 percent," and calls the book "a beacon of hope" rather than "a tale of despair."

It says what it is not. A medical disclaimer at the front states that the book "is not intended as medical advice" and that treatment decisions "should never be made based solely on personal stories or spiritual testimony."

It gives you the practical pages too. The back of the book includes a guide to navigating a cancer journey with faith and courage, a collection of patterns of God's interventions, family letters and supporting medical documentation.
It took a decade to write. Dan began in 2011, paused in 2012, and in 2021 felt, he writes, "clearly led by the Holy Spirit to finish it."

stories.h2: A sermon, and a life verse
paras: On August 30, 2009, just weeks after the diagnosis, Dan watched a sermon at the family cabin. The message was on Isaiah 41:10, and he writes that it "changed my life." The verse became his Life Verse: "So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand." It came two weeks before surgery, "exactly when I would need it most," and he still prays it before major tests.

stories.h2: One in the morning, day eleven
paras: Ten days after surgery, Dan was not improving. On Saturday, September 26, 2009, he could not sleep for pain. He writes that he turned his head and saw Jesus by his left shoulder, with a woman beside Him he later understood to be Mother Mary. He was in St. Mary's Hospital. According to Dan, Jesus said, "Today you will have a very rough day, but you will get better." That afternoon he vomited blood and lost consciousness, and Kay ran into the corridor calling for help. He writes that the visit "dramatically changed the level of my faith and trust in Him."

stories.h2: The message at the supper table
paras: Years of chemotherapy had passed when Dan, at a July 2021 appointment, asked his doctor, "How would I know if I still have cancer?" A liver biopsy followed on July 29. Two days later his family was together at a restaurant when his phone chirped with the pathology report. The lesion was benign. "I have been healed; I am cancer free!" he told the table. He also records that his children were skeptical at first, and that they shared a wonderful meal and believed, at the very least, that their dad would be around much longer.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Dan did not set out to write a book. "At the time, I had no desire to write a book and doubted that I had the ability to do so," he says of 2011, when it began. In 2021, he writes, "I felt clearly led by the Holy Spirit to finish it. This is truly His book, a testimony of miraculous healing from Stage IV pancreatic cancer."

His reason for sharing it is simple: "I am simply a vessel God has used to share that He is alive, faithful, and still working miracles today." Nothing in these pages is offered as a formula. It is one man's true story, with the records at the back, told so that others facing illness might find comfort, perspective and faith along their own journey.

faq.q: What is In the Hands of Our Heavenly Father about?
faq.a: It is Daniel Zebarth's true account of a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in July 2009 that became a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, spread to his liver as Stage IV, and, after years of chemotherapy, ended with a biopsy that came back benign.

faq.q: What was the diagnosis and the surgery?
faq.a: The first diagnosis was pancreatic cancer, and days later it became a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. The book describes his surgery at Mayo, which was extremely difficult and painful, and the hospital recovery that followed.

faq.q: Does the book describe Whipple surgery and recovery?
faq.a: Yes. Part III follows his cancer journey chapter by chapter, from the first news and the surgery through the darkest times to the healing. It is a personal account, not a medical guide, and it does not give treatment advice.

faq.q: Does the book promise healing?
faq.a: No. The author writes plainly about the statistics and the fear and does not promise that healing follows a formula; he offers his story as a testimony that God is alive and faithful.

faq.q: Who else tells the story?
faq.a: In Part IV the author's wife tells the same story from her side: the vigil, the email updates to family, fourteen blessings and answered prayers, and reflections on faith and marriage.

faq.q: Is it a medical book?
faq.a: No. A medical disclaimer at the front says the author's experience is personal and unique and that readers should consult qualified medical professionals before making healthcare decisions.

faq.q: Does it include medical documents?
faq.a: Yes. Appendix E collects supporting medical documentation, and the chapters point to specific documents, such as the pathology report that came back benign.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Anyone facing a serious illness who wants to read one man's account of faith and prayer, the families, friends and spouses who walk beside someone who is ill, and readers of Christian testimony and memoir.

book.about: In a small village in Austria, the yellow Heuriger hotel glows on summer nights and the smell of fresh bread drifts from the kitchen. The bread belongs to Big Leo, a barefoot baker with gentle eyes. His wife Rosina runs the front desk, always praying and blessing guests. When Emperor Gier decrees a military draft and officers arrive with Leo's military orders, he gives a plain answer: he will not go, because God does not want him to fight them or anyone else. At the center is Max, a wild-haired village boy who wants to be a baker and wants to know why grown-ups are always fighting. Rosina answers that we need love as we need water: if someone hits you, do not hit back, love them still and forgive them. Leo, Rosina and Max set out by carriage for Vienna, with a smoky roadside inn, a bar fight Leo ends with a song, and a night sky full of stars. In Vienna, Max sees cakes and church bells, kindness and anger on the same street. A warm, faith-filled story about mercy, family and grace.

sections.h2: For readers of faith-filled historical fiction
paras: This one has an emperor, a palace, an old city and an inn built in the 1600s, all seen through a boy's eyes. The faith in it is practical: people pray over a meal, bless a guest, ask a priest for help.

sections.h2: For book clubs
paras: What does Leo owe an emperor, and what does he owe God? Is Rosina right that anyone can be reached by love? Why does Max keep asking? A short book, but a club will find plenty to discuss in how it treats people who are poor, drunk, proud or afraid.

sections.h2: For readers who love small villages, bread and food
paras: Bread runs through every page. A baker lifts a fifty pound bag of flour and shows a boy how his starter stretches like a tongue. A basket of rolls with honey changes the mood of a standoff. A Vienna bakery changes hands in a day, and a soup the baker can never match is served in a cottage kitchen.

audience.headline: A baker who will not fight, a praying wife and a wild-haired boy set out for Vienna.
audience.body: For readers of warm, faith-filled historical fiction, book clubs that like a story about mercy and forgiveness, and anyone who enjoys a small village, fresh bread and a long ride to the big city. In a short novel of twenty-four chapters, a barefoot baker called Big Leo refuses to take up arms for his emperor, and a boy who wants to know why grown-ups are always fighting gets an answer he does not expect. A note on subjects: this is a gentle story with a tender heart, but it does not look away from hard things. It includes drinking and a bar fight, a child who has been frightened by her father, a mother in despair, and a scene in which a public execution is carried out in front of a crowd. These are told without graphic detail, and the book answers them with kindness. If any of this is close to your own life, please talk to someone you trust. If you or someone you know is in danger or thinking about suicide, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want a story of mercy
paras: Spring Birds begins in a small village in Austria, at a yellow inn called the Heuriger, where beer, sausage and bread fill the air. From there it follows one family of three, a baker, his wife and a village boy, to the capital and into the lives of the people they meet on its streets. The emperor in the story is named Gier, and in Chapter 17 a character confirms the year as 1910.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a refusal. When officers arrive with a conscription order, Leo does not argue about politics. He simply says what he believes God wants of him, and he sits the officers down to eat.
It is told through a child's questions. Max asks the question the whole book answers: why do grown-ups fight?
It puts forgiveness in plain words. A wife and a baker teach a boy to love people who do wrong, and the book then tests that teaching on a stranger's street.
It is funny. A teacher who calls a boy a loof, a grandmother who feeds blue birds at her window, a dough starter with a name and an emperor with a long neck all keep the mood light.
It is short. Twenty-four brief chapters, about eighty pages, easy to read in a weekend.

blocks.text: The story opens at night, in the village:

paras: It was lively and happy in the small village in the heart of Austria. The yellow Heuriger hotel glowed with light in the summer night, and there were people all in and around it. There was much laughter, and everyone's breath smelled like beer. The bar and restaurant of the hotel rang loud with banging and shouting, and the cooking made the whole village aromatic with fried foods, sausage, and bread.

blocks.text: In Chapter 2 Max asks his questions in the courtyard, and Rosina answers him:

paras: The whole world could be at war, but that doesn't mean you have to be. We are taught to love everyone and to forgive everyone.

blocks.text: She goes on, when Max asks whether he should love people who are bad:

paras: Maybe they are bad because no one loved them. Maybe no one loves them because they are bad. We need love as we need water. If someone is mean to you or hits you, don't hit them back. Love them still and forgive them, so there can be no evil in your heart, and then maybe it will make the evil in their heart go away.

blocks.text: The chapters are:

items: Chapters 1 to 4: the inn at night, the courtyard and a grandmother's cottage, the arrival of the officers, and Leo's morning prayer
Chapters 5 to 8: the carriage ride, the arrival in Vienna, a trumpet in the night and the first morning in the city
Chapters 9 to 12: a boy on a narrow street, a flower shop, a silent girl called Blue and three street musicians
Chapters 13 to 16: the meadow, a dark night, the clouds and a mother's long day
Chapters 17 to 20: the year 1910, an old photograph, the week of the royal feast and the walk to the palace
Chapters 21 to 24: the last four chapters, left for you to read

paras: Three men in uniform come to the hotel with a letter of military orders. Leo does not take it. He tells them plainly that "God doesn't want me to fight you or anyone else." One of the soldiers, an old friend, shrugs and apologizes. Another quietly empties the basket of rolls. Leo offers him more: "It's great with a drop of honey." Then he invites all three to the bar for coffee, because "I know you haven't had anything." The officer, careful not to look too pleased, asks how long Leo has been a baker, and the standoff turns into a new offer. Leo sums it up with a dry line: "A minute ago you wanted me to kill people, and now you want me to feed people."

One night soon after reaching Vienna, Leo lies awake listening to the city and hears a trumpet in the alley below. "It sounded honest and sad. There was a humble pain in it." The next morning he meets the man who played it, a street musician who has been told his music is too slow. Leo does not tell him to change. He says, "I heard you play at night, my friend. It was truly beautiful." Leo offers an idea that is also a blessing: "God's an artist, you're a musician, and I'm a baker."

A girl with a flower in her hair has never been heard to speak. When she meets Max, he takes the flower she offers and leads her out of the city to a green meadow. "It looked like two does were meeting each other." They lie on their backs and watch the clouds. When Max starts walking through the flowers, she speaks, and the book marks it plainly: "Don't step on the flowers." Max is not surprised. He thinks her voice is pretty.

paras: What the story itself says is plain. Its first question comes from a boy: "Do I have to fight when I grow up?" Its answer comes from a wife who prays: "The whole world could be at war, but that doesn't mean you have to be."

faq.q: What is Spring Birds about?
faq.a: A baker named Big Leo in a small Austrian village refuses to fight when his emperor orders a military call-up. He, his praying wife Rosina and a wild-haired boy named Max travel to Vienna, and the story asks why grown-ups fight and answers with love and forgiveness.

faq.q: Is it historical fiction?
faq.a: Yes, it is classed as historical fiction and Christian fiction. It is set in an Austrian village and in Vienna, with a fictional emperor named Gier, and in Chapter 17 a character gives the year as 1910.

faq.q: Is it a story about a conscientious objector?
faq.a: In effect, yes. The opening premise is that Leo refuses military service because he believes God does not want him to fight anyone. The words conscientious objector do not appear in the book. Leo's reason is his faith, he states it calmly, and the book follows what happens next.

faq.q: What does the book say about loving your enemies?
faq.a: Rosina tells Max that we are taught to love everyone and forgive everyone, and Leo prays for the soldiers who came for him. He tells Max that "Being hateful is exhausting. Also, they are my brothers." The phrase love your enemies is not in the book, but the idea runs through it.

faq.q: Is it a heartwarming novel?
faq.a: Yes. It is a warm, faith-filled story about mercy, family and grace, and much of it is funny. It also contains hard moments, and the note on subjects near the top says what they are.

faq.q: What does the title Spring Birds mean?
faq.a: The phrase appears in Chapter 10, where Rosina walks down a Vienna street and everyone she smiles at is happy for a while after. "She was pleasant like spring birds, innocent like their songs." Blue birds also gather at the window of Max's grandmother's kitchen in Chapter 2.

faq.q: What does the book say about forgiveness?
faq.a: Rosina tells Max to love people who do wrong and forgive them so there is no evil in his heart. Later in the book, forgiveness is asked for and given by people who have good reason to withhold it.

faq.q: How long is it, and who is it for?
faq.a: It is about eighty pages in twenty-four short chapters, for adult and teen readers who like warm historical fiction. Parents of younger readers should read the note on subjects first.

book.about: From Jesus 'til Now is a guided walk through two thousand years of the Christian church, told through the people who lived it. Julie Boone spent much of her life developing this text, and it was published after her passing by her son. A prologue sets the stage with Alexander the Great, the Maccabean revolt and the rise of Rome. Twenty-four chapters then move from Pentecost and the first sermon through persecutions recorded in Acts, the move from persecution to power, monks and monasteries, barbarians and scholars, Islam and icons, the Crusades, plague and mysticism, the sixteenth century, missions to the far corners of the world and on into the iPhone century. Readers meet real people and surprising details: only one in ten people in Rome in Jesus' lifetime could read, and Origen's mother hid his clothes to keep him from rushing out to be martyred. The book is honest about the church's failures as well as its faith. Every chapter ends with questions for thought and discussion, a Bible passage for study, questions for personal response and keywords for further research.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want church history they can actually enjoy
paras: A church history that reads like stories, and a study guide that sends you back to Scripture. It begins in the world of the Bible, which the introduction says is "geographically a good bit larger than the typical Holy Land tourist imagines," and it keeps going until now.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told through people. Each chapter details a period of church history "and the people who were notable in it," from Origen and Augustine to John Newton, William Wilberforce and John Woolman.

It is honest about failure. The introduction calls church history "a story of great faith lived out in challenges, of great fears overcome by faith, and sometimes – when we're honest -- of great failures by those who thought they were trying to do God's will."
It ends every chapter with something to do. Questions for thought and discussion, a Bible passage to study, questions for your response, and internet keywords to search if you want to go further.

It is built for a group. The questions compare the historic issues in the chapter with issues "that may be experienced in the contemporary church," which makes it easy to use in a class or small group.
It is a mother's life work. Julie Boone spent much of her life developing the text, and her son, Mark Boone, saw it into print after she passed into glory.

paras: In the 21st century world, many of us live as if the only history that matters is the one we've seen personally. That can narrow our frame of reference dangerously when it's time to consider how best to live as people of faith in our own time.

Readers will see ways that people in different times have sought to enact their similar desires to honor God and live according to God's will, and their responses – whether wise or not – can illuminate our responses to church and world today.
