stories.h2: The king who bowed to a priest
paras: When Alexander the Great reached Jerusalem, the high priest was frantic with fear that he would destroy the city. That night he saw in a dream the gates open, the people in white and the priests in their robes, and he asked everyone to recreate the scene. Alexander stopped his army, rode up alone, dismounted and bowed. Asked by an officer why he, before whom people showed adoration, would honor a priest, he replied that he honored, not the priest, but the God the priest worshiped. Jerusalem was not attacked.

Origen was born in Egypt around A.D. 185 and tutored by his father, and he learned to quote long passages from the Bible when he was only a boy. He asked so many questions that his father reproved him for being too inquisitive, yet "secretly thanked God for such a child." When Origen was seventeen, his father was arrested and killed because of his faith. The youth tried to join his father in death, but his mother kept him home by hiding his clothes. He went on to head a Christian school in Alexandria and to compile the Hexapla, a massive book of Bible translations set in parallel columns.

Augustine preferred the theater to church, and his mother, Monica, prayed and wept almost continuously for him. She asked a priest to talk with him, and he answered, "Leave me and go in peace. It cannot be that the son of those tears should be lost." In Milan, Augustine began attending Ambrose's church only to study his eloquence, then found he could not ignore the meaning. The book prints Augustine's own account of weeping beneath a fig tree: "How long shall I go on saying 'tomorrow, tomorrow'? Why not now?" Then a child's voice nearby chanted, "Take it and read, take it and read."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book exists so that readers can "both learn about the history of God's church and discover lessons from church history for church life today." In his introduction, Mark Boone writes that "helping you to find, reflect on, and make good use of those lessons is a primary goal of this book."

The conclusion is humble about it. "People usually think the time in which they live has unique challenges never before overcome," it begins, and it adds that monasteries, the Reformation and revivals "solved some problems and created others." Its closing hope is: "By God's grace, may each of us live closer to God's purposes for our own times."

book.about: Wherever Ryan Schraffenberger and his family park their RV, he sets out a sandwich-board sign: Can We Pray For You? One morning at a nearly empty RV resort in Texas, the resort's general manager read it and told him he had planned to end his life the night before; Ryan put his hand on the man's shoulder and prayed. That conversation became the launchpad for a movement and for this book. Ryan tells honestly how he went from the Florida Keys, bartending and partying, to full-time faith. Part 1, Inward Progression, builds the private foundation: living with open hands, relating to God as Father and learning to hear from Him, prayer in the family and workplace, praying Scripture, prayer and fasting, models for prayer and praying through lament. Part 2, Outward Expression, turns it outward: boldness in faith, sharing your testimony and the Gospel in plain words, walking with someone as they accept Christ, and becoming the local chaplain in your community. His message: outcomes are His, obedience is ours.

sections.h2: For believers who freeze at praying out loud
paras: The author knows the feeling and says so plainly: "Praying in public takes courage, no question." His answer is not a technique. It is a way of living that gives you room to say yes: hold life with open hands, and expect interruptions as invitations. He calls it going off script, and it begins long before you meet anyone who needs prayer.

sections.h2: For parents and families
paras: A chapter on prayer in the family opens with a joke that rings true: "If praying in public feels like jumping out of a plane, then praying with your family sometimes feels like jumping without a parachute." He walks through how to begin with your spouse, how to pray with children, and why a praying family does not need to be perfect.

sections.h2: For professionals and workplaces
paras: Most of us spend more waking hours at work than anywhere else. The workplace chapter makes the case for bringing prayer there, quietly and without a title: "Peace is magnetic, peace is noticeable, peace is evangelism without trying."

sections.h2: For people who want to hear from God
paras: The chapter Hearing from God is for anyone who finds prayer one-sided. The author says hearing from God is not mystical but relational, and he gives practical rhythms: coffee and Scripture in the morning, a walk, a drive, a quiet pause.

audience.headline: One simple question that can change a life.
audience.body: For believers who want to pray more but freeze when it comes to praying out loud with a stranger, parents who want prayer woven into family life, professionals who want to be a light at work, and anyone who has felt a nudge from God and talked themselves out of it. Ryan Schraffenberger tells how a sandwich-board sign at RV campgrounds led to a prayer movement, and gives a practical way to build a prayer life that grows into everyday boldness. A note on subjects: the opening chapter tells a true story about a man who had planned to end his life, and other chapters mention suicidal thoughts, grief, addiction and illness. They are told with care and no graphic detail, and the book points readers toward prayer, community and people who can help. It is a faith-based book, not medical advice or a substitute for care. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away, and talk to a physician or licensed counselor about what you are carrying.

stories.h2: One morning at a nearly empty RV resort
paras: Wherever his family parks their RV, the author sets a sandwich-board sign beside the campsite: Can We Pray For You? With it is a phone number and the words Call or Text. At a resort in Texas, assigned a site at the back, he laughs to himself that no one will see it. On Monday morning, reading outside, which he rarely does, he notices the resort's general manager come out of the woods, stop, and walk toward him to ask about the sign. The man tells him he had planned to end his life the night before. The author does not preach. "Tell me everything," I said. "But I want you to know something first—I'm broken too." He puts a hand on the man's shoulder and prays, and they both cry. He offers his number and an invitation: "Let's get together and start reading the Bible from the beginning. I'll give you as much time as you need." While the author is away for work, the man tells his closest friends everything. "They surrounded him with love." The author draws one lesson: "That's how God works. That's how He multiplies."

stories.h2: Keeping the phone off the hook
paras: Hearing from God, says the author, is simpler than most people imagine. He compares it to an old landline phone left off the hook, so the line stays open and the conversation never has to end. "You don't hang up the phone with Heaven. You keep the line open." The point is not constant talking but constant connection: "This is why hearing God isn't mystical; it's relational." Then comes the line that gives the chapter its weight: "You can't recognize a voice you never spend time with."

A chapter for hard seasons says what many readers need to hear. "Lament is not complaining, lament is not faithlessness. Lament is worship with tears in your eyes." The author reminds readers that "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit (Psalm 34:18)." He then turns to the one who prays for others: when someone is suffering, real compassion begins with humility, not a quick spiritual answer.

faq.q: What is Can I Pray for You? about?
faq.a: It is Ryan Schraffenberger's account of setting out a Can We Pray For You? sign wherever his family parks their RV, and a practical guide to building a prayer life that flows naturally into everyday boldness.

faq.q: Is it a book about praying for others?
faq.a: Yes. Part 2, Outward Expression, covers boldness in faith, telling your testimony and the Gospel in plain words, supporting people after the moment has passed, and becoming the local chaplain of the places you already go. Part 1 builds the private prayer life that makes that possible.

faq.q: Does it teach praying Scripture?
faq.a: Yes. A full chapter, Praying Scripture, explains why to do it and gives simple methods, such as turning a verse into a personal prayer, praying slowly through a passage, and praying Scripture over someone else. The author writes that "when you pray Scripture, you are praying God's thoughts back to God."

faq.q: Is there a chapter on prayer and fasting?
faq.a: Yes. Prayer and Fasting is in Part 1. It looks at fasting in the Bible and in modern life and says, "Prayer connects you to God; fasting clears space so you can hear Him."

faq.q: Does it help with building a relationship with God?
faq.a: That is the foundation of the book. In Relationship with Your Father the author writes that "you must understand something foundational: God is your Father, and He desires a relationship with you." He adds that "Your Father wants your presence more than your perfection."

faq.q: Does it teach how to hear God's voice?
faq.a: It has a full chapter, Hearing from God. The author says God most often speaks in a whisper, that He may use a nudge, a Scripture or a moment of peace, and that "The more you quiet your life, the louder His whisper becomes." The book offers habits, not guarantees.

faq.q: Do I need to be a pastor to use this book?
faq.a: No. It is written for believers, parents and professionals. The local chaplain chapter says "You don't need a title. You just need a heart that says, Lord, use me here."

faq.q: Is it only for people who already pray out loud?
faq.a: No. It is written for people who find it hard. A chapter called Looking Like Weirdos says that the feeling of awkwardness is common, and that "The awkwardness is temporary, but the fruit is eternal."

book.short: A practical, faith-grounded guide for everyone who does vital work without holding the top title: followership as an active, intentional skill.
book.about: Why do we celebrate leaders so often, yet rarely acknowledge the followers who make their success possible? In Humble Influence: The Strength of True Followership, Jim Matuga answers with a practical, faith-grounded guide for everyone who does vital work without holding the top title. The idea took root at a leadership conference at West Virginia University in 2007 and grew through a 36-year business career, years of mentoring from accomplished leaders and hundreds of interviews on his weekly podcast, Positively West Virginia. Followership, he argues, is not passive obedience or a fallback role but an active, intentional skill that demands humility, courage, loyalty, critical thinking and initiative. Across fourteen chapters readers learn why followership is not intuitive, how to connect rather than merely communicate, how close to get to a leader, how to gain real empowerment, when to withhold judgment, and why it does not matter who gets the credit. The book draws on biblical wisdom, from Joshua serving under Moses for forty years to Ruth following Naomi and Peter following Jesus, and closes with Jesus Christ as the greatest follower. Additional resources include the Humble Influence Roadmap to becoming an effective follower.

Five things set it apart:
list: It speaks to the person leadership books skip. The author asks why we celebrate leaders so often "yet rarely acknowledge the followers who make their success possible," and then writes for those followers.

It treats humility as a working skill. Humility to serve without seeking the spotlight comes first among the traits he names, beside courage to speak up respectfully, loyalty to the mission, and initiative.

It is rooted in Scripture. Joshua serving under Moses for forty years, Ruth following Naomi, John the Baptist stepping aside, and Peter following Jesus all appear, and the final chapter closes on Jesus Christ as the greatest follower.

It is full of people you will recognize. Short stories follow a new trainee, a software engineer, a team leader who shares credit, and a friend who spent fifteen years learning beside a demanding chief executive.

paras: In the opening chapter, a mentor named Mr. Doug hands the young author a Bible open to Joshua. Joshua led battles, carried out Moses' instructions and watched, up close, what leadership cost, including the day twelve spies went out and only two came back with faith. When Moses died, God chose Joshua. The author draws one conclusion: the mantle was not handed over by chance, it was earned through years of faithful service. A friend named Angela shows the same pattern in a modern office. She spent fifteen years under a demanding chief executive, studied how he decided, supported his vision, and was the natural choice to succeed him.

Lisa has an MBA and big plans, and a trainee program that has her shadowing department heads and compiling reports. She grumbles, "I didn't endure years of case studies and late-night group projects just to follow others around." Then a senior executive, Mr. Reed, tells her where he started and says, "Leadership isn't just about making decisions—it's about making informed decisions." Lisa begins asking questions in marketing and operations, and three years later she is asked to manage a struggling department, which she turns around within a year. Looking back, she decides her time as a follower "wasn't a detour—it was a masterclass in leadership."

stories.h2: Who cares who gets the credit?
paras: Chapter 11 opens in a marketing agency. A team leader named Lisa, in the middle of a client pitch, pauses to say that the concept would not exist without a colleague's creativity on the visuals. The room responds with admiration, and her team sees what kind of leader she is. The chapter pairs that scene with John the Baptist, who drew a large following and still said of Jesus, "He must increase, but I must decrease." The author's point is that great followers care more about the success of the mission than about their own recognition.

author.bio: Jim Matuga has spent a 36-year business career talking with thousands of business leaders. Since 2017 he has interviewed hundreds of business owners and leaders on his weekly podcast, "Positively West Virginia," and he asks each one about leadership. He writes that he has worked with extraordinary leaders and mentors, among them Milan Puskar, founder of Mylan Laboratories, Doug Leech, founder of Centra Bank, and John Maxwell. The idea for this book was planted on April 17, 2007, when he heard author James Kouzes speak at a leadership conference at West Virginia University. It took eighteen years of experience, conversation and study before he found the courage to put it on the page.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author traces the book to a coffee shop in New York City, where a young professional named Michael told him, "Everyone talks about leadership, but what about people like me?" That conversation was the spark. He writes that "Over the years, I've met countless individuals who feel overshadowed by the leadership narrative."

He also saw a gap: "Surprisingly, resources for followers are scarce." His answer is a book that is not about stepping out of the shadows but about understanding the role you already play. In his words, "This book is a celebration of followership." It is meant for "the quiet contributors, the team players, and the behind-the-scenes problem-solvers who know that their work matters just as much—if not more—than the person at the top."

faq.q: What is Humble Influence about?
faq.a: It is a faith-grounded guide to followership for people who do vital work without holding the top title. Jim Matuga argues that following is an active, intentional skill, not blind obedience.

faq.q: Is it a book about biblical humility?
faq.a: Humility is central. The author names humility to serve without seeking the spotlight as the first trait of great followership, and the book closes with Jesus Christ as the greatest follower, whose submission to the Father's will became the path to ultimate leadership.

faq.q: Is it about servant leadership?
faq.a: It is about following rather than leading. Chapter 14 does look at Jesus as a servant who "did not come to be served," but the subject of the book is the strength of true followership.

faq.q: What does it say about Joshua and Moses?
faq.a: Joshua served under Moses for forty years before leading the Israelites into the Promised Land. The author uses that story to show that following prepares a person to lead, because Joshua learned discipline, empathy and humility along the way.

faq.q: Does it cover Ruth and Naomi?
faq.a: Yes. In chapter 5 Ruth chooses to follow Naomi back to Bethlehem. The author quotes her words, "Where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay," and points to her gleaning in the fields as proof that she followed with initiative, not passively.

faq.q: Is it about leading without authority or leading from the middle?
faq.a: In spirit, yes. The book is for people who want to lead "from the middle," to serve quietly and to influence with humility without a formal leadership role.

faq.q: Is it a Christian leadership book?
faq.a: It is a Christian book about the other half of leadership. It draws on Scripture, including Joshua, Ruth, John the Baptist, Peter and Jesus, alongside history and real-world examples.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Quiet contributors, team players and behind-the-scenes problem-solvers, and anyone who wants to lead well by first learning to follow faithfully. It has fourteen chapters, an epilogue and a Humble Influence Roadmap.

book.short: Thirteen-year-old RJ and his nine cousins meet every day under the oak tree in Johnny D's field, and trouble is never far behind, in a warm, funny Christian story of simpler times.
book.about: Growing up on the ridge was fun, and it was a safe place. For thirteen-year-old RJ and his nine cousins, every day begins under the big oak tree in Johnny D's field, with no cell phones and no video games, just a field, a family and endless ideas, some of them very bad ones. RJ's dad and his three brothers were raised by Grandma after Pa died, and every Saturday night the cousins sleep on her hardwood floors under hand-made quilts and every Sunday morning eat her famous cathead biscuits and gravy before Sunday school. The cousins build a campfire that brings the fire department, take a dare that ends with Dad's prize pig and turn a muddy kitchen floor into a sock-sliding rink right before Mom walks through the door. Through every scrape RJ learns that actions have consequences and that family sticks together. Sister Pearl brings Bible stories to life, and the parents live out the Golden Rule.

audience.headline: Ten cousins, one oak tree and a lot of very bad ideas.
audience.body: For families who want a warm, funny, Christian story of growing up in simpler times, for grandparents and parents who remember a field, a party line and Grandma's biscuits, and for young readers who like stories about cousins who always get into trouble and always stick together. Thirteen-year-old RJ tells seven short chapters about the summer days, Sunday mornings and scrapes that made his family what it is. A note on subjects: this is a gentle story with mischief and a few bumps. A fire brings the fire department, a boy breaks his arm falling off a van, the cousins are spanked and grounded as boys were in that day, and one evening the television news mentions a war, which upsets the family for a moment before a board game turns the evening around. There is no graphic detail.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for families who miss the good old days
paras: A short story in seven chapters, told by a boy who is proud of his family and honest about his mistakes. The first page sets the tone: "We each had a phone, but it was connected to a cord in our homes." There are no games to play and no texting, only a field, a baseball and ten cousins who "are the best of friends."
Five things set it apart:
list: It is told by a kid. RJ is the oldest of three brothers, and his chapters read like a storyteller at Grandma's table.
It is funny without being unkind. Every mishap is followed by a consequence and by a laugh, and the narrator says of the fire, "To this day, we still laugh about that day."

It remembers real details of a simpler time: a party line, a station wagon, cathead biscuits, a wooden bat, a three-wheeler and a cake walk at the fire station dance. Hard words are explained in parentheses right in the text, so a young reader never gets lost.
Faith is part of the week, not an add-on. Sunday school, a fiery preacher, the blessing before meals and the Golden Rule all show up in ordinary scenes.
It ends with a short, sincere word to the reader about the Bible and prayer.

stories.h2: The fire under the oak tree
paras: It is a week before Thanksgiving, and the cousins decide to build a fire. "It burned so high that we started sweating." A neighbor sees the smoke and calls for help, and the cousins run, leaving their jackets hanging on the oak tree. The firefighters know whose they are. The narrator adds, in parentheses, that "Firefighters come quickly when there's a fire, even a small one."

A new water well sends up black mud, and the boys play in it for hours. When they trudge inside for lunch, Dad walks in. They clean with the water hose, then one cousin brings it indoors, and soon they are all in their socks. "We all took turns sliding across the wet, muddy floor." The ending is a spanking and a week of being grounded, which was "the longest week of my life," saved only by an hour a day on the party line.

Chapter 6 ends at the pastor's dinner table, where the narrator, a picky eater, hides his brussels sprouts and peas in his pockets until the pastor's wife offers him more. "You must love green peas! Let me give you some more." One look at his mother settles it: "My pockets were stuffed with green peas that night."

faq.q: Is it a book about the good old days?

book.about: In 1836 ten-year-old Robie went out to feed the animals in a blizzard, struck his head and woke up a ghost. Before he could follow the beautiful light that came for him, a red-haired girl hurried him away, insisting the light was evil, and he spent the next 175 years exploring the world alone. Then he learns the truth: the Bad Man is Bebop, a shape-changer whose monsters keep children who have just died locked in underground caves. When two children, Jimmy and Sarah, escape one of those caves, Robie knows he has to help. In Heaven an angel named Mary has noticed that too many children are missing, and she is sent to Earth with a daring plan and a song, Jesus Loves Me. The four friends work out how to slip into Bebop's caves, teach the captive children to jump from place to place and gather them in a desert where the Bad Man's power cannot reach. When every child is safe they will sing Jesus' song and call for help. Across thirteen chapters the rescue grows into a mission that spans the planet.

paras: Each rescue is followed by healing, and Robie's friends take care of one another. The monsters are frightening but foolish, and the children are never left without help. The foreword calls it a story about "the joys of helping others."

sections.h2: For families who want to talk about purpose
paras: Jimmy asks Mary whether Jesus really needs them. She answers: "Yes, Jimmy. That is how the universe is set up. We each have tasks to fulfill. God waits to see if we will accept those tasks and do them." It is a good place to stop reading and ask what task a young reader might be given.

sections.h2: For readers who like a team and a plan
paras: By chapter 8 the rescue has become an organization. Teams are trained to make the jumps, border guards watch the desert, and Robie briefs the team leaders before a big raid in Liberia: "Tell them ChaCha is coming for them." When a leader asks how he knows Heaven is behind them, he answers, "Because they glow, and they don't hurt you but help you." Readers who like to see how a plan is made, tested and fixed will find a lot to enjoy.

audience.headline: A ghost boy, an angel named Mary and ten thousand lost children to bring home.
audience.body: For readers ages 8 to 12 who love adventure, angels and monsters with a hopeful ending, and for parents who want a clean middle-grade story about courage, purpose and helping others. Robie has been a ghost since a blizzard in 1836. When he meets two children who have just escaped a monster's cave, he finally learns what has been happening to children like him, and what he can do about it. A note on subjects: this is an adventure about children who have died and are being kept from Heaven. Robie falls in a blizzard, another boy drowned in a storm, and the captive children are hurt by monsters who feed on pain. The hurt is described briefly, and the story turns on hope, healing and rescue. Parents of younger or more sensitive readers may want to read the first chapters first.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who love a story of good versus evil
paras: A thirteen-chapter adventure that sets a shape-changing villain and his band of small monsters against a handful of children and an angel with a plan. The plan is a song, "Jesus Loves Me", and a desert where the Bad Man cannot use his power.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with an unusual hero. Robie is not a scary ghost. He is a lonely ten-year-old boy, and when a stranger finally speaks to him he says, "You're the first person to talk back to me in one hundred seventy years."
The villain is clever and foolish at once. Bebop can "change his shape to be anyone or anything he wants," and yet he forgets to lock the cage doors.
Heaven is involved from the first chapters. An angel named Mary and her supervising angel, Mac, talk about the missing children, and Jesus Himself comes to meet the four friends.
The children are the rescuers. They learn to jump from place to place by thinking about it very hard, and then teach others to do the same.
It says what it is for. The foreword to parents begins with its theme, purpose, and ends with the joy of helping others.

stories.h2: The light that was not evil
paras: In chapter 1, a very bright light full of color and music comes down from the sky, and Robie turns to follow it. A red-haired girl screams, "No-o-o! That is an evil light. It will hurt you." The light is gone before he can reach it, and he spends a hundred and seventy-five years alone. Only later does he understand who the girl really was.

In Heaven, Mary tells Mac that "there are ten thousand missing children." Mac tells her about Bebop and then lays out the plan: "Teach it to the kids. When the time is right and all of the children have been gathered, sing it loud and clear." On Earth, Jimmy supplies the missing piece: "We jump into the caves while the monsters are sleeping or gone, free the kids, teach them how to jump out," and the four friends choose the Mojave Desert as the place to take them.

When Jimmy shouts that Mary sounds just like the rest of them, the sky grows bright and a man with a kind face stands before the children. "I am Jesus, the One you seek, even though you knew Me not." Robie bursts into tears as all the pain and loneliness he has carried finally leave him, and Jimmy hugs Him. Jesus tells Sarah, "Keep the faith before them, and all will come home."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in the foreword to parents: "This is a story about purpose." She writes that "It is important for each person to find their place in life and use their talents to better the human experience." Her hope is that a child reading it will discover "the joys of helping others." The story shows that idea in action. Each of the four friends has a different gift, from teaching to healing to fighting, and each is needed.

faq.q: What is Robie the Ghost about?
faq.a: A boy who has been a ghost since a blizzard in 1836 joins two escaped children and an angel named Mary to rescue lost children from a shape-changer called Bebop and his monsters, and to call Jesus to bring them home.

faq.q: Is it a story of good versus evil?
faq.a: Yes. Bebop and his small monsters keep new souls in cages and "feed off pain and negative emotions," while Heaven sends an angel, a plan and warrior angels to bring the children home. The words "good versus evil" are not used in the book. The contest is the whole plot.

faq.q: Is it scary for kids?
faq.a: It has monsters and underground caves, and the captive children have been hurt. The story is hopeful, the hurt is described briefly and healing follows each rescue. Parents of younger readers may want to read it first.

faq.q: What is the song in the story?
faq.a: Mary's plan includes "Jesus Loves Me," which the children sing together when all of them are gathered. The book names the song early, and the familiar words of the first verse and chorus appear in the final chapters when the children sing. It is a story that uses the song, not a songbook.

faq.q: Does it have angels?
faq.a: Yes. Mary is an angel sent to Earth, her supervising angel is Mac, and other angels, including warrior angels, appear throughout. Mac teases Mary when she is alarmed: "Don't get your wings all bunched up."

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: It is written for ages 8 to 12 as a middle-grade chapter book of thirteen chapters.

faq.q: Is it a story about finding your purpose?
faq.a: The foreword says so in its first line, and each child finds a job that fits: Jimmy teaches the jumps, Sarah heals, and Kono, who has waited five hundred years, joins the rescue. It is not a self-help book. It is an adventure that shows what purpose looks like.

faq.q: Is it a guardian angel story?
faq.a: Partly. Mary explains to Sarah that everyone has a guardian angel, and Sarah's own helper begins to speak up in the cabin. It is one thread of the story, not the whole of it.

sections.h2: For young readers who love fairies and talking animals
paras: If your child likes tiny creatures with big opinions, this is for them. A queen bee holds court over a forest of honey. A snail at a bark desk speaks in a whisper and a caterpillar named Bobbin goes to fetch his sister. A blue bird named Indigo carries the fairies home in a woven basket shaped like a nest.

sections.h2: For parents who read aloud
paras: The chapters are short and end where a bedtime can. The language is simple and the dialogue carries the story, so it reads well out loud. The questions come up the way a child would ask them: "Where did God come from?" is answered honestly with "Nobody knows," and the book says plainly that believing takes trust.

sections.h2: For teachers and families who want to talk afterward
paras: The back of the book has Discovery Questions for chapter groups. They ask a child how it feels not to get the color of flower you wanted, what you think came first and why, how to answer a question you do not know, what helps when you are scared, which verse in Genesis chapter 1 talks about the creation of birds, where you can learn about God, and whether everyone who hears about God will believe. They work as a read-aloud guide for a family, a classroom or a small group.

sections.h2: For children who wonder where everything came from
paras: The question of the chicken and the egg is really a question about beginnings. The book takes it seriously and answers it inside the story, with a Creator who made birds, trees, mushrooms and fairies. It is a children's story that gives one clear answer and invites a child to think it over.

audience.headline: Two fairy best friends ask what came first, the chicken or the egg, and set out to find the answer.
audience.body: For children ages 6 to 10 who love fairies, talking animals and a good adventure, and for the parents and teachers who read to them. Jenna Kris sends Rose Petal and Raindrop from the land of Whimsy through the Honey Forest, the Garden of the Gnomes and Flutter Butterfly Meadow to the mushroom libraries of the Questing Woods, where an answer waits that is bigger than the question. A note on subjects: this is a gentle fantasy for young readers. There is a loud argument at a festival, a long trip with a few scary moments, including a butterfly ride in which one fairy falls and is caught, and a worry about whether everyone will agree at the end. The book presents God as the Creator who made everything, and it does that through a scroll about the fifth day of creation.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who ask big questions
paras: It begins with a spring festival and a question that sounds silly. By the last chapter the whole land of Whimsy has stopped to listen. Rose Petal and Raindrop go looking for an answer to calm everyone down, and they come home with more than they asked for.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a question every child has heard. At the animal booths, fairies argue about the chicken and the egg until the chickens squawk and the baby chicks hide. Nobody actually knows the answer, and that is why the two friends leave.

It is a quest with places you can picture. The path runs past the Honey Forest and its Queen Bee, the Garden of the Gnomes, Flutter Butterfly Meadow, Lake Mystery, the Questing Woods and Singing Bird Haven, and then home to Whimsy.

It is about friendship that holds when things get hard. Rose Petal charges ahead and Raindrop stops to take notes. When Raindrop slips from a butterfly's back, Rose Petal is the one who reaches for her hand.

The answer comes from the first chapter of Genesis. A scroll called Birds and Fowl says that on the fifth day God created "every winged bird according to its kind," and a hyper young fairy named Dickens explains what that means.

It leaves room for doubt and for choosing. Raindrop worries that not everyone will like the answer, and Rose Petal answers, "All we can do is share what we learned about God, and they have to decide for themselves."

stories.h2: The question at the animal booths
paras: Chapter 3 finds Raindrop and Rose Petal at the festival, hoping to see baby chicks. Instead they find animal fairies bickering. The argument turns into a scene: worms wiggle everywhere, chickens squawk and baby chicks hide, and the arguing fairies are too busy to notice. Raindrop shouts "Stop!" and nobody hears her. Mother Kit tells them the only place that could hold the answer is "more than a week away," a place called The Questing Woods, and the two friends decide to go.

In Chapter 4 the fairies walk into the Honey Forest without asking, and the worker bees drop their honey. Queen Bee comes out to ask who is there. Rose Petal tells the truth, that fairies back home are bickering. Then the queen asks what Rose Petal believes the answer is, and Rose Petal has to admit that she does not know. The queen lets them pass and asks them to come back and tell her what they find. They keep that promise on the way home, and Queen Bee says, "I have heard of this God before."

Chapters 9 and 10 take place in a tall orange mushroom library with stairs winding to the top. It takes most of a day to find the shelf for farm animals. Dickens unrolls the scroll and reads the first sentence aloud, and then explains it in his rapid way: God made birds, not a pile of eggs left to hatch on their own. Raindrop is not sure. She asks who God is and where He came from. Dickens says nobody knows, and that you have to trust that He is real. She leaves the chapter thinking it over.

Much of her inspiration comes from being outdoors and from time with her little niece. This book was inspired by the Lord and by a couple of little girls she used to babysit and their love of fairies.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's note in the book is short, and it says where the story came from: "This book was inspired by the Lord and a couple of little girls she used to babysit and their love of fairies."

The story itself says what she wants a child to carry away. When Raindrop worries that the fairies of Whimsy will not accept the answer, Rose Petal says, "What matters is that we believe." In the last chapter Raindrop says that even if the others do not, "we do, and I know that I will continue to believe in God and creation no matter what."

faq.q: What is The Fairies Quest about?
faq.a: Two fairy best friends, Rose Petal and Raindrop, leave the land of Whimsy to find out what came first, the chicken or the egg, after the question splits the spring festival into two sides. They travel through forests, a garden, a meadow and past a mysterious lake to the Questing Woods, and they come home with an answer about the Creator.

faq.q: Does the book answer the chicken or the egg?
faq.a: Inside the story, yes. The fairies read that God created birds on the fifth day, so for them the chicken came first. It is a children's faith adventure. It is not a science text, and it does not claim to be one. The exact phrase chicken or the egg appears about ten times in the book, and the question drives every chapter.

faq.q: Is it for kids who like talking animals?
faq.a: Yes. Queen Bee speaks in the Honey Forest, Quickie the snail greets visitors at the Questing Woods, Bobbin the caterpillar and his sister Windy talk to the fairies, and Indigo the blue bird gives them a ride home. The festival opens with animal booths, baby chicks, squirrels and toads.

faq.q: Is there a water fairy in it?
faq.a: Raindrop is called a water fairy once, in Chapter 5, when a bucket falls down the gnomes' well and she raises the water level to bring it back. The rest of the time she is the careful friend with a notebook, drawing water wheels and thinking about how to feed the picky sparkle spike fish.

faq.q: Are there gnomes as well as fairies?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 5 takes place in the Garden of the Gnomes, where Greenie shows the fairies how water flows through the trenches and Daisy gives them a place to sleep.

faq.q: Where did animals come from, according to the book?
faq.a: The book answers with the scroll in the Questing Woods library, which says that God created "every winged bird according to its kind" on the fifth day, and Dickens explains that He made the birds first and not a pile of eggs. The question is about birds, and the book keeps to birds.

faq.q: Does it teach about God?
faq.a: Yes. The subtitle names discovering the Creator. The fairies learn about God in the library, they take a scroll of the creation story home, and the new idea spreads through Whimsy. The story is a conversation between friends who are still working it out.

faq.q: Is it a fairy tale adventure for ages 6 to 10?
faq.a: It is an early chapter book of 88 pages for read-aloud or for children who read on their own. It has thirteen chapters and a gentle pace.

book.short: A devotional for the divorced and relationship impaired, written by a pastor's daughter who found grace waiting on the other side: God will restore.
book.about: Thirty years, three marriages and five kids after giving her heart away for the first time, Carol Renee Gitthens tells the truth about the mess that relationships can make of a life, and about the God who restores it. Lessons from the Well is a devotional for the divorced and relationship impaired, written by a pastor's daughter who knows what it is to fail herself, her father and God, and to find grace waiting on the other side. The book opens with an allegory: Virtue is a sanctuary of meadows, a clear stream and a well as pure as a young girl's heart, until storms come and the well is walled in with stones of fear and distrust. From there she moves through nine chapters drawn from her own story and from Scripture, on growing up in a Christian home, the shame that asks who told you that you were naked, and, at the heart of the book, the woman at the well and the Living Water Jesus offered her. Each chapter closes with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, Scripture from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles, and a prayer. This is not a book that justifies divorce. It points to the healing power of Jesus despite our choices.

sections.h2: For readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: If you are tired of explaining yourself, this book does not ask you to. It asks you to sit down at the well. The author tells her own failures without excuses and then shows, chapter by chapter, where she found grace. You can read one chapter at a time, write your answers on the questions at the end, and pray the prayer when you are ready.

sections.h2: For anyone who has asked what a loss did to their worth
paras: The author writes about a belief that took hold after her first heartbreak: that she was "unworthy of anything better than what I had lost." If that sentence sounds like something you have thought, you will find company here, and you will find the story of a woman in John 4 who was treated the same way and was met by Jesus anyway.

sections.h2: For personal study and small groups
paras: Each chapter lists its Scripture passages up front and closes with questions that suit a quiet morning or a circle of women or men. The discussion questions are honest, for example asking how a breakup or divorce affected your outlook on love and on your sense of self-worth. Groups that want to talk about shame, forgiveness and judgment will find plenty to open up.

audience.headline: After the breakup, the divorce and the shame, Jesus is still waiting at the well.
audience.body: For readers healing from divorce and broken relationships, and for anyone who has asked how a loss changed their sense of worth. Carol Renee Gitthens, a pastor's daughter, tells the truth about her own failures and about the grace that met her on the other side. Each chapter closes with Scripture for healing, questions to journal and a prayer. A note on subjects: this devotional speaks openly about divorce, shame, grief and a season of depression, and about the author's own mistakes. Nothing is described in graphic detail. It is a personal testimony and a book of Scripture and prayer, not counseling or medical advice.

quote.text: Virtue was a sanctuary; the well was my heart.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: A devotional in nine chapters, built from one woman's story and from Scripture. It opens with an allegory of a place called Virtue, moves through shame and failure, sits for a long chapter with the woman at the well, and ends with steps toward moving forward.
Five things set it apart:
list: It does not excuse and it does not condemn. The foreword says the book does not praise or justify one of the most divisive subjects in the church, and that "it points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices in life."
It is told by someone who has been there. The author writes that after "Thirty years, three marriages, and five kids," she had failed herself, her father and God, and she says so plainly.

It stays close to Scripture. Chapters draw on Genesis, John 4, the Psalms, Isaiah, Romans, Paul's letters and more, quoted from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles, with the references listed at the start of each chapter.
It is built for journaling and groups. Every chapter ends with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, then a prayer.
It centers on the woman at the well. At the heart of the book, a close reading of John 4 shows Jesus choosing to meet one outcast woman, and the author shows how that same love reaches readers today.

paras: Virtue was mine. It was a landscape adorned with the beauty of innocence, unspoiled, and blooming with endless possibilities. Nothing was dead or brittle. Every plant flourished in youthful anticipation, and every fruit and flower thrived with hope. The meadow was clothed with wild flowers of many vibrant colors, descending gracefully to the clear, babbling stream. Near the stream was a well encircled with large stones, and the water from it was as clean and pure as a young girl's heart. Virtue was a sanctuary; the well was my heart.

blocks.text: A few lines later the story turns:

paras: But with all the love I had shown him, he slowly grew distant. More often, I walked to the well alone. At times, I would find him at the bluff, his eyes fixed on the horizon. His heart seemed a thousand miles from me.

stories.h2: A well walled in with stones
paras: The allegory begins in a sanctuary of meadows and a clear stream, with a well as pure as a young girl's heart. A young man draws close and then slowly pulls away, and a storm follows. Years later, after much loss, the author describes herself as guarding her heart so fiercely that "I encapsulated the well with thick, impenetrable walls, built up with stones of fear and distrust." At the gate she staked a sign with a new name, "Vulnerable, population: one." The chapter ends with questions that ask readers where they see themselves in the picture.

stories.h2: Jesus sat by the well, and He waited for her
paras: In Chapter Five the author looks hard at John 4. The Samaritan woman came to draw water alone at noon, when the other women were gone. The author writes, "She was an outcast among outcasts." Then comes the line the chapter turns on: "But Jesus, being weary from His journey, sat by the well, and He waited for her." The author admits she once shut people out, did not answer the door or the phone, and that in her aloneness Jesus came to her well too, through His Word and through prayer.

stories.h2: The radio, the roadside and the fear
paras: In Chapter Four the author remembers being seventeen and driving a big maroon car her friends nicknamed "The Tank." A wave of fear hit her while she listened to pop music, so she switched off the radio, pulled over and prayed to be forgiven. Looking back she writes, "As a true believer, I should never have been so afraid." The chapter uses that memory to ask, with Genesis in view, who told us we were naked, and what fear was handed to us long before we made our own mistakes. In Chapter Seven her father's question comes back: "Are you a victim or a victor?"

author.bio: Carol Renee Gitthens is a pastor's daughter who grew up in a Christian home. She is the mother of five children and has been through three marriages and the divorces that followed, and she writes about guilt, shame and the grace of God without hiding any of it. The book is dedicated to her father, Bishop and Pastor Ronald Keith Gitthens. At his bedside in April 2023 she made him two promises, to carry the torch of his ministry and to finish this book. Stephanie Hensley, author of When the Lilacs Bloom, wrote the foreword.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's dedication explains it. "First, I promised my dad that I would carry the torch of his ministry." "Second, I promised him I would finish my book." She found a Father's Day letter to him folded in his Bible, written after their first reconciliation, which thanked him for pointing her to God.

Of the mistakes she mentions there, she writes, "It was through my divorces and, as a result, the ups and downs of our father-daughter relationship, that we both came to a fuller understanding of the grace of God." The book is her way of passing on what that grace taught her. Its purpose, in the foreword's words, is to point readers to "the healing power of Jesus."

faq.q: What is Lessons from the Well about?
faq.a: It is a devotional for the divorced and relationship impaired by Carol Renee Gitthens, a pastor's daughter and mother of five who has been through three marriages and divorces. It combines her story, Scripture and prayer.

faq.q: Does the book include Bible verses for healing?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter lists its Scripture at the start, and chapters quote passages such as "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3). The Scripture is from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles.

faq.q: What is the woman at the well chapter about?
faq.a: Chapter Five, "Lessons from the Well," is the longest in the book. It looks at John 4, where Jesus waits for a woman the town had pushed to the edges, and it shows what He offered her: Living Water, and a love with no boundaries.

faq.q: Does it justify divorce?
faq.a: No. The foreword says it is not a book that praises or justifies one of the most divisive topics in the church. It points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices.

faq.q: Is it a devotional I can use as a journal?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter closes with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, lined space to write, Scripture and a prayer.

faq.q: Does it speak to the fear of being abandoned or to feeling worthless after a breakup?
faq.a: The author writes honestly about both. She describes believing she was unworthy after her first heartbreak, and she shows how the woman at the well, and later her own Bible and prayer, answered that belief.

faq.q: Does it speak to being judged by other Christians?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Eight, "To Judge, or not to Judge, that is the Question," is subtitled "A Plea to Christ Followers." In it she asks, "Why did I feel like I had to make excuses for myself?"

faq.q: Can I use it in a small group or a women's Bible study?
faq.a: Yes. It suits personal study or small group discussion, with questions at the end of each chapter. It is written for women and men who are healing from broken relationships.

book.meta: My Perfect Daddy by Kelly Pexton: on dads' day at school, a boy whose father left tells his class about God as Father, a story of courage for ages 4 to 8.
book.short: On Friday the dads are coming to school, and Caleb has not seen his father since he was little. When it is his turn he whispers a prayer for courage and tells his class about a different kind of Father who will never leave.
book.about: Every child in Mrs. Mackin's class will stand at the front of the room with their father and tell everyone about him. For most of the kids it sounds like fun. For Caleb, whose dad stopped living with his family and whom he has not seen since, it is the scariest day of the year. All week he prays one small prayer: "Please don't let them laugh at me." On Friday he walks to the front, whispers "Give me courage," and tells his classmates about his Father, the One who goes to school with him every day, takes care of everyone in the whole world and will never leave. Some kids giggle, but a warm feeling comes back like a gentle hug from the inside. Then come the questions: how can God be everyone's Father, how does Caleb know God is always with him, and how can anyone believe in Someone they cannot see? Caleb answers as a child would, simply, honestly and with faith, that everyone has two dads: one on earth and God, our Father in heaven.
who_for: Children ages 4 to 8 whose father is absent or who feel different from classmates
Parents, grandparents and teachers who want a gentle story about God as our Father

sections.h2: For children whose father is absent
paras: This book does not hide the hole. Caleb says so out loud, and then he says what helped. His mom took him to church, and at Sunday School he learned about God. The story does not promise that the father returns. It gives a child a way to say that he has a Father who stays.

sections.h2: For parents, grandparents and caregivers
paras: If a child in your care misses a father, this is a story you can read together without a long explanation. The pages leave room for a child to talk. Caleb's answers to his classmates are the kind a young child can repeat at bedtime: "You have two dads. You have your dad here on earth. And you have God, your Father in heaven."

sections.h2: For Sunday School teachers and classroom readers
paras: The questions are the ones a Sunday School class asks. David says he already has a dad, and Sam wants to know how Caleb can believe in something he cannot see. Teachers can stop after each answer and ask the group what they would say.

audience.headline: A boy whose father left stands up on dads' day at school and tells his class about the Father who never will.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 8, especially children whose own father is absent or who feel different from the kids around them, and for the parents, grandparents and teachers who read to them. Kelly Pexton tells the story of Caleb, who dreads the Friday when every dad comes to class, prays for courage, and finds the words to describe the One who goes to school with him every day. A note on subjects: the story begins with a boy who has not seen his father since he was little. He is nervous and some classmates giggle. It is told simply and ends warmly. It is a picture book about faith and courage, not a guide for parents or counseling advice. If a child in your care is grieving or struggling, please talk with a pastor, a school counselor or a licensed professional.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who feel different from the kids around them
paras: Every child in Mrs. Mackin's class is supposed to stand at the front with their dad. For Caleb it is the scariest day of the year.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with dread, not a lesson. On a Friday morning in October Caleb's hands will not stop shaking, and all week he has thought about staying home and pretending to be sick, then decided that would be a lie.

stories.h2: The teacher who offers a way out
paras: On Monday Mrs. Mackin told the class that on Friday everyone would bring their dad to school and tell the class all about him. All the kids cheered, but not Caleb. The book says "Caleb did not have a dad." Mrs. Mackin bends down close and says softly, "Caleb, you don't have to do this." Caleb nods, but he has an idea. All week he thinks about staying home, decides that would be a lie, and prays every night with his eyes squeezed shut.

When Mrs. Mackin looks right at Caleb, his heart jumps into his throat. He nods yes and stands up. "The walk to the front of the room felt very, very long." He looks up at the ceiling and whispers, and "right away, something warm spread through his chest." His shoulders relax. He says, "I want to tell you about my Father," and his voice is small but steady.

stories.h2: Two questions from the back of the room
paras: David asks how God can be everyone's Father when he has a dad sitting right there, and Caleb answers that he has two dads. Sam asks how Caleb knows God is always with him, and Caleb smiles for the first time all day. He puts his hand on his chest and says, "I talk to Him all day long. Even without words." And when Sam asks how anyone can believe in something they cannot see, Caleb says, "That's called faith."

faq.q: What is My Perfect Daddy about?
faq.a: It is a picture book about Caleb, whose father left the family, and the Friday when every child in his class introduces their dad. He prays for courage, stands up, and tells his classmates about God as his Father, who goes to school with him and never leaves.

faq.q: Is it a book about God as Father?
faq.a: Yes. That is the whole story. The phrase God as Father is not printed in the book. The book says it in a child's words: "God made the whole wide world. He made people so He could have children to love. We are all His children. He is a Father to all of us."

faq.q: Is it a show and tell story?
faq.a: It has the same shape: a child stands at the front and tells the class about someone special. The words show and tell do not appear in it, and Caleb has no dad beside him, so he brings the One he cannot see.

faq.q: Does it speak about a heavenly Father?
faq.a: Yes. Caleb tells David that he has God, his Father in heaven. The word heavenly is not used, and the idea comes in plain language: a dad on earth and God in heaven.

faq.q: Is it for a child with an absent father?
faq.a: Caleb's father stopped living with the family, and he has not seen him since. The book shows a boy missing his dad and finding comfort in prayer. It does not offer counseling or promise any change in a real father.

faq.q: Does it teach a prayer for courage?
faq.a: It shows one. Caleb whispers "Give me courage" and then feels warm in his chest. He also prays at night that the others will not laugh at him. The book shows a child praying in his own words.

faq.q: Does it say God is always with me?
faq.a: Yes. Caleb says that when he is scared he asks God for help and "the scared feeling goes away," and that "He always listens." He tells Sam, "He is always there."

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Ages 4 to 8, as a read-aloud. A parent or teacher can finish it in one sitting.

Readers will find main dishes such as chicken and dumplings, baked salmon, meatloaf and chicken piccata; casseroles; Southern favorites like fried catfish and chicken fried steak; pasta from cacio e pepe to lasagna; egg dishes; soups and stews; side dishes; sourdough bread and buttermilk biscuits; sweets; and a generous chapter of appetizers and dips. Rooted in the conviction that cooking is a love language, it invites beginners and seasoned cooks alike to give themselves grace and never give up.

sections.h2: For busy people who say "I don't have time to cook"
paras: The author has an answer for you, and it is arithmetic. "The process of preparing and eating a meal takes the same amount of time whether you cook it yourself, wait in a drive through, or go out to eat." Her advice is to choose one dish to master and fill in the rest with store-bought sides, and she shows you how little a good weeknight dinner needs.

sections.h2: For beginners and self-described kitchen failures
paras: If your dinner has never looked like the photo, this book is on your side. The author defines "failure" in a way that lets you off the hook, then points you to simple recipes you can make from the start. The glossary, the equipment tips and the notes on prepping fruits, vegetables and meats are written for people just beginning to expand their cooking skills.

sections.h2: For home cooks who want easy recipes for weeknights and company
paras: Weekend guests who arrive on Friday after work, kids who bring friends home for dinner, or a table planned for four that ends up serving eight: the author has fed all of them. You will find casseroles, soups, Southern mains and a large chapter of appetizers and dips, plus tips for keeping food fresh, using leftovers on purpose and throwing away less.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for busy people and beginner cooks
paras: A 319-page, full-color cookbook of everyday recipes that "are simple and have only a few steps," with ingredients that are "inexpensive and easy to buy." It is as much a cooking teacher as a recipe book.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts where beginners start. Two short chapters answer "But I've Always Been a Kitchen Failure!" and "But I Don't Have Time to Cook!" before a single recipe appears, and a glossary of cooking terms waits at the back.

It covers the whole week. Main dishes, casseroles, Southern favorites, pasta, egg dishes, soups and stews, sides, breads, candies, cookies, cakes, pies and cobblers, and a long chapter of appetizers and dips.

It gives you ways to bend each recipe. Many recipes carry time-saving tips, cooking-for-one tips and variations, and a section teaches you to create your own recipe variations by testing an idea on a single portion.
It plans for company. There is a section on how to stretch dinner for unexpected guests and how to enhance a boxed cake mix, drawn from years of feeding a full house.
It is rooted in faith and love. The author reminds you that Jesus cooked fish on a fire to feed His followers, and that "God cares to feed all the people He loves."

paras: The cookbook began when the author, then a traveling nurse in North Carolina, taught a coworker how to cook. He wanted to break the fast-food habit, so he told her what he wanted to make and they made it together. He did all the work and she helped him succeed. When he mastered a baked-salmon main course, she told him, "Go buy some frozen peas and Uncle Ben's ninety-second rice, and that's your dinner!" It is the book's whole philosophy in one line: master one dish, then buy the rest.

stories.h2: A dish that does not look like the picture
paras: The chapter for self-described kitchen failures begins by asking whether your dish failed if it does not look like the one in a cooking magazine. "No way!" is the author's answer. She tells readers that "Perfection is elusive and appearances are just that—appearances," and she makes her point with a tomato: "Not every tomato is worthy of a picture on the cover of a magazine, but every tomato adds flavor to tomato sauce." The lesson is to give yourself grace, learn a few terms and techniques, and grow as you go.

stories.h2: Chicken and dumplings, and cooking for one
paras: Chicken and Dumplings is the first recipe in the book, a simple stew for cold fall days that the author likes to make from scratch. When she taught a friend, Cathy Vau, the hardest part was recognizing when the noodle dough was the right texture. Once you have felt it, the author says, "you'll never forget how to make this dough perfectly." A time-saving tip shows how to use the cooked chicken three ways in one week, and a cooking-for-one tip says that if you make a full pot, "your coworkers will love you."

author.bio: Toni R. Young-Huber grew up on a farm watching her grandmother cook three big meals a day. In her culture, she writes, feeding family is a point of pride and a love language, so cooking for and with other people comes naturally to her. She has worked as a traveling nurse in North Carolina, where she spent many Sunday afternoons teaching a coworker to cook American foods. She lived for a time in the foothills above Denver, where weekend and weeknight guests were common and she learned to stretch a meal. For her, cooking can be therapeutic, and she encourages every cook to give themselves grace when they make mistakes.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author wrote it for people who think cooking is out of reach. "If you're telling me you don't have time to cook, I'm thinking you're intimidated. That's why I wrote this book—to let you know how easy it can be to make meals for yourself, your family, and your friends."

She also wrote it because feeding people is an act of love. "When you go to cook, you're speaking a love language," she writes, and "When we share food we offer friendship, hospitality, and love." Her invitation to every reader, seasoned or new, is this: "You can feed yourself tonight and sustain yourself until tomorrow."

book.short: A short Bible study that invites readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine Scripture with fresh eyes, to move from knowing about God to truly knowing Him.
book.about: There is a profound difference between knowing about God and truly knowing Him. Philip Guenaga grew up in a deeply religious household and moved through several denominations, noticing that the Bible stories stayed the same from church to church while the teaching on salvation changed dramatically: some churches emphasized baptism while others dismissed it, some required speaking in tongues while others called it unnecessary. In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God invites readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine Scripture with fresh eyes. Chapter by chapter he returns to familiar passages: did God name both the first man and the first woman Adam (Genesis 5:2)? What does it mean that male and female were created in God's image? Did Adam and Eve have children in the Garden of Eden? He lays out six pieces of textual evidence, and later chapters ask whether Job's children really died, whether the seals of Revelation have already been opened, and what it means to be born again. The author shares his personal testimony, and a bonus chapter offers a theory on dinosaurs and creation. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes.

faq.q: What is In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God about?
faq.a: It is a short Bible study in which Philip Guenaga asks readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine familiar passages with fresh eyes, moving from knowing about God to a genuine relationship with Him through Jesus Christ.

faq.q: What topics does the book cover?
faq.a: It covers questions about Adam and Eve and the Garden of Eden, the image of God, the fall, Cain's wife, Job's children, the seals of Revelation, what it means to be born again, and the author's testimony, plus a bonus chapter on dinosaurs and creation.

faq.q: Does it discuss salvation, baptism and speaking in tongues?
faq.a: The author's starting point is that teaching on salvation changes from church to church, with some stressing baptism and others dismissing it, some requiring speaking in tongues and others calling it unnecessary. These are his questions and his reading of Scripture.

faq.q: Is it good for a small group or personal study?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes, which suits personal study, small groups and Bible classes.

faq.q: Does the book cover the plan of salvation?
faq.a: Salvation is the issue that opens the book, and the born again chapter asks what it means. It is the author's own study, not a denominational statement.

sections.h2: For believers who want more than religion
paras: If you have attended church for years and still sense a gap between what you know and Who you know, this book speaks to you. The author says that "genuine relationship with Him often remains elusive" for people raised in religious traditions, and he writes the whole study to move you from knowing about God toward knowing Him. His own testimony in Chapter 8 ends with this conviction: "That's why the relationship matters more than religious knowledge."

sections.h2: For personal Bible study, small groups and Bible classes
paras: Each chapter is short enough to read in one sitting and ends with questions you can answer alone or with others. One asks what other familiar Bible facts might benefit from closer examination of the original text. A group can take a chapter a week, compare the passages, and use the notes pages to record where members agree and where they would like to keep digging.

sections.h2: For readers who still wonder whether there is more
paras: Some readers have sat through sermons on Adam and Eve, Job and Revelation for decades and never been asked to read the verses themselves. This book is for you. It assumes you can read Scripture carefully, and it invites you to weigh what the author finds. He is open that these are his questions and his reading of the text, and he asks you to test them for yourself.

audience.headline: What if you know a great deal about God and still wonder whether there is more?
audience.body: For believers who want a relationship with God, not just religion, and for Bible study groups ready to look at familiar passages with fresh eyes. Philip Guenaga grew up in a deeply religious household, moved through several denominations, and noticed that the Bible stories stayed the same while the teaching on salvation changed. This short study invites you to open Scripture and ask your own questions. A note on subjects: the author's personal testimony in Chapter 8 briefly mentions an abusive childhood and a time of despair. It is told without graphic detail and ends in hope. The rest of the book is Bible study, offered as one man's reading of Scripture, not as the statement of any church or denomination.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want more than religion
paras: A short Bible study in nine chapters. Each chapter takes one familiar passage or question, lays out what the text says, and closes with reflection questions and lined pages for your own notes.
Five things set it apart:
list: It asks questions instead of handing down answers. The author says he wants you to examine Scripture "with fresh eyes" and to see what you find when you "look closely at familiar passages."

It goes back to the text. In Chapter 1 he points to Genesis 5:2; in Chapter 4 he lays out "six pieces of textual evidence" for children in the Garden of Eden; in Chapter 5 he compares the Hebrew words used in Job 1.

It covers the questions people whisper in Bible class: what Adam and Eve were really called, what the image of God means, who first got the blame for the fall, whether Job's children died, and whether the seals of Revelation have already been opened.
It speaks plainly about salvation. Chapter 7 begins, "How can my name be written in the Book of Life?" and the author says the chapter is "an invitation to examine the Scriptures afresh."
It is made for personal study. Every chapter ends with reflection questions and a notes page, so it works as a small workbook for a quiet week or a group meeting.

paras: Chapter 1 begins with an assumption most readers share, that the first man and woman were named Adam and Eve. The author points to Genesis 5:2: "Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, on the day when they were created." In his reading, God named them both Adam, the name Eve was given later by the man, and the change reflects a human perspective that developed over time. The chapter closes with reflection questions about how our understanding of gender roles might change if both were first given the same name.

Chapter 5 takes up one of the hardest passages in Scripture. The author looks at the Hebrew word used by each messenger who brings Job bad news, notes that translators rendered it as "servants" in three reports and as "young men" in the fourth, and asks why. He also notices that Job's wife seems distraught only once Job himself is afflicted. He offers a possibility, and he is clear about his purpose: "This perspective doesn't diminish the trials Job endured." The chapter closes with questions about how translation shapes the way we read.

In Chapter 8 the author tells how God changed his life. He grew up in a home where love was absent, one of seven children, and at seventeen he gave his life to God. He writes that "He spoke to me, saying He would be my friend," and that from that moment his life changed. He went on to marry, to serve ten years in the Army and to walk with God through the years. He admits that "some wounds from my childhood linger" and that God continues to heal him. The chapter ends with three questions for the reader about transformation, God's voice and personal struggles that might become testimonies.

author.bio: Philip Guenaga grew up in a deeply religious household and moved through several denominations, where he noticed that the teaching on salvation differed sharply from church to church. As a young man he had an experience with God that carried him through difficult times. He served in the Army for ten years and was stationed at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. He came to Rolla in 1986 and attended the church pastored by Larry Thornhill, who wrote the foreword and says he has known him for 34 years. Pastor Thornhill calls the book "first, an act of love, and second, a true understanding of God's word." The author wrote this study at the encouragement of friends.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the book began with a curious observation: Bible stories stayed the same from church to church, but "interpretations of salvation varied dramatically." He wrote it as "an invitation to examine the Scriptures afresh" and as a journey of personal discovery. In his words, "Rather than accepting traditional interpretations without question, I encourage you to examine Scripture with fresh eyes."

His friend and editor, Dr. Precious Taylor, recalls that he gave her every excuse for why he could not write a book, and she is proud that he finished it. The foreword says the book "is dedicated to those that are searching for a genuine relationship with the giver of life, Jesus Christ."

faq.q: What is In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God about?
faq.a: It is a short Bible study in which Philip Guenaga asks readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine familiar passages with fresh eyes, moving from knowing about God to a genuine relationship with Him through Jesus Christ.

faq.q: What does the book say about the plan of salvation?
faq.a: Salvation is the issue that opens the book, and Chapter 7, "The Plan of Salvation," asks what it means to be born again. The author says the chapter is not written to condemn any religion or denomination, and that Jesus told Nicodemus the path into the kingdom is to be born again. He writes that the path is "repentance, baptism in Jesus' name, and receiving the Spirit." It is his reading of Scripture, not a denominational statement.

faq.q: Does it discuss baptism and speaking in tongues?
faq.a: Yes. The Introduction notes that some churches emphasize baptism while others dismiss it, and that some require speaking in tongues while others consider it unnecessary. Chapter 7 gives the author's view of both, in the context of being born of water and of the Spirit.

faq.q: Does it talk about the Garden of Eden?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 asks whether Adam and Eve had children in the Garden of Eden and lists six pieces of textual evidence. Chapter 3 looks at the sequence of events in the garden, and the bonus chapter returns to Eden in a question about creation.

faq.q: What does it say about the story of Job?
faq.a: Chapter 5 compares the Hebrew words used in Job 1 and asks whether Job's children died at all. The author offers it as a possibility to consider and says Job's suffering "was still immense."

faq.q: Does it cover the return of Jesus and the seals of Revelation?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 compares Jesus' words in Matthew 24 with the first five seals of Revelation 6 and asks whether several seals may already have been opened. It does not set dates.

faq.q: What is the image of God, according to the book?
faq.a: Chapter 2 asks what "His image" means when both man and woman were created in it. The author suggests that the union of marriage reflects God's complete image, and he presents it as insight gained through prayer and reflection.

faq.q: Is it good for a Bible study workbook or small group?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes, which suits personal study, small groups and Bible classes.

book.about: Chicago, 1987. A young mother wakes to cold hands tapping her leg; a tall figure stands at the foot of the bed and beckons. She cries out in the name of Jesus and the figure is gone. Her two-year-old son sleeps beside her, and he would inherit her sight. In The Seer's Journey, Frank Theurer II tells his own story in the first person: raised on Bible stories in a home rich in prayer, a small boy who asked God to show him an eagle and watched one circle above the skyline, a reckless young man whose mother never stopped praying. He writes that when you surrender your life to Christ you become a target, and that Jesus holds the keys to Death and Hell. He explains the biblical role of the seer and the marks of the gift: spiritual sensitivity, discernment of spirits, and visions and dreams. A prologue describes an encounter before the throne, and twelve chapters follow the road to it, including Angels Over Iraq, Visions of Hell, The Rapture Revealed and The Seer's Commission. Scripture is quoted from the New International Version.
