sections.h2: For believers who want to understand prophetic gifts
paras: If you have wondered what the Bible means by a seer, Chapter 2 gives a plain definition and a list. The author writes that the gift cannot be earned by study. It is given by the Holy Spirit. The same chapter lists the marks of the gift and says the Holy Spirit helps a seer interpret and pass on what is received.

sections.h2: For readers drawn to true accounts of angels and demons
paras: The Angel of Death in his mother's room, a spirit who visits him after his cousin's death, small demons that hold him down, thousands of angels lining a road in Iraq: the accounts are direct, and the author does not decorate them. Chapter 10 states its position without hedging. He writes that demons are real and warns readers about the occult goods now sold as toys. You do not need to agree with every claim to see what he believes and why.

sections.h2: For parents who have prayed for a wandering child
paras: His mother appears on almost every page of the early chapters. She prays in the night, tells him Bible stories at bedtime, and keeps praying through his reckless years. He writes that her prayers were "the invisible architecture that preserved my life." A parent who is waiting for a child to come back will find company here.

sections.h2: For soldiers, veterans and families who have waited at home
paras: Chapters 5 and 6 follow the author through basic training and a deployment to a war zone where improvised explosive devices were buried in roads. He writes about fear, about praying for each member of his unit by name, and about asking God for protection. Not every reader will share his view of what protected his unit, and the book offers it as his own account.

audience.headline: The son of a prophetess tells what he saw of angels, demons and the living God.
audience.body: For believers who want to understand prophetic gifts and spiritual warfare, for readers drawn to first-person accounts of the unseen, and for parents who have prayed through the night for a wandering child. Frank Theurer II writes in twelve chapters, most dated by year and age, about a Chicago childhood, years in the U.S. Army, a deployment to Iraq, visions and dreams, and a prologue that ends before the throne of God. A note on subjects: this is one man's account of his own experiences, written from a Christian faith that believes God still speaks in dreams and visions. It describes spiritual warfare, demons, hell, war and violent deaths of people he knew, told without graphic detail. Chapter 7 states that it is a prophetic vision and not an account of events that physically occurred. It is a testimony and a teaching on the gift of a seer, not medical or mental health advice. If you are troubled by what you read, please speak with a pastor or a licensed professional.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a first-person account of the unseen
paras: It does not argue from a distance. A man who says he has seen angels, demons and Christ tells what happened, when, and what it cost. Then he explains what a seer is and what the Bible says about the gift.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a family inheritance story. The book begins with his mother, a prophetess, who wakes in Chicago in 1987 to a figure at the foot of her bed and cries out in the name of Jesus.

It teaches as well as tells. Chapter 2 explains the biblical role of the seer, names Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Ezekiel and Daniel, and lists three marks of the gift: spiritual sensitivity, discernment of spirits, and visions and dreams.
It is dated. Most sections carry the year and his age, from 1990 at age five to 2014 at age twenty-nine, so a reader can follow how the gift grew.
It goes to war. Two chapters follow his enlistment and his deployment to Iraq, and a third tells of a prophetic vision of the soldiers around him.
It ends with a call. The last pages are a plain invitation to believe the Gospel and "come to Jesus while there is still time."

paras: Chapter 1 begins before he can remember. His mother and her two-year-old son are asleep in the same bed. Cold hands tap her leg. A tall figure stands at the foot of the bed and raises one arm to beckon her. She cries out to God in the name of Jesus to save her life and her child's, and the figure is gone. In her heart she understands that she met the Angel of Death and was rescued by the One who "holds the keys to Death and Hell." From that night, the book says, her life was lived entirely for Christ.

Later in the same chapter, a small boy waiting for a Chicago bus asks his mother whether he can ask God for anything. She says yes, according to His will. He kneels on the sidewalk and prays, "I asked God to show me an eagle." An eagle appears over the skyline and circles overhead "as if responding to my prayer." His mother smiles. The chapter says his sight was beginning to awaken.

In Chapter 6, a young soldier deployed to Iraq prays for each member of his unit by name. One night he asks God to send angels, and he hears a question: "How many?" He answers with one word, legions, and asks that they guard the unit whenever it leaves the base. From then on, he writes, he saw angels standing along both sides of every road, "like an honor guard stretching into infinity." He also writes that no soldier in his unit was killed or seriously injured on missions outside the gates, and that bombs were found before they could go off.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author answers in the last lines of the prologue. After describing an encounter before the throne, he writes: "This is why I write. This is why I speak. Not to entertain, not to impress, but to declare: God is real, His eyes are upon us, and His call is urgent."

He also gives a sentence of purpose at the start of the book: "I exist to glorify Christ through the testimony of transformation." And in the closing pages he leaves the reader with a charge: "Believe the Gospel. Trust in Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins."

faq.q: What is The Seer's Journey about?
faq.a: It is Frank Theurer II's first-person account of growing up the son of a prophetess, his encounters with angels and demons, his years as a soldier, visions and dreams, and a prologue encounter before the throne of God. It also teaches what the Bible says about the seer.

faq.q: Does the book describe angels and demons?
faq.a: Yes. Angels line the roads in Chapter 6, demons attack in Chapter 4, Chapter 9 describes visions of hell, and Chapter 10 is a direct teaching on the unseen world. The exact phrase angels and demons does not appear in the book, but both are central to it.

faq.q: Is it a book that says demons are real?
faq.a: It does, plainly. Chapter 10 opens with these words: "Let me state this clearly and without equivocation: Demons are real." The chapter goes on to warn about the occult and says that "The Devil requires permission to take over a human life." The closing pages urge the reader to put on the full armor of God daily.

faq.q: What does the book say a seer is?
faq.a: A person given the gift of prophecy by God. Chapter 2 traces the role through Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, Ezekiel and Daniel and gives three marks: spiritual sensitivity, discernment, and visions and dreams. The author adds that the gift is not earned by study.

faq.q: Does it talk about prophetic dreams?
faq.a: Yes. Visions and dreams are one of the three marks of the gift. The book describes dreams and visions from his childhood on and presents them as ways God gives insight, warning and comfort. The exact words prophetic dreams are not used, but dreams run through the chapters.

faq.q: What does the book say about the gift of discernment?
faq.a: Discernment is the second mark of the seer. Chapter 6 says that in a combat zone he received the ability to perceive the hearts and intentions of the people around him, and calls it a gift that "proved invaluable." Chapter 7 is presented as a vision about the people around him.

faq.q: Is the book about a prophetic gift passed from mother to son?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 3 says, "The gift I had inherited from my mother, the mantle of seeing that had been passed down through her night of deliverance from the Angel of Death, was now manifesting in my own life." The words prophetic gifting are not in the book, and the idea is.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. Scripture runs through it, quoted from the New International Version. The last chapter ends in prayer, and the author's stated aim is to declare that God is real.

book.meta: Too Stubborn to Die by Susan Mahon: a nurse, teacher and Army linguist's testimony of God's faithfulness through autoimmune disease and chronic illness.
book.short: A pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army German linguist tells how she kept going through a lifetime of illness, and what God's faithfulness looked like along the way.
book.about: At seventeen, Susan Mahon heard a pharmacist say that when she got sick she was down for the count, and wondered for the first time whether being sick all the time was normal. Chickenpox, meningitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, pleurisy, staph pneumonia and surgery had filled her childhood, yet she kept going. Too Stubborn to Die began as a record for her loved ones of God's faithfulness through years of medical illness; friends urged her to share it so others facing illness might find comfort, perspective and faith. She is honest about what faith is and is not: healing does not follow a formula and faith does not guarantee an outcome. The story opens at the kitchen table of a frugal family of seven children, moves through her years as a pediatric registered nurse, a math teacher and an Army German linguist during the Cold War, and a season when illness left her bedridden. Four chapters, Foundations, Service, Homecoming, and Rise and Thrive, are followed by reflections including 35 Terms and Conditions of My Body and Blue Zones and the Circle of Health. This is a personal story, not medical advice.

faq.q: What is Too Stubborn to Die about?
faq.a: It is Susan Mahon's personal testimony of God's faithfulness through years of medical illness, from a childhood of repeated sickness to a career as a pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army German linguist.

faq.q: Is Too Stubborn to Die about living with autoimmune disease?
faq.a: Yes. The author lives with several autoimmune conditions, which the book describes in the story and in a closing reflection, 35 Terms and Conditions of My Body. It is a faith memoir, not a medical guide.

faq.q: Does the book promise healing?
faq.a: No. Susan does not believe healing follows a formula or that faith guarantees a specific outcome; God's work in our lives is personal, sovereign and often mysterious.

faq.q: Who is the book for?
faq.a: Anyone living with chronic illness, caregivers and family members who walk alongside them, and believers who want to hold on to God when the answers are slow in coming.

faq.q: Is it medical advice?
faq.a: No. The book is a personal story, and readers are told to consult qualified medical professionals before making healthcare decisions.

book.bio: Susan Mahon grew up in Arizona, one of seven children in a close, frugal family whose motto was 'The Mahons stick together.' She graduated from nursing school in 1975 and began her career as a pediatric registered nurse at age twenty. She later taught math and religion and coached volleyball at a Catholic middle school, then joined the U.S. Army and trained as a German linguist during the Cold War. She went on to teach for twenty years at Springstead High School in Spring Hill, Florida. Too Stubborn to Die began as a testimony for her loved ones about God's faithfulness through years of medical illness.

sections.h2: For anyone living with chronic illness
paras: If you have been told to expect less, you may recognize a voice here. The author spent thirty years trying to outrun a prognosis, and then could not. She does not claim to have found a cure. She writes about what it was like to lose her independence, and about small things that helped: a class, a letter, a brother who called every day.

sections.h2: For caregivers, family and friends
paras: The book shows what it looks like from the bed. Her husband runs the household, her mother-in-law drives her to appointments for over a year, and her brother calls almost every day. If you are caring for someone who is sick, you will see what their small improvements cost and what an ordinary compliment can mean.

sections.h2: For nurses, teachers and veterans
paras: Her working life runs through the book. She writes about the pediatric ward, and about taking a bottle to a baby who needed feeding and using those twenty minutes to cry quietly after losing a young patient. She writes about the classroom and the years of teaching German. She writes about basic training, the language school and a veterans' hospital program.

sections.h2: For believers who want to hold on to God when answers are slow
paras: The book is open about prayer and about what faith did and did not do. She asks God to let her live, and she says that once she accepted the outcome was no longer hers to decide, a burden lifted. She does not say God healed her on request. She writes that she almost feels He walked beside her her whole life, and she leaves the reader to weigh that.

audience.headline: A pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army linguist tells how she kept going through a lifetime of illness, and where God was in it.
audience.body: For anyone living with chronic illness, for the caregivers and family who walk beside them, and for believers who want to hold on to God when the answers come slowly. Susan Mahon writes in four short chapters about a frugal family of seven children, a nursing career that began at twenty, Army training as a German linguist during the Cold War, a diagnosis she put on a shelf, and the long stretch when illness left her bedridden. A note on subjects: this is a personal memoir about serious chronic illness. It describes childhood sickness, hospital work with very sick children and the death of a young patient, years of pain, a long period in bed, depression, and a time when the author believed she was dying. It is told honestly and without graphic detail, and it contains one use of strong language near the end. It is not medical advice. If you are living with illness, please talk with your physician or another qualified health professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people living with chronic illness
paras: This is a testimony, not a treatment plan. The author is blunt about that in the pages before chapter one, and then she tells what happened. She was a tough, stubborn girl who kept going, and she was sicker than she knew.
Five things set it apart:
list: It says what faith is not. A statement at the front says healing does not follow a formula, that faith does not guarantee a result, and that "God's work in our lives is personal, sovereign, and often mysterious."
It starts small. A pharmacist tells a seventeen-year-old cashier, "When you get sick, you're down for the count!" and she wonders for the first time whether being sick all the time is normal.
It comes from real work. She was a pediatric registered nurse at twenty, a math teacher, an Army German linguist during the Cold War, and a high school teacher for twenty years.
It tells the hardest years. A year and a half in bed, a scooter for almost six years, classes through a veterans' health program, and small steps that finally added up.

It ends with tributes and plain explanations. Former students and colleagues write short pieces about her, and a closing list, 35 Terms and Conditions of My Body, explains the author's diagnoses in everyday words.

paras: In Chapter 2, a classmate at the Defense Language Institute asks what is wrong with her eyes. A tear test and lip biopsy follow, and months later a physician tells her she has Sjögren's syndrome and that she will be "in a wheelchair, disabled and dead by fifty." She is twenty-nine, fit, and in the best shape of her life. She writes, "I decided to put the diagnosis on a shelf, high up and out of sight." Another diagnosis, rheumatoid arthritis, goes onto the same shelf.

Chapter 4 opens with the hardest stretch. She spends a year and a half in bed, cannot read or drive for a year, and is told there is too much organ damage for more to be done. She writes that she resigned herself to dying, bought a dress for her casket and spoke with her family. Then she prayed and asked God, if He would allow her to live, to let her spend her life helping others become healthy. "I felt a burden lift. Hope returned. So did strength."

At a veterans' program she takes a class for people with chronic pain and depression. One assignment is to write a letter consoling a friend who is going through what she is going through. She writes, and tears run down her face. "The compassion I had for this imaginary friend was the compassion I realized I needed for myself." A year later an instructor says, "You must be feeling better now." She frowns. He says, "You're wearing makeup. And you fixed your hair."

author.bio: Susan Mahon grew up in Arizona, one of seven children in a close, frugal family whose motto was "The Mahons stick together." She graduated from nursing school in 1975 and began her career as a pediatric registered nurse at age twenty. She later taught math and religion and coached volleyball at a Catholic middle school, then joined the U.S. Army and trained as a German linguist during the Cold War. She went on to teach for twenty years at Springstead High School in Spring Hill, Florida.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says it plainly at the front of the book: "This book began as a personal testimony written for my loved ones, a record of God's faithfulness during my journey through various medical illnesses."

She did not plan to publish it. "Friends who walked alongside me encouraged me to share it more broadly, in the hope that others facing illness might find comfort, perspective, and faith along their own journey." In her closing she names what she hopes readers will carry away: "I would like anyone struggling with health issues, mobility issues, or negative changes in these areas to have hope that things can improve in many situations."

faq.q: What is Too Stubborn to Die about?
faq.a: It is Susan Mahon's personal testimony of God's faithfulness through years of illness, from a childhood of repeated sickness to a career as a pediatric nurse, math teacher and Army German linguist, and a long period when illness left her bedridden. It is told in four chapters with a closing, tributes and two reference sections.

faq.q: Is it a book about autoimmune disease?
faq.a: In part. The author lives with several autoimmune conditions, and by one count in the book had "twenty-six diagnosed autoimmune diseases." They appear in the story and in the closing list of 35 conditions. It is a faith memoir by someone who lives with them, not a medical guide, and it says so: "This book is not intended as medical advice."

faq.q: Does it talk about rheumatoid arthritis?
faq.a: Yes, briefly. In Chapter 2 she describes knee pain she first blamed on running in military boots, and then writes that she was developing rheumatoid arthritis, which means her immune system was attacking healthy tissue. It also appears as term 29 in the closing list. It is one condition among many, and the book is about the whole story and not this diagnosis.

faq.q: Does it talk about Sjögren's syndrome?
faq.a: Yes. Sjögren's was her first diagnosis, given at the Defense Language Institute when she was twenty-nine. The book explains that it is an autoimmune disease in which glands do not produce moisture, and that for her it affected much more than dry eyes and mouth. Most of the other conditions in her closing list are described as related to it.

faq.q: Is it a personal memoir or a how-to?
faq.a: It is a personal memoir. It includes a few pages on lifestyle ideas she drew from a veterans' program and from Blue Zone research, but the notice at the front says medical treatment decisions should never be made solely on personal stories or spiritual testimony. Readers are told to consult qualified professionals.

faq.q: Does the book promise healing?
faq.a: No. The statement at the front says she does not believe healing follows a formula. The book speaks of hope, and the Closing says things can improve in many situations. It does not offer a cure or a guarantee.

faq.q: Who is the book for?
faq.a: Anyone living with chronic illness, the caregivers and family who walk alongside them, and believers who want to hold on to God when the answers are slow in coming. Nurses, teachers and veterans may recognize their own work in it.

book.short: Michele Wilson shares a lifetime of true stories in which God answered prayer, gave direction and drew near through His Word, a vision in the night, dreams and quiet nudges.
book.about: Have you ever longed to hear God speak to you personally? In thirty-four short chapters Michele Wilson walks through the seasons of a real life: marriage at nineteen, raising four children, moving from town to town, a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder and the day God set her free, a blinding light in her bedroom at three in the morning, a season of deep depression, a ten-year prayer finally answered, a man saved on his deathbed, an unexpected job as a general contractor, a day lost at Disney World, and encounters with God in places as ordinary as a back porch and a Walmart aisle. Each story is anchored in Scripture, with passages quoted so readers can see how God used His Word at the very moment it was needed. Written with warmth, honesty and humor.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to read the Bible with fresh expectation
paras: The author believed for decades, as many do, that the Bible was old words about other people. When a friend showed her how God speaks to her in Scripture, it changed everything. Here she shows what that looks like in real moments, with real verses. If you have ever opened your Bible and wondered what it has to do with Tuesday, her stories will give you something to look for.

sections.h2: For believers who want to pray about real decisions
paras: Where to live, whether to sell a home, whether to move a family, how to take an unexpected job: these are the decisions at the center of the book. The author prays about each and tells what she says God said in return. Whatever you think of her interpretations, you will see a woman who asks, listens and checks what she hears against the Bible, which is the habit the book encourages.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy a warm, honest and humorous Christian memoir
paras: If you like a memoir that is both sincere and funny, you are in the right place. The twins who are nothing alike, the husband who is an engineer and rarely wrong, the baby girl she prayed for, and the day she was lost at Disney World make the pages move quickly. The thirty-four chapters are short enough to read one at a time.

quote.text: I am thrilled that you desire to truly hear the voice of God.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want to hear God speak
paras: A Christian memoir in thirty-four short chapters, grouped into parts on foundations of faith, visions and dreams, trials and triumphs, walking in faith, prayer, provision, humility, everyday miracles, gratitude, and times and seasons. Each chapter is a true story and each is anchored in a Bible passage.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is built on a simple discovery. After nearly thirty years in church, the author learned in 1995 that God speaks through the Bible, and she writes so that you do not have to wait that long.
Every story points back to Scripture. Passages are quoted in full so you can see how God used His Word at the very moment it was needed.
It is honest about hard seasons. The author writes about fear, depression, moving from town to town, and years of waiting, along with the moments she says God answered.
It is warm and funny. A day lost at Disney World, an unexpected job as a general contractor, and a conversation in a Walmart aisle sit beside the weighty chapters.

It tells you how to respond. The closing chapter explains that salvation is a gift received by grace through faith, and invites you to pray, to read the Bible daily and to join a Bible-centered church.

stories.h2: A vision in the night, and a home by February 28
paras: In a rental home the family disliked, the author prayed for help by February 28, the end of the lease. Months later she cried out to God to reveal Himself. Two days after, around 3:00 a.m., she saw a blinding white light in the upper corner of her bedroom, and she writes that she heard, "The whole ordeal you have been through for the last four months will be over very soon." Chapter Five tells what came next. A friend from church called about her house for sale. On the morning of February 28 the author read John 4:50, "You may go, your son will live," and the next word she saw was "pool," and the family bought that home the same day.

For ten years the author had prayed for a baby girl, and she writes that "I had been praying for a baby girl for ten years." On June 19 she asked God to show her in her Bible the word "her" or "she," and it opened to Psalm 87:5. Her husband, an engineer, thought they would have all boys. She kept the promise in her heart through ultrasounds, mailed Christmas cards announcing a girl, and met her daughter three days after the due date. The chapter also tells, honestly, how hard the first months at home were.

stories.h2: An encounter with God in Walmart
paras: On the twenty-first anniversary of a frightening accident in which her son was spared, the author called her older son and asked, for the first time, what he had seen that day. Later, shopping at Walmart, she writes that God said, "For twenty-one years now you have been asking me how you can pay me back for saving your son's life. Let's get something straight; you can't pay me back, so don't ever ask me again." The message she took from it was that she should share the story, and tell others that Jesus died to save their lives eternally.

author.bio: Michele Wilson was raised in West Columbia, South Carolina, by Christian parents who took their four children to church almost every time the doors were open. She has a twin sister and a brother who became a pastor. She accepted Jesus at about age twelve and married at nineteen, and she and her husband raised four children. In 1995 a friend named Lelia showed her how God speaks through the Bible, a discovery that changed her life. She writes so that readers will learn to hear His voice and come to know Jesus as Savior.

paras: The author says God directed her to write it: "The very reason I am writing this book is because God directed me to do so in Jeremiah 30:2." She hopes readers will do two things: "learn how to hear His voice," and, if they do not yet belong to Him, "come to know Him as your Savior."

She also wants you to see why the Bible matters. "Salvation is a gift from God, not something we can earn by church attendance, good works, or family heritage." And she ends with a promise she says she has seen kept: "As I have testified throughout this book, God keeps His promises."

book.about: God is raising up His End-Times Warriors: men and women who will dare to believe, trust and obey Him at any cost. The End-Times Warrior is a 40-day devotional by Patricia A. Daniel, a roadmap to help believers be ready for the Lord's return. The author grew up a child of military parents and saw the discipline and commitment of those who serve; a poem she wrote, Marching Orders, inspired the book. The forty days move through four sections: The Lord, Our Commander; The Warrior's Identity in Christ; The Warrior's Special Training; and The Warrior's Mindset, thirty-three days on truths such as wearing the armor of God, being hidden in Christ, counting suffering for Christ an honor, living in the peace of God and being clothed in humility. Each day opens with New King James Scripture and affirmations, then a biblical truth, a reflection, ideas for applying it, a prayer and journal pages. It closes with a final prayer.

sections.h2: For believers who want to be ready for the Lord's return
paras: If you have been wondering how to prepare your heart for the days ahead, this book gives you a daily rhythm instead of speculation. The author calls it "a roadmap to help us be ready for His return." It does not set dates. It asks you, one day at a time, to surrender, to trust the Commander and to obey.

sections.h2: For readers who want a 40-day devotional on identity, surrender and fearless faith
paras: Forty days is long enough to build a habit and short enough to finish. The first week focuses on who you are in Christ, and the remaining days on how a person who belongs to Him thinks and lives. Each day gives you something to say aloud, something to think about and something to do, so the truth reaches your week and not only your reading.

sections.h2: For men and women who want Scripture, a prayer and journal pages every day
paras: You will find a Bible verse and a set of affirmations at the start of each day, a prayer at the end, and a journal page you can fill in. The reflection questions are practical, such as asking where you still struggle with fear, what you have not yet fully surrendered, and where you have been relying on your own strength. You can read alone or share it with a friend or small group.

audience.headline: Forty days to stand fearless, surrendered and ready for the Lord's return.
audience.body: For believers who want a 40-day devotional on identity in Christ, surrender and faith over fear. Patricia A. Daniel, who grew up the child of military parents, gives you Scripture, affirmations, a reflection, ways to apply it, a prayer and a journal page for every day, so that you can begin each morning with daily Bible reading and a prayer for strength. A note on subjects: the book uses military imagery as a picture of spiritual life under Christ's command, and it speaks of a possible season of persecution and even martyrdom for believers. It gives no instructions for violence and sets no dates. It is a devotional, written to encourage readers toward courage and trust.

quote.text: May this devotional serve as our trumpet call, awakening us to new levels of faith, commitment, and obedience.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for believers who want to be ready for the Lord's return
paras: A devotional in four sections and forty days. It begins by asking who your Commander is, builds up your identity in Christ, speaks of the training God allows, and then spends thirty-three days on the mindset of a believer who is hidden in Christ and fixed on Jesus.
Five things set it apart:
list: It gives you a plan. Each day has the same shape: New King James Scripture and affirmations, a biblical truth, a reflection, ideas for how to apply it, a prayer, and a closing affirmation of faith, with a page for notes.

It was born from a poem. The author wrote "Marching Orders" about being prepared to serve faithfully in the end-times, and "God would eventually use this poem to be the inspiration behind the devotional."

It is rooted in identity. Section Two takes five days on the surrendered, equipped, authorized, fearless and victorious warrior, so that you start from who you are in Christ, not from what you must achieve.
It tackles fear head on. Day 5 begins, "Fear is the first weapon the enemy deploys against a warrior," and the day closes with a prayer to renounce fear and entrust your life to the Lord.

It pairs courage with humility. Day 29 says true humility is "an accurate assessment of ourselves before God," and the book repeatedly describes the warrior as one who serves without seeking recognition.

stories.h2: Day 1: We serve a man of war
paras: Day 1 begins with the verse "The LORD is a man of war; The LORD is His name" from Exodus 15:3. The author reminds readers that when Moses and the Israelites stood at the Red Sea, "they didn't sing praises to their own strength or strategy," but recognized the true source of their victory. Under His command, she says, "we are offensive, not merely defensive; unstoppable, not easily deterred; and victorious, not defeated." The reflection asks you to take inventory of your readiness, to name what you have not yet surrendered and to write a personal declaration of surrender.

Day 5 names fear as the first weapon of the enemy, "because he knows that a frightened soldier cannot fight effectively." The author reminds readers that they stand in a long line of believers: Stephen faced stoning with a face like an angel, and "Paul and Silas sang hymns in prison at midnight." The action for the day is small and practical. Speak truth when it would be easier to stay silent, take a step of faith when you would rather play it safe, and reach out to someone when rejection seems possible. The prayer renounces fear and embraces the spirit of power, love and a sound mind.

stories.h2: Day 9: He is hidden in Christ
paras: Day 9 turns to Colossians. The author writes that when we come to Christ, our old self dies and our new life is hidden in Him, and that "This sacred concealment offers both protection and a new identity." She says the hidden position does not make us ineffective, but gives access to resources beyond human understanding. The reflection asks you to rest in that security today, especially when criticism or attack comes, and to remember that your worth cannot be touched.

author.bio: Patricia Daniel grew up a child of military parents and saw firsthand the discipline, order and commitment of those who served. She has served in multiple ministries over several decades, but most enjoys the Missions ministry, and has served in India and Brazil. She uses her administrative gift, her English as a Second Language certification and her writing gifts to edify the body of Christ. She is the author of three other books: a poetry collection, In Heaven I Can Fly, a children's book, The Purple Swan, and A Block From Grace, a memorial tribute to her parents that she co-authored. Her ministry blog, Destination Jesus, is where she shares her poetry, short stories and Bible teaching. She believes in what she calls legacy living, intentionally living so that your impact outlives you.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It began with a poem. The author writes, "It was not too long ago that I penned a poem called Marching Orders about being prepared to serve faithfully in the end-times." She never imagined it would become the inspiration for a devotional.

She also wrote it because she believes God is preparing believers now. "God is raising up His End-Times Warriors," she writes, "men and women who will dare to believe, trust, and obey Him at ANY COST." She is clear about the limits of the book: "This 40-day devotional by no means captures the full breadth of all God is doing in us and for us in these end-times, but it can serve as a roadmap to help us be ready for His return." Her closing hope is that readers will "rest in the fullness of His grace."

faq.q: What is The End-Times Warrior?
faq.a: A 40-day devotional by Patricia A. Daniel that helps believers prepare to serve Christ as surrendered, fearless warriors and be ready for His return.

faq.q: How is each day built?
faq.a: New King James Scripture and affirmations, a biblical truth, a reflection, ways to apply it, a prayer and journal pages.

faq.q: What are the four sections?
faq.a: The Lord, Our Commander; The Warrior's Identity in Christ; The Warrior's Special Training; and The Warrior's Mindset, which spans thirty-three days.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for strength?
faq.a: Each day ends with a written prayer. Day 5, for example, asks the Lord to "Strengthen me to stand fearlessly against every scheme of the enemy," and Day 11 prays that Christ's life will supply what the reader needs.

faq.q: Does it cover the armor of God?
faq.a: Yes, as one of the truths in the Warrior's Mindset section. Day 8 is titled He Wears The Armor of God, 24/7. It is one theme among forty days, not the whole book.

faq.q: Does it help with fear?
faq.a: Yes. Day 5 is devoted to the fearless warrior, and the book returns to fear throughout, pointing you to peace, to being hidden in Christ and to the truth that "We're not fighting for victory; we're fighting from victory."

faq.q: Is it a book about the second coming of Jesus?
faq.a: It is a devotional and a roadmap to be ready for the Lord's return, with daily Scripture and prayer. It does not predict dates.

faq.q: Does it speak to identity in Christ?
faq.a: Yes. Section Two is entirely about the warrior's identity in Christ, and later days speak of being crucified with Christ, hidden in Christ and one of many living stones.

book.about: Forty Days of Prayer and Reflection is a guided devotional journal by Pastor Andre d'Arden for believers who want to grow closer to God one day at a time. Each of the forty days opens with a passage of Scripture from the New King James Version, followed by a heartfelt prayer, a brief reflection, and thoughtful questions with lined space for your own answers and prayers. The introduction explores why forty matters in Scripture: Moses on Mount Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Elijah's journey to Horeb, and Jesus fasting in the wilderness. The days are not tied to Lent, though they echo its call to reflection and renewal. The prayers follow the unpredictability of life: healing and wholeness of mind, body and soul, removing limitations, overcoming obstacles, feeling insignificant, resisting fear, recovery, enduring pain, resting in the arms of Jesus, and believing in the unlimited power of God. The prayers grew out of a pastor's own prayer life, and a friend's encouragement planted the seed for the book.

sections.h2: For believers who want a daily quiet time
paras: If you want to start the day in prayer but do not know what to say, this book gives you words and then asks you to find your own. The author invites you to "take a breath," to "take the days as they come," and to "walk them with God." One day's passage, prayer and questions is enough to begin.

sections.h2: For anyone in a hard season
paras: The prayers do not pretend life is tidy. Day 17 is titled Life Is Not a Bed of Roses, Day 27 is about resisting fear, Day 29 asks to be pulled through, Day 30 is a prayer for recovery and Day 40 is about enduring pain. If you are tired, anxious or grieving, you can open the day that matches where you are and pray it as your own.

sections.h2: For small groups and prayer partners
paras: The introduction calls the forty days a "sacred rhythm" and a "deliberate space to pause, reflect, and realign." Each day ends with questions that a group can talk through, from how fear has played a role in your spiritual life to which lessons we can learn from Israel's failures. A group can take a day at a time, or pick days by theme.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to pray with more confidence
paras: A guided devotional journal in forty short days. It grew straight out of a pastor's own prayer life, after a friend who loved hearing his prayers told him, "I would love to have a collection of them. Put them in a book."
Five things set it apart:
list: Every day has the same simple rhythm. A Scripture passage from the New King James Version, a prayer written out for you to pray along with, a brief reflection, then questions with lined space for your own answers.

It explains why forty. The introduction traces the number through Scripture: Moses on Mount Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Elijah's trip to Horeb, the spies in the land and Jesus fasting in the wilderness, each one a threshold between what was and what would be.

It is honest about real life. The introduction says the devotional "reflects the unpredictability of life itself," so the days move from healing and wholeness to fear, frustration, recovery, feeling insignificant and enduring pain.
It teaches by example. If you have ever wondered how to pray, forty finished prayers show how a believer can thank, ask, confess and trust, and each day invites you to write one of your own.

It is not tied to a season. The days are "not bound to a particular liturgical season like Lent," though they echo Lent's call to reflection, repentance and renewal, so you can start on any morning of the year.

paras: The prayer begins, "Lord God, in a universe that seems so immense, it is easy to feel insignificant." It answers by reminding the reader of being "precious in Your sight" and "created in Your image: to shine in the world, to reflect Your love and character." The passage beside it is Psalm 8:3-4, which asks what man is that God is mindful of him. The questions are simple and personal: how important are God's children to Him, and what would you say to Him about the depth of His love for you?

stories.h2: Day 27: Resistance to the Effect of Fear
paras: This day sits beside 2 Timothy 1:7, "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind." The prayer asks to live "not in fear, but in faith," and is careful about what it is not asking: "We are not asking You to allow us to walk on serpents or coals of fire without harm, not even that. We are simply asking to live our lives in peace, without fear." The reflection that follows asks how fear has played a role in your spiritual life and what tools you need to overcome it.

The last day pairs James 1:2-4 with a prayer for hard times: "Heavenly Father, when times are difficult and heartbreaking, I need to remember that You are the One who strengthens me." It closes on hope, "The darkness of night makes the dawn of morning brighter," and a reflection that admits it is not easy to consider trials a joyful experience. The questions ask whether there is a trial you need to thank God for and whether the Scriptures have given you a way to endure.

faq.q: What is Forty Days of Prayer and Reflection?
faq.a: A guided devotional journal by Pastor Andre d'Arden: forty days, each with New King James Version Scripture, a prayer, a short reflection and questions with lined space to write.

faq.q: How do I use it?
faq.a: Take one day at a time. Read the passage, pray the written prayer, read the reflection, then answer the questions and write your own prayer in the lined space. The introduction asks you not to rush.

faq.q: Is it a book of Bible verses for encouragement?
faq.a: Every day is paired with a Scripture passage, and the book is meant to encourage, but it is a prayer journal rather than a list of verses. Each passage comes with a prayer, a reflection and questions.

faq.q: Can it help me learn how to pray?
faq.a: It models forty prayers, in a pastor's own words, for different needs, and every day asks you to write a prayer of your own. It is a good companion if you want to learn how to pray by praying alongside someone.

faq.q: Does it pray for healing?
faq.a: Healing and wholeness of mind, body and soul is the theme of Day 1, and Day 30 is a prayer for recovery. These are prayers of petition and trust. The book is not medical advice and makes no medical claims.

faq.q: Does it speak to fear?
faq.a: Yes. Day 1 includes Isaiah 41, "Fear not, for I am with you," and Day 27 is devoted to resisting the effect of fear, beside the verse that God has not given us a spirit of fear.

sections.h2: For Christian professionals
paras: If you lead a team, solve problems and make decisions all week and rarely connect any of it to your faith, this guide is for you. It promises to help you "lead with integrity, wisdom, and spiritual authority without being preachy, awkward, or irrelevant." The weekly challenges are small and concrete: ask a colleague about their story, tell your own, ask someone you trust for input on a decision, invite someone to coffee.

sections.h2: For pastors and ministry leaders
paras: A section is written just for you. It says this study is a tool for discipling "staff, volunteers, donors, or business leaders in your congregation," and it gives a way to start: "Hand-select 6–12 people who show leadership, curiosity, and relational strength," walk through the ten weeks together, then use the group to train the next facilitators.

sections.h2: For marketplace leaders who want to start a group
paras: "You don't need permission to start a group." The guide gives three steps for an owner, an executive or a team leader: pray and prepare, choose a time and place (a lunch hour, an early morning, a virtual meeting, "whatever works"), and follow the weekly rhythm. It works in a church, a workplace lunchroom, a virtual group or a living room.

audience.headline: Church taught them how to worship. Work taught them how to perform. This study teaches how to bring the two together.
audience.body: For Christian professionals who are tired of keeping their faith in a Sunday box, and for pastors and ministry leaders who want a practical way to disciple people beyond Sunday. Mark Thompson, a business coach and Chief Revenue Officer, gives you a ten-week small-group study with a weekly Scripture theme, discussion questions, an at-work challenge, a midweek message and a closing prayer. A note on subjects: Week Nine talks about stress, burnout and temptation at work, and the author shares from his own life and invites you to share from yours. It is a faith study guide, not professional counseling.

quote.text: Church taught them how to worship. Work taught them how to perform. But no one taught them how to integrate the two.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want faith and work to meet
paras: A short, practical guide of ten weekly sessions, an eight-step communication framework and a plan for launching your own group. It began when the author noticed that his own faith stopped at the office door.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts from honest experience. The preface describes a faith that stayed "compartmentalized" for years, "a box I checked on Sunday mornings, not a lens through which I lived," until small groups helped the author and his wife weave God into daily life.

It gives each session a clear shape. A meeting is about sixty minutes: a check-in, a guided discussion, then a wrap-up with the at-work challenge and a closing prayer, with a short message sent midweek to keep the study alive.

It teaches relationship skills, not just ideas. The Four Spaces of Belonging (public, social, personal, intimate) and the eight-step Communication Framework give you tactical ways to move from surface-level connection toward trust.
It does not require a seminary degree. The group leader's job, the guide says, is "to facilitate," not to teach, and you do not need to be "a pastor, teacher, or expert to lead this study."
It is built to multiply. The guide ends with how to launch a group in a church or an office, and invites finishing groups to start new ones.

stories.h2: Week One: Building authentic relationships at work
paras: The theme is "Trust is the foundation of spiritual leadership." The guide says that "Most people don't struggle with knowing what's right, they struggle with knowing who's safe," and it opens with icebreaker questions about your name, your work, what drew you to the group and how you would describe your relationship with God right now. Then it teaches the Four Spaces: public, social, personal and intimate. The first two steps of the Communication Framework, being curious about someone else's story and telling your own, become that week's practice.

stories.h2: Week Three: Integrity and ethics in business
paras: The theme is that integrity "isn't just about avoiding wrongdoing, it's about aligning our decisions with God's character." The Scripture focus includes Proverbs 11:3 and Psalm 15:1-2. The midweek message asks, "Where are you tempted to compromise this week? Who could you invite into that moment?" The challenge is step three of the framework, seek counsel, and the closing prayer asks for "courage to ask for help" and "humility to receive it."

stories.h2: Week Nine: Handling stress, burnout and temptations at work
paras: This session begins from a plain statement: "Stress, burnout, and temptation are part of every workplace. But they don't have to define our story." The Scripture focus runs from Matthew 11:28-30 ("Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest") to Isaiah 40:31. The teaching moment says, "We're not called to power through, but we are called to abide," and invites the leader to share a personal story of burnout, temptation or pressure.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author calls the problem a firewall. "Everything shifted," he writes, when he and his wife joined a church where small groups showed them a faith that "permeated every aspect of our lives." One frontier remained, the workplace. Working with clients who brought their faith to their jobs was "a revelation." It "exposed the firewall I'd unknowingly accepted," the place where his faith stopped at the office door.

Conversations with other Christians echoed the same frustration, so he wrote a study to close the gap. "It's not about perfection, it's about progress," he says, and the goal is to "transform your workplace into a mission field, where you live boldly as a witness to God's love and truth."

faq.q: What is Bringing Jesus to Work?
faq.a: A practical ten-week study by Mark Thompson for Christian professionals, with a weekly Scripture theme, discussion questions, an at-work challenge, a midweek message and a closing prayer. It works in a church, a workplace or a living room.

faq.q: What topics do the ten weeks cover?
faq.a: Authentic relationships, wise decisions, integrity and ethics, hard work and diligence, communication and listening, resilience, financial responsibility and generosity, mentorship and discipleship, handling stress and burnout, and legacy and impact.

faq.q: Is it good for workplace relationships and communication?
faq.a: Yes. Relationships are the thread through all ten weeks. Week One teaches the Four Spaces of Belonging, and the eight-step Communication Framework gives practical steps such as being curious about someone's story and inviting someone to coffee.

faq.q: Does it cover business ethics?
faq.a: One weekly session, Week Three, is about integrity and ethics in business, with Scripture, discussion questions and a challenge to seek counsel. It is a faith study with one session on ethics, not a business ethics textbook.

faq.q: Does it help with workplace stress and burnout?
faq.a: Week Nine is devoted to stress, burnout and temptation, with Scripture on rest, peace and perseverance and a call to bring burdens to God. It is a faith study, not counseling or medical advice.

faq.q: Is there a communication framework?
faq.a: Yes. The appendix lays out the eight steps, from being curious about someone else's story to asking about someone's faith history, and the weekly sessions introduce them one at a time.

faq.q: Does it include prayers for the workplace?
faq.a: Every weekly session ends with a written closing prayer, for example one for integrity and wise counsel and one for carrying a legacy of grace, truth and spiritual impact.

faq.q: Does it cover mentoring and leaving a legacy?
faq.a: Week Eight is about mentorship and discipleship, and Week Ten is about living and leaving a spiritual legacy, with 2 Timothy 4:7 and Psalm 78:4 among its Scriptures.

book.short: A work of fiction inspired by real events: a five-year-old Dalit orphan in rural India flees a violent father and searches for survival while a young man builds a refuge for children no one else will take.
book.about: At five years old, Naggya has already learned to run. In a makeshift hut outside a village in rural Andhra Pradesh, India, his father drinks day and night, and when the money runs out he comes looking for whatever his wife has hidden. One morning Naggya and his mother flee toward the jungle, and she does not survive. Orphaned, he wanders for days in search of the only relative he has ever met, and repeats his mother's words: Son, you must be strong. When his aunt finally finds him she takes him into her single-room hovel, but she is a childless widow, sick, and cannot see how to raise him. Not far away a young man named Elijah has walked away from the philosophies he once preached at university. One encounter with a homeless six-year-old changed everything, and in his parents' mud house he began Son-Shine, a refuge and school for Dalit children. Untouchable is a work of fiction inspired by real events. It opens a window on India's Dalits, the people at the bottom of the traditional caste hierarchy, in a story of cruelty and discrimination and of compassion that reaches one child at a time.

paras: A 478-page work of fiction that the author describes as "lifted directly from the life-and-death experiences" of the founder of Son-Shine, an orphanage and school in India that has rescued, housed and educated many thousands of Dalit children since 2006.

paras: Chapter One opens on a dawn chase. Naggya, who is five, urges his mother to run faster toward the jungle where his father, a drinker, will not find them. What follows costs him his mother, and the next pages follow a child alone: three days and three lonely nights of wandering, a search for water, and an effort to find "Aunty," the only relative he has ever met. When he is most afraid, "he silently repeated his mother's words: 'Son, you must be strong!'"

In a chapter about the young man who will found the refuge, a university student who spent his days "spruiking the philosophies of Lenin or Marx or Mao" comes home for a visit and meets a homeless six-year-old. One thought changes him: "if my parents had died like so many others, this boy could so easily be me." The next lines say that "An indescribable glow filled Elijah," and that he returned home determined "to start a revolution, not to the masses, but merely to one." The refuge begins in his parents' two-room house.

Years later, Naggya is a teenager when his mentor shows him something on a screen. "Ballet." "Ballet?" He watches the grace and strength of the dancers in amazement, and then asks, "But how, how do they do that? It looks so, they must be so strong!" It is a lighter scene, and it opens a door that leads to the other half of the book's title.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author met the founder of Son-Shine in 2009. In the thirteen years since, he writes, he has "relied countless times" on him "for insight and understanding," as "a westerner from Australia" trying to shed light on the lives of Dalits. He is clear about what kind of book this is: "Although Untouchable is a work of fiction, much of the content of this novel has been lifted directly from the life-and-death experiences" of the founder's world.

The founder, in his own foreword, writes of why he welcomes it: "Through this book, may your eyes be open to see the other side of the world of the Untouchable Dalits." He adds, "May God speak to you through this book."

faq.q: What is Untouchable about?
faq.a: A novel inspired by real events: Naggya, a five-year-old Dalit orphan in rural India, flees a violent father and searches for survival while a young man builds a refuge and school for Dalit children.

faq.q: Is it a true story?
faq.a: It is a work of fiction inspired by real events, much of it drawn from the life-and-death experiences of the founder of Son-Shine, who wrote one of the book's forewords.

faq.q: Does it explain the caste system?
faq.a: It opens a window on India's Dalits, the people at the bottom of the traditional caste hierarchy, through a story, and the first pages define the traditional categories. It is a novel, not a history or a guide to caste.

faq.q: What does the title mean?
faq.a: The book's own definition says that those at the bottom of the traditional hierarchy are "considered 'untouchables' or Dalits." The title names the people the story is about.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: It follows a faith-based refuge and is shelved with Christian and world fiction, but it is a novel and not labeled devotional.

faq.q: What does Broadway have to do with it?
faq.a: The subtitle From Beatings To Broadway reflects the boy's arc. The book includes ballet and New York theater scenes, and the path from one to the other is left unspoiled here.

faq.q: Does it deal with social injustice?
faq.a: Yes. Discrimination, poverty and unequal treatment of Dalit families run through the story, and so does the response of a young man who decides to take in one child at a time.

faq.q: Is it suitable for every reader?
faq.a: It is written for adults and includes violence against a child and a parent's death. If these themes are difficult for you, read the note under the hero first.

book.meta: Write Before Coffee by Carlene Hill Byron: a short, encouraging guide to write a book from the story God gave you, even if you think you're not a writer.
book.short: A short, warm guide from a writer and editor of more than 40 years for people who believe they are not writers: why your story matters, where the words for a book come from and how to start.
book.about: Many people carry a story God has given them but freeze at the thought of writing a book. Carlene Hill Byron, a professional writer and editor for more than 40 years, begins with the most basic question: why write at all? Her answer is that we write to build bridges. Drawing on the old one-lane bridges of her home state of Maine, she shows how stories carry people closer to God and to one another and invites readers to ask what bridge God has prepared them to build. Grounded in Ephesians 2:8-10, the book reminds readers that God is with them, working in and through them, and is not finished with them yet. It explains that the words for a book come from three places: words already written (blogs, sermons, speeches), words found and saved from reading, and words created fresh. It offers simple ways to collect material, from bins and folders by subtopic to journals, 3x5 cards, sticky tabs and online tools, and shares two secrets for facing the blank page. The author uses the example of Joeth Strickland, who began with a few boxes of supplies in her breezeway.

sections.h2: For Christians who sense God gave them a story
paras: If you freeze at the thought of writing a book, start with the questions the booklet asks: "What bridge has God prepared you to build? How can your story carry others closer to God and each other?" Those questions are meant to be answered before the first page is written. The author also asks "What experiences can you share?" and "What lessons have you learned?"

sections.h2: For pastors, ministry leaders and speakers
paras: You may already be good with words in sermons, devotionals and conference talks, and the author says so: "You may be an experienced wordsmith, but a book is a different thing." Blogs, opinion pieces, sermons and speeches "can become part of your book project," and she explains how a person who prepares talks tends to think in blocks that take twenty to forty minutes to read aloud, and how to turn those into chapters.

sections.h2: For first-time authors
paras: The advice is practical and gentle. "Write. Don't edit!" is tip number three, because writing and editing are two different ways of working on text. The author says that if you try to edit as you go, "you'll get caught up in polishing the first sentences for days on end," and she adds, "Trust me, this is the voice of experience speaking!"

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who think they are not writers
paras: A short, warm, illustrated guide in small pages, written for the person who is holding it because they are "at least beginning to know inside you what message God wants you to carry forward."
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with why. The first question is not how to write, it is "Why write?" Her answer, drawn from the one-lane bridges of her home state of Maine, is that we write to build bridges between people and God and between one person and another.
It names where the words come from. Words you have already written, words you find and save, and words you create fresh: three sources, so you are never starting from nothing.
It gives you a way to collect. Bins or folders by subtopic, an online tool, journal books, 3x5 cards, even the little sticky tabs the author puts in books she reads.
It is honest about the blank page. Two secrets from a long-time professional writer come before four practical tips, one of them the "WEIRDEST TIP" you will ever hear about how to write.

It shows what a finished bridge can look like. The author tells the story of one volunteer who began with a few boxes in a breezeway and built a ministry that has reached more than a hundred nations, with a book to explain how.

paras: The fourth tip is the one she calls weird, and she is careful to say it is not about getting up at four in the morning. It is a trick for your brain. "The part of your brain that creates, the writing part, actually 'wakes up' earlier than the part of your brain that edits." Her own practice: "What has worked for me is to get up at least 30 minutes earlier than I'm used to and go straight to my desk. NO COFFEE. The editor loves coffee!" After a few weeks, she says, you will know what it feels like to write without an interrupting editor.

Where do the words for a book come from? "You can collect them from things that you and other people have already written, and you can create them fresh." The booklet draws three pictures: words you have already written (blogs, opinion pieces, sermons, speeches), words you find and save (books, streaming media, news), and words you create for this project. For the blank page, she offers a comparison: "Would you step onto a Broadway stage and start dancing without feeling intimidated?"

stories.h2: One volunteer, a few boxes and a breezeway
paras: To show what God can do with a story, the author tells about a woman who began about forty years ago by having her Sunday School class and friends fill a few boxes with things missionaries needed. She kept them in the breezeway of her home until she could ship them. Today she runs a 17,000-square-foot warehouse and has shipped to Christian organizations in more than a hundred nations. The author asks whether God is finished with her yet and answers, "I don't think so!" Her book explaining the ministry was written in three months.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author comes at it as a writer and an editor who has heard many stories. "Fabulous stories from God's people that I've been privileged to help share" is how she describes her work with authors. She believes those stories matter because "The stories we have been given to tell encourage and uplift others who need to know the truths we've learned."

Her message to the reader is that you are not too late and not too unskilled: "God is with you. God is working in and through you. God isn't finished with you yet!" She invites you to listen to God about the message He wants you to share, and then to take the first small step. "You bring the inspiration," she writes. "We bring the experience and skill that build your bridge effectively to your readers."

faq.q: What is Write Before Coffee about?
faq.a: A short guide for people who think they are not writers: why your story matters, where the words for a book come from and how to begin, with practical tips from a writer and editor of more than forty years.

faq.q: Can I write a book if I am not a writer?
faq.a: The author says yes, and starts with why. She argues that the purpose is to write, not to produce finished text on day one, and that a professional editor is there to help with the rest. "The purpose of writing is to write, not to produce the finished text today."

faq.q: How do I start a book?
faq.a: Choose a strategy, either "Establish an outline and write to it" or "Write until you discover the outline," then gather words from three sources and start writing without editing. The four pro tips are Write, Write whenever and wherever, Write and do not edit, and Write before you wake up.

faq.q: How do I start a memoir or a testimony?
faq.a: The booklet is about telling stories of how God has changed people's lives, and about how to find the shape of your story. One of its tools is the Hero's Journey, a story structure that "often applies to stories from Christian living."

faq.q: How do I plan or organize a book?
faq.a: Collect your material by subtopic in bins or folders, an online tool, journals or 3x5 cards. The author shows her own sticky-note system: green for chapter heads, pink for chapter subdivisions, yellow for key scriptures and blue for applications.

faq.q: Is this a book for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for people who are not used to writing, and it says plainly that you are not expected to be highly skilled. That is why an editor gets involved.

faq.q: Is it a book about self-publishing?
faq.a: It is a guide to getting a story onto the page, not a step-by-step guide to publishing. It does explain how a team of writers and editors at Spirit Media can help with planning, writing, design and getting a finished book into readers' hands.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Christians who sense God gave them a story, pastors and speakers with material that could become a book, and first-time authors who want a simple, encouraging place to start.

book.meta: A Shepherd's Story by Leivon Canary Kom: a testimony of God's love from a poor village in Manipur, India, for anyone suffering and needing hope.
book.short: Leivon Canary Kom's plain, honest testimony of God's love, from a poor village in Manipur, India, through miracles, ministry and loss, offered to encourage poor people wherever his own voice cannot go.
book.about: Leivon Canary Kom grew up the fifth of seven children in a nominally Christian family in a tiny, underprivileged village in Manipur, India. His parents were daily wage laborers who worked long hours in the woods and fields for little more than one day's plain meals. In A Shepherd's Story he tells that life plainly and honestly as a testimony of God's love. He writes of the homeland he calls a Garden of Eden spoiled by selfishness and violence, of a grandfather who taught him that the Holy Bible is where God speaks to man, and of the King James Bible that became the first book he ever loved. He recounts miracles God has shown him, his early education, his teaching and Bible ministries, his fondest childhood memories and his regrets. Since 2000 he has worked in different parts of India, not as a pastor but as a daily bread earner, sharing God's love and plan of salvation. Later chapters speak about social, political and religious systems, Satan, selfishness and where true peace and security are found, and the book closes with testimonies from his family.

sections.h2: For anyone who is suffering physically or spiritually
paras: The author says he likes "to share my story with others who are suffering physically and spiritually." His message is simple: "We are His. So, we don't need to worry about anything in life. The only thing that matters is to trust and obey Him." If you are tired of being told to try harder, a short book in the voice of someone who has little may be easier to hear than a long argument.

sections.h2: For readers who want a testimony from Manipur, India
paras: Few books in English come from this corner of northeast India. The first chapter describes a homeland he compares to "the Garden of Eden that the serpent spoiled," and then he turns to the reader: "So, dear friend, if you are in a similar situation, never give up your faith in God. Manipur may be gone forever, but you don't have to be. Keep trusting in His promises."

sections.h2: For readers who love stories of hope, miracles and trusting God
paras: If you enjoy first-person testimonies, this one is plain, specific and told with dates. The miracle chapter says, "God has shown me several miracles. They testified of His existence to me." It is a book of faith rather than of argument, offered to be read in a sitting or two.

audience.headline: A plain, honest testimony from a poor village in Manipur, India, for anyone who needs to hear that God is good.
audience.body: For readers who are suffering physically or spiritually, who want a true story of hope, miracles and trusting God when a situation looks hopeless, and who would like to hear it in the voice of a man who has little and has known God's love. Leivon Canary Kom grew up the fifth of seven children in a tiny, underprivileged village, the son of daily wage laborers, and he wrote this book to "encourage poor people like me wherever my voice can't go to testify of God." paras: Chapter 5 begins, "The first book that I ever fell in love with was the Holy Bible in King James Version." His grandfather had told him the Bible "is where God speaks to man and gives him all the information that he needs for the welfare of his physical and spiritual life," so the boy grew interested. At thirteen he began studying it, praying every day, and used the Manipuri Bible and English grammar books to understand each verse. He became a bookworm, and writes that, "if I didn't get to read a book during the day, I couldn't sleep at night."

In Chapter 6 he tells of three miracles. In one, on a Sunday morning in June 1997, he climbed a mountain near his village to fast and pray, and studied Psalms and Proverbs for hours. Then the sky darkened and thunder began, and he prayed that it would not rain on him and his Bible. He writes that it rained at a distance and that "my Bible and I didn't even get one drop of rain." Looking around afterward, he says, "a circle with a diameter of 10 meters where I prayed wasn't wet!" He offers it as his testimony.

Chapter 10 begins on a quiet note: "Regrets and mistakes are inseparable parts of life. Every person on earth has regrets and mistakes." He then lists a few of his own, beginning with a childhood in which relatives teased him for growing fast and he decided to eat less to slow his growth, which he now calls foolishness. He finds comfort in 1 Samuel 16:7, that the Lord looks on the heart, and closes with a line of his own: "And nothing can ever stunt my spiritual growth!"

book.short: Kevin White tells how a prayer for food that others might eat, while his family lived on less than $500 a month, grew into a ministry feeding 500 families, and shows three steps to set God, yourself and others free.
book.about: In the year 2000 Kevin White was living on less than $500 a month in Cary, North Carolina, with his wife Shelly, three young children and a foster son. There was no food in the cabinets. He prayed, "Father, give us food that others might eat." Days later a grocery store deli manager handed him three carts of expired but edible food, and it happened again the next day. Within a year his family and twenty-five volunteer families were feeding five hundred needy families every month, and his family never missed a meal. That season became With Love from Jesus Ministries in Raleigh. Audacious Generosity defines the title as a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks by being kind and plentiful, an attribute of God seen throughout Scripture, and it is not about pressure, guilt or prosperity. The book follows three steps: Set God Free, to live recklessly and discover why you need courage; Set Yourself Free, to move from fear to freedom; and Set Others Free. A trip to India after he was fired from a church as an insecure workaholic is where he committed to pursue God's presence.

faq.q: What is Audacious Generosity about?
faq.a: It is Kevin White's story of a prayer for food that others might eat, which grew into a ministry feeding 500 families a month, and a three-step guide to live with bold, openhanded generosity.

faq.q: What are the three steps?
faq.a: Set God Free, to live recklessly, ask God for more and find courage; Set Yourself Free, to receive more and move from fear to freedom; and Set Others Free.

faq.q: Is it about pressure to give?
faq.a: No. It is not about beating you up for not giving, pressuring you to give what you can produce, or giving for personal gain. God is the Giver and giving means releasing what He puts in your hands.

faq.q: What does the book say about fear and courage?

stories.h2: Father, give us food that others might eat
paras: Chapter 1 tells of the year the author's support dropped to less than $500 a month and the cupboards were bare. He prayed and looked for work, and God gave him new words to pray: "Father, give us food that others might eat." One morning he stopped a store employee, learned she was the deli manager and asked what she did with expired products. The next day she "pointed to three grocery carts full of rotisserie chicken, pizza, pasta, and everything the deli and bakery sold." It happened the next day, and the next. "One year later, we were feeding five hundred needy families per month with the help of twenty-five volunteer families."

Chapter 3 begins with a question, "Have you ever realized a gift you didn't know you'd been given?" The author's answer is courage. He writes that "Courage is a choice and an act of obedience," that "Courage results from yielding to the Holy Spirit," and he points to 2 Timothy 1:7, where God has given "a spirit of fear and timidity, but of power, love, and self-discipline." He adds that his own need for courage has grown over four decades as a Christ-follower, not shrunk, because it "keeps me dependent on God."

Chapter 7 opens bluntly: "Fear is a B-word, a bully." The author describes living in fear for years: "I lived in fear for twenty years after I accepted Jesus for salvation. It wasn't until I was thirty years old that I began to understand what the Bible says about our identity in Christ." The chapter ends with the shift: "Once we are alive in Christ, we are secure, significant, and accepted in Christ," and the boxing match between fear and freedom comes to an end.

faq.q: What is Audacious Generosity about?
faq.a: Kevin White tells how a prayer for food that others might eat, while his family lived on less than $500 a month, grew into a ministry feeding five hundred families, and shows three steps to set God, yourself and others free.

faq.q: What are the three steps?
faq.a: Set God free, by living recklessly for God and asking Him for more; set yourself free, by moving from fear to freedom; and set others free, by turning from getting to giving.

faq.q: Is it about faith over fear?
faq.a: Courage and fear run through all three steps. Two chapters are about courage, one is titled Fear Versus Freedom, and the author builds on 2 Timothy 1:7, which says God has not given us "a spirit of fear and timidity, but of power, love, and self-discipline." The exact phrase faith over fear is not used.

faq.q: Is it about pressure to give?
faq.a: No. The author says audacious generosity is not about beating you up for not giving, pressuring you to give what you can produce, or giving for personal gain. He says it is not about faith being "some force that guarantees prosperity."

faq.q: Is it about biblical generosity and stewardship?
faq.a: It is about biblical generosity as an attribute of God, with Scripture throughout. Stewardship of money is a smaller subject: it appears briefly, and the book is not a financial guide.

faq.q: What does the book say about freedom in Christ and the presence of God?
faq.a: The second step, Set Yourself Free, is about identity in Christ, "secure, significant, and accepted," and the author says that on a flight home from India he committed to "passionately pursue the presence of God."

faq.q: What is the link to India and the Great Commission?
faq.a: The author has traveled to India over fifty times and writes that for over twenty years "God has had me staring at the 1.3 billion Indian Nationals who desperately need to know about Jesus." The book keeps the Great Commission in view.

faq.q: Does it speak of the joy of giving?
faq.a: The author wants readers to "exchange any sense of pressure and regret for genuine confidence and satisfaction," and says "The surprising thing is the more I give, the more I receive."

book.about: Do You Know? is a gentle, read-aloud picture book that introduces young children to who God is and how deeply He loves them. Written by Katherine Robinson and paired with full-page illustrations, it asks one simple question again and again, inviting little listeners to discover the truth for themselves. Page by page children learn that God is the creator of the heavens and the earth, that He was there in the beginning, and that even though we cannot see or touch Him, we can know Him and see the work of His hands. They hear that He is all holy, all sovereign and all mighty, and that He is also our heavenly Father who loves us and wants a relationship with each of us. The story explains, in words a child can follow, that everyone struggles with sin and needs help making godly choices, and that this is why God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, to save us. When Jesus returned to Heaven, He left us His Holy Spirit. Children are reminded that God made them with special care, on purpose and with purpose.

book.meta: A Journey Through Grief by Annie Brown: a short, compassionate guide for anyone who has lost someone, from a grief counselor who knows loss herself.
book.short: A grief counselor widowed in her mid-thirties walks grieving readers through the pain of loss in short lessons with key takeaways, rooted in Scripture and honest about the process.
book.about: A Journey Through Grief is a short, compassionate guide for anyone who has lost someone they love and wonders whether life can ever feel right again. Annie Brown writes from more than fifteen years of grief counseling and ministry and from almost thirty-four years of knowing grief personally. Arranged as lessons, each closing with key takeaways, the book describes what grief can look and feel like, the secondary losses that follow a death, the tangled emotions and the endless why and what-if questions, and the temptation to numb pain, which only prolongs the hurt. It addresses anticipated deaths after a long illness as well as sudden tragedies. Throughout, she says there is no right or wrong way to grieve, no schedule and no timeframe, that tears are therapeutic, and that time is not a healer but a great buffer. Rooted in Scripture, including Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8, it holds that faith sustains us through tragedy. Her message: grief is a process, life will get better, and there is life after death.
