what_makes.title: What makes this book for people walking through loss
paras: A short, compassionate guide arranged as six lessons, from an author whose own husband was killed when she was in her mid-thirties. It was not the ministry she would have chosen, she says, but "out of my loss, out of the deepest darkest season of my life, my ministry was born."
Five things set it apart:
list: It tells the truth about grief. There is "no right way or wrong way to grieve," no schedule and no timeframe, and the book says it plainly, and it explains secondary losses, such as the nightly phone call, the family connection and the dreams you had.

It keeps each lesson short. Every lesson ends with key takeaways you can reread when your mind cannot hold much.
It is rooted in Scripture without being heavy-handed. It draws on Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8 and says that "Faith does not isolate us from tragedy."
It is honest about helpers. It includes lessons gathered from people who lost someone and practical things to do and not do, and advice for friends who do not know what to say.

paras: In the introduction, the author recalls the weeks after her husband was killed, when she and her sixteen-year-old son moved in with her mother and she could not manage the house. One day she stepped on a glass plate hidden in the overgrown grass, and it broke. "Even after all these years, I remember looking down at the broken plate and saying aloud, 'You might as well break....everything else in my life is broken.'" Out of that sorrow, she says, she learned how to connect with hurting people.

Lesson 2 says "There is no right way or wrong way to grieve," and gives her own example. "I found comfort in sleeping with my husband's blue jeans." She brought five pairs to her mother's house, and her mother could tell what kind of day she had had by how many pairs she tucked around her at night. A physician who knew her situation told her she wasn't losing her mind and that the need would fade, and "you know, he was right." Her point: "it's OK to take comfort in different measures."

Lesson 5 explains that children do not grieve like adults. "Children move in and out of grief." The book gives an everyday picture: "One minute they are playing basketball with their buddies, the next, they are in their room sitting in the dark." It adds that children revisit grief at milestones such as graduation and weddings, and that parents should not grieve behind closed doors: "It's appropriate for your children to see you sad."

paras: The author's reason is simple. "Out of my sorrow, I learned how to connect with hurting people, how to minister to them, help them, and show them that although they cannot believe it now, in the middle of their darkest season, there IS life after death."

She wrote it as a manual for people in grief and for those who walk beside them, and her closing words say so: "God bless you in this ministry." Throughout, her message is that "Grief recovery is intentional and it takes work," and that "Faith does not isolate us from tragedy. What faith does, is sustain us through our loss."

faq.q: What is A Journey Through Grief about?
faq.a: A short guide for anyone who has lost someone they love, from a grief counselor who was widowed in her mid-thirties: lessons on what grief looks and feels like, each ending with key takeaways.

faq.q: What is the grieving process?
faq.a: The author says grief is a process, not an event. "Grief recovery is a process." She says it is something we get through, that there are good days and bad days, and that "Grief recovery is intentional and it takes work."

faq.q: Does it cover sudden loss?
faq.a: Yes. It addresses anticipated deaths after a long illness and sudden tragedies, including accidents, suicide and murder, and the guilt and "what if" questions that follow.

faq.q: Is it a grief support book for individuals or groups?
faq.a: Both. It is written for individuals in fresh loss and for friends and family, and its closing words are addressed to anyone "helping others walk their Journey Through Grief." The lessons suit a support group or class.

faq.q: Does it help with losing a spouse?
faq.a: Lesson 4 is entirely about it: loneliness, "firsts" without a spouse, fear of the future, and a caution about hasty decisions. The author lost her own husband in her mid-thirties.

faq.q: Does it speak to healing after loss?
faq.a: It says "Even though you cannot believe that you will EVER feel right again, you will," and that grief is a process you walk through, not one you live in. It does not promise a timetable: "There is no schedule to stick to, and there is no timeframe."

faq.q: Is it a Christian book, and is it therapy?
faq.a: It is rooted in Scripture, including Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8, and holds that faith sustains us through tragedy. It is one counselor's guide and personal account, not therapy or medical advice.

faq.q: What about loss to suicide?
faq.a: Lesson 3 speaks about suicide and the "haunting questions" that follow, in a short section. It is one part of a book on many kinds of loss, not a book devoted to suicide loss, and it is not a crisis resource.

audience.headline: Choose faith over fear, one short reading at a time.

Dr. James E. Kilgore draws on more than sixty-five years as a marriage and family therapist and pastor to offer fifty-nine short readings, each a power idea for turning difficulties into discoveries. If anxiety or low mood is affecting your daily life, please contact a physician or licensed mental health professional, and if you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to choose faith over fear
paras: A collection of brief readings from a pastor and family therapist, arranged in five sections and written to be read in a few minutes. The author is candid that anxiety is common: "Everyone who lives has some anxious moments." His answer is not a technique but a change of mind, and he takes Paul's call to be "transformed by the renewing of your mind" as the guide for the whole book.
Five things set it apart:
list: It comes from the counseling office. The author has listened to people struggle with anxiety for more than sixty-five years, and the readings carry stories from that work.
Each reading is short. Fifty-nine readings across five sections, from escaping anxiety and positive wholeness to seasonal lessons, family and marriage, and turning the mundane into the magnificent.

It names more than one cure and says where grace fits. The introduction notes that medicine is necessary for some, that groups can help belonging and that psychology offers guiding ideas, then says "Only the transformational power of grace can bring real change."
It takes Scripture seriously. Verses run through the readings, quoted mainly from the Holman Christian Standard Bible, with the Living Bible, The Message and the King James Version where marked.
It reaches past the individual. A full section on family and marriage, and readings on forgiveness, grief and listening, speak to the relationships where worry often lives.

paras: In the first reading, Delete Anxious Thinking, the author recalls that "Over forty years ago, a couple I had worked with in marriage counseling brought me a small gift." It was a framed plaque, and he has never forgotten its words. Fear, he says, "locks us in place and keeps the key to freedom," while "Faith is the key that unlocks the prison cell." He sets that beside David and Goliath: every one of us faces giants, and a small stone in a practiced sling is faith used with the skills we already have.

A short Christmas reading begins with a little boy who was just learning to read and saw the word backwards. He was trying to read Isaiah's "God with us!" The author thinks of the dogs he has known, including a friend's old dog that, nearly blind and deaf, crawled into bed at night and patted his owner on the leg. It was no longer a sign that he needed to go out. He "simply wanted to know that his master was still there." A country physician sitting at the bedside of a dying man tells him that "My dog doesn't know what else is in this room, but he knows I'm in here." The author's point for anxious hours is that "It doesn't really matter what's behind the door when we know Who is behind it."

stories.h2: How do you fill a hole in your heart?
paras: Coping with Grief at Christmas begins at a funeral, where a young woman looks up through tears and asks, "How do you fill a hole in your heart?" The author answers with permission and honesty. Start with "good grief," he says: "Don't deny yourself the right to feel anything, whatever it is." Feelings "are neither right nor wrong," tears "assure us that we are neither pain less nor dead," and out of opening ourselves to pain we often discover strength to help others.

author.bio: James E. Kilgore, Ph.D., has served as a marriage and family therapist and a pastor for more than sixty-five years. Across six decades in the counseling office he has listened to couples and individuals wrestle with anxiety, bitterness, grief and the search for identity, and has watched forgiveness open the way to happiness. He dedicates this book to his wife, Ruth, whose faith and love, he writes, have helped him escape anxiety for over sixty-five years.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says the book is "the result of discovering the ideas that transform our difficulties into discoveries." He wrote it because culture, medicine, groups and psychology each offer a partial cure, and he believes a deeper change is needed: "We can be transformed only by a powerful change within us."
His hope for the reader is stated in his last lines to them: "May these power ideas create a foundation for positive living for you!"

faq.q: What is Escaping Anxiety about?
faq.a: Short, practical readings from a marriage and family therapist and pastor, each a power idea for turning anxious thinking into a calmer, more hopeful life through faith and grace. The author says each is one way of discovering that difficulties can become discoveries.

faq.q: Is it a book of words of encouragement?
faq.a: It is a book of short faith-filled readings meant to encourage. One reading is titled Be an Encourager, and others speak to forgiveness, grief and hope. It is not a collection of quotations, and it is written as readings, not as daily affirmations.

faq.q: What does faith over fear mean in this book?
faq.a: The first reading says "I choose faith over fear!" and uses a plaque on the author's wall to make the point: when faith answers the door, fear is gone. It is also one of the book's recurring themes, from the reading on David and Goliath to Fear is Our Enemy.

faq.q: What does renewing your mind mean here?
faq.a: The author says he has been "captured by Paul's admonition" to be "transformed by the renewing of your mind," and that a transformed mind leads to a more satisfying day-by-day experience of life. The book's power ideas are meant to feed that renewal.

faq.q: Does it have Scripture about fear?
faq.a: Yes. Scripture runs through every reading. In Fear is Our Enemy, the author notes that so many angelic announcements in the Gospels begin "Do not be afraid" and writes that "God does NOT want you to live in fear."

faq.q: Does it say anything about the power of prayer?
faq.a: In a reading on prayer he describes a crusade he worked on in 1957 and calls the result "a marvelous example of the power of prayer." He also says prayer "includes speaking and listening," and that too often "all we do is talk."

faq.q: Does it help with forgiving others or yourself?
faq.a: It has a full reading on forgiveness, Forgiven to Forgive, built on the story of a father and two sons. It speaks mainly of forgiving others and of receiving forgiveness, not of a program for forgiving yourself.

faq.q: Is it medical advice or therapy?
faq.a: No. It is a collection of readings from one counselor's experience and from Scripture. If anxiety is affecting your health or daily life, please talk with a physician or licensed professional, and contact a crisis line if you are in danger.

book.short: A true story of a successful businessman who hid anxiety and old wounds behind a full calendar and a 7:30 AM screwdriver, and the hope that held when willpower could not.
book.about: It was spring of 2014 and John P. Boyle sat on a cafe patio in Las Vegas, hands shaking, ordering vodka with his English muffin. He was thirty-seven, his businesses were profitable and no one had voiced a concern. He was, in his own words, a highly functioning, ultra-successful alcoholic. Hope That Anchors the Soul is his honest account of what that life costs and of the hope that finally held when willpower could not. Across eight short chapters and an epilogue he walks through the turning points of his recovery: the 7:30 AM screwdriver, the night he chose treatment so his son would not grow up without a father, a friend's invitation at the lowest point of his life, the diagnosis he had been searching for, the sobering reality of the 90 percent who do not make it, when the pink clouds of early recovery hold, and a closing word about forgiveness. He blames no one for a single drink, and Scripture and the conviction that God was present run through the story. Each chapter closes with a direct, compassionate challenge to the reader.

sections.h2: For high-functioning drinkers who keep promising to stop
paras: If you know what it is to manage a day around the next drink, this book speaks your language. The author describes waking at night with anxiety that only a drink would quiet, knowing exactly what he was doing and doing it anyway, and tries more than once to quit on his own. He writes that "The thinking was sound. The follow-through was not." There is no lecture, only a man who has been there saying what it cost.

sections.h2: For people who love someone who looks fine from the outside
paras: Nobody voiced a concern for years. When he told his staff and his closest friends he was going to treatment, none of them were surprised, and that made it lonelier, not easier. If you have said nothing, or said something that was not heard, this book shows what it took for one person to listen. The turning point was a sister who was furious and then, the next morning, someone he could tell she had been right.

sections.h2: For anyone with old wounds and no name for them
paras: Many readers will see themselves in the chapter on the diagnosis. For twenty years he had fought what he calls an invisible enemy, and a name arrived late. He asks the physician whether this is the disorder soldiers get. The chapter does not tell you what you have. It shows that a name can change how a person understands the years behind them.

sections.h2: For readers in or seeking recovery, and for Christian readers
paras: Faith runs through every chapter and is never presented as a shortcut. He started with day four, a Bible he could not yet read, and sermons he could listen to from his bed. He writes that the grace of God was no pink cloud. He also writes that he told his sister he needed help and could not solve the problem alone.

audience.headline: A successful businessman hid behind a full calendar and a 7:30 AM screwdriver. This is what held when willpower could not.
audience.body: For high-functioning drinkers who keep promising themselves they will stop, for people who love someone whose life looks fine from the outside while it quietly falls apart, and for anyone who feels broken, forgotten or burdened by the past and wonders if healing is possible. John P. Boyle writes eight short chapters and an epilogue, and each chapter speaks straight to the reader. It is the true story of addiction, a late diagnosis, treatment and lasting recovery, grounded in faith. A note on subjects: this memoir is about alcohol addiction and recovery. It describes heavy drinking and withdrawal, anxiety, a diagnosis of Complex PTSD, relapse among other patients in treatment, and, in one chapter, a school visit where students describe family violence and one shows signs of self-harm. It is told without graphic detail. It is one man's story and not medical or mental health advice. If you are struggling with alcohol, trauma or thoughts of harming yourself, please contact a physician or licensed treatment professional, and in a crisis contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who are carrying a hidden struggle
paras: It does not start with a rock bottom that anyone could see. It starts with a man who looks fine to everyone, sitting on a cafe patio in Las Vegas with shaking hands, ordering vodka at breakfast.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins at 7:30 in the morning. It is the spring of 2014, the author is thirty-seven, his businesses are profitable, and he asks a server for a double screwdriver with his English muffin.
It takes no shortcuts about blame. He writes, "Every drink I ever took was my own decision," and he says that knowing what he was doing and doing it anyway is "not evidence of freedom."

It names the thing under the drinking. In treatment a physician tells him, "We've diagnosed you with Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder," and the author calls it the diagnosis he had been searching for.
It is honest about odds. The book cites a figure that 90 percent of the few who seek treatment are drinking again within four years, and then looks hard at what might hold.

It is built on a verse and an image. The verse is Hebrews 6:19, "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure." The image is a ship's anchor system that is a tiny fraction of the ship's weight and holds because of what it is set into.

paras: Chapter 1 opens at a small table on the patio of a cafe, under a replica Eiffel Tower. The morning is blue and the fountain across the street is running, and none of it reaches him. He has barely slept. His hands are shaking and his side hurts. He settles on coffee and an English muffin, and then adds one more item. "Can I get a double screwdriver?" The time is seven-thirty and he is thirty-seven years old.

Chapter 2 begins after a Las Vegas trip that ended with a failed attempt to quit cold turkey on the flight home. He spends a sleepless night weighing what treatment would cost him: his career, his reputation, and the privacy he had kept for years. Then one thought will not leave. He did not want his son to grow up without a father. In the morning he walks into his sister's office and tells her she had been right. He agreed to go. She helped him find a facility in Florida, and he left days before his son's birthday, feeling guilty and certain.

In Chapter 4 he lands in Florida sweating and shaking, and a driver offers to stop at a liquor store. He says no. During his intake exam a physician asks if he wants to add anything to his chart. "Write this down: I'm going to beat this." A second physician snarls a warning, "Be wary of pink clouds," and then tells him the symptoms are rooted in one disorder. The book gives the line that follows: "Addiction won't be the only hurdle you'll need to overcome." The diagnosis follows in the next lines.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author says it in the Introduction: "I wrote this book to help others. I believe God will use it for good."

He says who he is writing for: "If you've ever felt broken, forgotten, unloved, or burdened by things that happened to you, this book is for you." And he says what he hopes a reader will find: "By sharing this story, my story, I hope to help others find what I have found: that God loves them, that God was at work in their lives from their childhood, that He's been there all along, and that He'll be there if you call upon him."

faq.q: What is Hope That Anchors the Soul about?
faq.a: It is John P. Boyle's true story of addiction, alcoholism and lasting recovery. A successful businessman who was a highly functioning alcoholic tells what that life cost him, how he chose treatment so his son would not grow up without a father, and the hope that held when willpower could not.

faq.q: Is it a book for a high-functioning alcoholic?
faq.a: Yes. The author's own words are "highly functioning, ultra-successful alcoholic," and the book is written for people like him, who look fine and are not. It is also for those who love them. It is not a treatment guide, and it says that help from professionals mattered.

faq.q: Does it deal with Complex PTSD?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 4 covers the diagnosis he received in treatment, Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, which he describes as the single disorder beneath years of symptoms. It is his account of receiving the diagnosis, not a clinical explanation.

faq.q: What is the pink cloud in early recovery?
faq.a: The book explains that a pink cloud is a term for the false euphoria of early sobriety, and that other patients warned him his would crash. Chapter 6 argues that it is not the feeling that holds, but what the feeling is attached to. "If they wanted to call the grace of God a pink cloud, it was fine by me."

faq.q: Is it a book about trying to quit drinking?
faq.a: It is about what he tried and what finally held. He had tried to quit before and could not do it on his own, then chose treatment. The book does not give a program to follow. It tells a story, names what he learned, and encourages the reader to get help.

faq.q: What is the 154-ton anchor?
faq.a: It is the author's image from Chapter 7. A modern aircraft carrier's two anchors and their chains weigh 154 tons on a ship of 100,000 tons, a very small part of the whole. He writes that the question is not how much anchor you carry but "what your anchor is set into," and links it to the verse that gives the book its title.

faq.q: Is it a Christian book?
faq.a: Yes. It is short, candid and grounded in faith. Scripture runs through the story, along with the author's conviction that God was present even when he could not recognize Him, and a closing word on forgiveness.

book.about: Elisha Chowtapalli was born into an impoverished Dalit Christian family in a remote village in Andhra Pradesh, South India. His parents were illiterate quarry laborers earning about a dollar a day, the family lived in one mud room, and he studied at night under a street light because the home had no electricity until he was nineteen. He was the first in his family to go to school, carried there by the prayers and sacrifices of his grandmother. God's Dream is his own account of what God did with a life that began with nothing; he insists the book is about the One who called him. Across thirteen chapters he recounts growing up among the people India once called untouchable, his conversion, Bible college, answered prayer and a vision that took shape as LIGHT Home for orphaned children, an English medium school, tailoring training, feeding the hungry, church planting and a hospital for at-risk mothers. He writes honestly about betrayal, forgiveness and child begging and labor, and closes with the children's dreams and a sponsorship plan.

sections.h2: For readers who want to see God at work in a life that began with nothing
paras: The author says plainly that he had nothing special to offer: "I truly felt there was nothing special about it." His story is told so that you can see what God did with empty hands. One of its last lines puts it this way: "Empty hands don't matter so long as you have God's dream in your heart."

sections.h2: For supporters of missions and children's ministry in India
paras: If you give, pray for or visit ministries in India, this book is the story behind one of them. It shows how LIGHT Home began with one boy, how provision arrived week by week, and how the home grew into schools, feeding programs and a hospital project. Its last chapters invite readers to take part.

sections.h2: For readers who want to understand what education changes
paras: The conclusion argues that education is "one of the most powerful tools for driving positive change in society" and says that "only a few Dalit children are given the opportunity to be educated." The author writes from experience: he was the first in his family to go to school.

audience.headline: Born with nothing in an Indian village, he followed God's dream for orphaned children.
audience.body: For readers who want to see God at work in a life that began with nothing, supporters of missions and children's ministry in India who want the story behind LIGHT, and anyone who wants to understand what education changes for Dalit children. Elisha Chowtapalli tells it in his own words, across thirteen chapters, from a one-room mud home to a children's home, schools, a feeding program and a hospital for mothers. A note on subjects: this is a memoir of poverty and of caste discrimination in India, written by someone who lived it. It speaks of hunger, deaths in families, children who beg or work instead of going to school, and, briefly, of violence and abuse that children face. It is one man's account and testimony, not a history of the caste system, and it is told without graphic detail.

quote.text: Though I am part of this story, it's not really about me. Mainly, it is about the One who created me, who called me, who guided me, who gave me the vision, who entrusted me with work, and who is using me for His glory in India.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to see God work through an empty-handed life
paras: A memoir in thirteen chapters and a conclusion, by the founder and president of LIGHT Society. He was born into a Dalit Christian family in a remote village in Andhra Pradesh, South India, and he insists the book is about God, not himself.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with real poverty and does not soften it. His father was a quarry laborer paid about one U.S. dollar a day, the family lived in one room with a palm-leaf roof, and there was no electricity in the home until he was nineteen.

It explains what it means to be a Dalit from the inside. A full chapter, Untouchables of India, includes a section on the caste system, and the author says his friends urged him to write about his people so the rest of the world could understand.

It follows one calling to concrete results. From a prayer and a first child in 2006, the work grew into LIGHT Home, an English medium school, a tailoring training program, a feeding program for the elderly, a Bible school, church building and rural healthcare.
It is honest about betrayal and forgiveness. One short section tells of a painful email that questioned his integrity while he was traveling, and of how God helped him forgive.
It ends with the children. The conclusion speaks of children's dreams, of what education can change, and of a sponsorship plan for readers who want to help.

paras: In the section Our Humble Home, the author describes the one-room house his family lived in. "The roof was made of palm leaves and the walls made of mud, with no proper floor." When the rains came, the family moved everything to the one corner that still had a roof. There was no electricity. "I use to study under a street light pole at night where I could get some light to study." He remembers the group study with other children as fun at the time, and anger at his poverty came later. "We got electricity when I was nineteen years old."

stories.h2: One boy, three children, no stove
paras: LIGHT Home began on August 1, 2006, with one boy, and in a week there were three children and no regular support. He kept praying, and in the days that followed gifts arrived from friends in Australia. The early months were hard. "My mother used to cook food with firewood. It used to produce a lot of smoke but she never complained and didn't give up." For a time there was no running water. "My father took the responsibility of bringing water to us from the village tap and well." He carried it on his head, and the author writes that he did it "with great joy as it was part of God's dream."

stories.h2: A woman who had not eaten
paras: On January 1, 2008, the author was praying for the new year when a passage from Matthew 25 came to his mind. Then a woman who "hadn't eaten for the last few days" came to his office and begged for food, and she came again each day. He realized that this was how God was sharing His dream: to look after widows and old people who were dying for lack of food. Land was bought, a building went up, and in February 2009 the feeding of fifty widows and old people began. "Though we had a place to give food we didn't have the finances to feed them on a regular basis." He started anyway, "just looking to Jesus for guidance."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is stated at the start. "It is my sincere prayer and hope that God will speak to you through this book to be able to see the need and to take action together to show His love to the orphan, poor, and needy children of India."

He ends with the same invitation. "I do not know what God's dream is for your life, but I do know that He will speak to you and guide you in the right path." faq.q: What is God's Dream about?
faq.a: Elisha Chowtapalli's own account of a life that began in a poor Dalit village in South India and how, he says, God used it to build a children's home, schools, churches and a hospital.

faq.q: Does the book explain the caste system in India?
faq.a: It gives the author's view of it in a chapter on who the Dalits are, and says Dalits "are still in a hopeless situation with no hope for the future." It is a memoir, not a history of caste, and it tells one man's life among the people India once called untouchable.

faq.q: Where is it set? Is it about South India and Andhra Pradesh?
faq.a: Yes. The author was "born and brought up in an impoverished, Dalit Christian family in a remote village" in the state of Andhra Pradesh, South India, and has spent his life there.

faq.q: What is LIGHT?
faq.a: LIGHT Home cares for orphaned and needy children, alongside an English medium school, tailoring training, feeding the hungry, Light Bible School, church building and rural healthcare growing toward a hospital for at-risk mothers.

faq.q: Does it tell the story of feeding the hungry and of food for the poor?
faq.a: Yes. The section Feeding the Hungry tells how one passage in Matthew 25 and a hungry woman at his office became a feeding program for fifty widows and old people.

faq.q: Is it about the power of prayer?
faq.a: Prayer runs through it. When he wanted land for a garden beside the home and had no money, he writes, "My hands were empty, but I did know one thing – the power of prayer!" Gifts and land arrive again and again after he prays.

faq.q: What does it say about poverty in India?
faq.a: It speaks from the inside: a quarry wage of about a dollar a day, a family without electricity, children who beg or work instead of going to school. It is the author's testimony, not a statistical study.

faq.q: Can readers help?
faq.a: Yes. The book closes with a sponsorship plan and says "just the act of sharing God's plan with LIGHT Society will already be a huge blessing."

book.meta: Monday Morning Preacher by Roger Loomis: forty church issues from forty-three years of ministry, with biblical answers and a heart of worship chapter.
book.short: Forty-three years of pastoral ministry distilled into forty behind-the-scenes church issues, each paired with biblical principles, for pastors and church leaders.
book.about: Most American churches now gather fewer than one hundred people on a weekend, pastors are stepping down at a sobering rate, and many believers treat attendance as optional. Roger Loomis believes much of the answer, and much of the solution, can be found inside churches themselves. Drawing on forty-three years of pastoral ministry, Monday Morning Preacher identifies forty issues that arise in contemporary evangelical churches at some point and pairs each with biblical principles. Like Monday morning quarterbacks reviewing the game, pastors are invited to revisit Sunday on Monday: to celebrate their wins and spot the in-house issues that drain time, energy and attendance. Short chapters include Pastors Are People Too, Virtual Church, Pastor or Hireling?, No-Drama Zone, Church Hoppers, Peacemakers Not Peacekeepers, The Ten Suggestions, Bring Back Honor, The Heart of Worship and Money, Money, Money. Loomis shares his own missteps, including a season when he vented anger from the pulpit, and speaks directly to former pastors: you are not alone and not a second-class Christian.

faq.q: Does the book have a chapter on the heart of worship?
faq.a: Yes. The Heart of Worship is one of the book's chapters; the table of contents also lists chapters such as Pastors Are People Too, Virtual Church, Pastor or Hireling?, No-Drama Zone and Church Hoppers.

faq.q: Is Monday Morning Preacher a book about church leadership?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for pastors, church planters, staff, elders and lay leaders, and covers pastoral and church-leadership issues such as conflict, critics, unreasonable leaders and money, from the point of view of a fellow pastor.

faq.q: Why is it called Monday Morning Preacher?
faq.a: Like Monday morning quarterbacks who review the game, pastors are invited to revisit their Sunday service on Monday, to celebrate their wins and to identify the in-house issues that need wise and righteous attention.

faq.q: Is there anything in the book for former pastors?
faq.a: Yes. A closing word speaks to people now in the secular marketplace who fight rejection, anger or a sense of failure, telling them they are not alone, not second-class Christians, and that purposeful life and kingdom productivity exist beyond formal ministry.

book.bio: Roger Loomis has served in pastoral ministry for more than four decades, leading six churches in three states. He came to faith in 1970 and took Bible classes at Evangel University, though he credits much of his training to what he calls God's School of Hard Knocks. In 2012 he resigned from pastoral ministry to become a hospice chaplain, and in 2017 he and his wife planted a church in a village in rural northeastern Ohio. A self-described Christian pragmatist, he has a heart to help pastors succeed in their noble calling.

sections.h2: For pastors and church planters
paras: If you are tired, discouraged or just beginning, the author is blunt and kind: "I'm not a self-made martyr, just a fellow pastor who wants to see you and your church reach its highest potential." He also says that "Pulpit ministry counts for approximately 12 percent of their weekly schedule," and that too many of the remaining hours go to damage control.

sections.h2: For elders, staff and lay leaders
paras: Most of his observations relate to churches of fewer than two hundred in attendance, though he says "any leader can benefit from the information presented." Each chapter is short enough to read before a board or leadership meeting.

sections.h2: For believers who want a passion for the local church
paras: The author writes that "Christ-honoring local churches are God's gift to every community," and he asks the Holy Spirit to "rekindle a desire in the hearts of true Christians everywhere and renew their passion for God's house, the local church."

sections.h2: For former pastors
paras: If you left the pulpit and carry rejection or a sense of failure, the introduction speaks to you directly: "You are not a failure! A failure is defined as someone who, after getting knocked down, refused to get back up."

audience.headline: Forty things behind the back-door exits, from a pastor who has been there.
audience.body: For pastors, church planters, staff and elders, lay leaders in churches of every size, believers who want to rekindle a passion for the local church, and former pastors who carry rejection or a sense of failure. Roger Loomis draws on forty-three years of pastoral ministry to name forty issues that arise in contemporary evangelical churches and pairs each with biblical principles. A note on subjects: the book speaks plainly about church conflict, criticism, burnout, pastors who leave the ministry and people who leave a church angry, and it names hurts the author carried. It is one pastor's view from the pulpit, not counseling or a substitute for it. If a hard season is weighing on you, please talk with a trusted pastor, counselor or physician, and if you are in crisis, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for pastors and church leaders
paras: A book of short chapters on church leadership, each pairing a problem that surfaces in many congregations with biblical principles for answering it. The author calls himself a Christian pragmatist: "one who recognizes symptoms, then searches out root causes."
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts from the numbers and does not stop there. The introduction cites research that most American churches now have fewer than one hundred in weekend attendance and asks the hard question of why so many pastors are stepping down.
It looks inside the church first. The enemy and the culture are real, he writes, yet "the answers to much church decline, and solutions, can be found within churches themselves."

It is short on theory and long on cases. Chapters carry titles such as Pastors Are People Too, Virtual Church, Pastor or Hireling?, No-Drama Zone, Church Hoppers, Peacemakers, Not Peacekeepers, The Ten Suggestions, Bring Back Honor, The Heart of Worship and Money, Money, Money.
It is honest about the author's own missteps. He admits that in his third pastorate he used the pulpit to vent his anger, and he says so in order to warn others.
It speaks to people who have left the pulpit. A closing word tells former pastors, now in the secular marketplace, that they are not alone and not second-class Christians.

paras: In the first chapter of Part 1 the author recalls the people who loved his family unconditionally. "Most understood that we lived in a glass house but remained unwilling to throw rocks." He also turns the lens on himself. He tells pastors that other pastors usually do not want to hear their war stories, and admits he has rehearsed his own too often, "and for that, I'm embarrassed and sorry." His advice comes from an old saying: "Write your hurts in dust and your benefits in marble."

The Heart of Worship chapter begins with a song and a conviction that "worship is all about Jesus." He describes praise as "ascribing honor and worth to our King," and says that while praise extols the goodness of the Lord, "worship brings heaven to earth!" He asks worship leaders for humility above skill: "To me, the greatest attribute any worship leader can possess is humility." Skilled musicians can bring excellence to the platform, he says, but without yielded hearts a church will have "a performance but not a life-altering venue."

In Church Hoppers he gives a pastor's reason for staying planted, quoting Psalm 92:13 and asking, "What does it mean to be planted?" His answer is "to be faithful to one church." He tells of a man in his twenties who attended a different church almost every Sunday and eventually gave up on church altogether, and he writes that no one church has all the right answers: "while the Bible remains inerrant and infallible, we are not!"

author.bio: Roger Loomis has served in pastoral ministry for more than four decades, leading six churches in three states. He came to faith in 1970 and took Bible classes at Evangel University, though he credits much of his training to what he calls God's School of Hard Knocks. In 2012 he resigned from pastoral ministry to become a hospice chaplain, and in 2017 he and his wife planted a church in a village in rural northeastern Ohio. A self-described Christian pragmatist, he has a heart to help pastors succeed in their noble calling.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author gives his reason in a single line. "My sincere desire is that pastors everywhere learn from my mistakes and successes in order to sidestep any potential church setbacks."

He is candid about the exits he lived through. "My intention is to openly confront the reasons people left every church I served." And he sends the book out with a blessing for the people who lead local churches: "May you experience the favor of the Lord!"

faq.q: What is Monday Morning Preacher about?
faq.a: Roger Loomis's look at why people leave the local church and what pastors can do about it. Drawing on forty-three years of pastoral ministry, he identifies forty issues that arise in contemporary evangelical churches and pairs each with biblical principles.

faq.q: Is it a book about church leadership?
faq.a: Yes. It is written for pastors, church planters, staff, elders and lay leaders, and it covers conflict, critics, unreasonable leaders, offenses and money from the point of view of a fellow pastor.

faq.q: Does it have a chapter on the heart of worship?
faq.a: Yes. The Heart of Worship is one chapter. It is about the posture of worship leaders and of the church, not a manual for song selection, and it sits among chapters on conflict, honor and money.

faq.q: Is it about biblical preaching?
faq.a: Not as a how-to. The author calls for "balanced biblical preaching that draws from the entire canon of Scripture" in one chapter, and the introduction urges pastors to preach "the unsearchable riches of Christ" from the pulpit and deal with the other matters in private. It is a book about church life, not a preaching course.

faq.q: What does the book say about prophetic worship?
faq.a: In The Ten Suggestions, one suggestion says so-called prophetic worship songs are meant for private praise and not public worship, and he writes that the object of worship "is Jesus." It is his view as a pastor, offered as a point for leaders to weigh.

faq.q: Does it help with church growth?
faq.a: It addresses declining attendance directly, and says that "a lot of church problems develop from within." It is a book of observations and biblical principles, not a growth system or a set of metrics.

faq.q: Why is it called Monday Morning Preacher?
faq.a: Like Monday morning quarterbacks who review the game, pastors are invited to revisit their Sunday service on Monday, to celebrate their wins and to identify the in-house issues that need wise and righteous attention.

faq.q: Is there anything for former pastors?
faq.a: Yes. A closing word to people now in the secular marketplace who fight rejection, anger or a sense of failure tells them they are not alone, not second-class Christians, and that there is purposeful life and kingdom productivity beyond formal ministry.

sections.h2: Para papás, mamás y abuelos que quieren hablarles de Dios en español
paras: Si usted quiere que su hijo escuche el nombre de Dios en su idioma de casa, este libro le da las palabras. Son frases cortas, de las que se pueden leer de un tirón y repetir después. Cada página abre la conversación y deja que el niño pregunte.

sections.h2: Para maestros de escuela dominical y lectura en voz alta
paras: Las preguntas se prestan para detenerse. Después de cada una, el maestro puede mirar a los niños y preguntarles si ya lo sabían. El libro responde, pero también deja espacio para que el niño conteste con sus propias palabras, y al final lo invita a escribir su oración.

sections.h2: Para niños que empiezan a hablar con su Padre celestial
paras: El último tema del libro es la oración. Dice que se puede rezarle directamente a Dios, y la autora muestra cómo con una oración corta dirigida al Padre Celestial. Luego, en una página con espacio en blanco, le toca al niño.

audience.headline: Una conversación sencilla con los más pequeños: ¿Sabes quién es Dios? ¿Sabes que te conoce por nombre?
audience.body: Para papás, mamás y abuelos hispanohablantes que quieren presentar a Dios a sus hijos de 4 a 8 años, para maestros de escuela dominical y para las familias que leen juntas en voz alta. Katherine Robinson le habla a cada niño con preguntas cortas y versículos de la Biblia Reina-Valera Antigua: quién es Dios, quién es Cristo Jesús, quién es el Espíritu Santo, que Dios conoce a cada niño por nombre, que tiene un plan para su vida y que puede hablar con Él directamente. Una nota sobre los temas: es un libro ilustrado, tierno y breve. Habla del pecado y del perdón en palabras sencillas, sin imágenes duras. Es una introducción a la fe cristiana para niños, no un manual para padres ni un consejo profesional. Si su hijo tiene preguntas difíciles, hable con su pastor o con un maestro de confianza.

what_makes.title: Qué hace especial este libro para niños que empiezan a conocer a Dios
paras: Es un libro de treinta páginas construido sobre una sola pregunta que se repite, la que todo niño hace con los ojos muy abiertos: "¿Sabes...?". Cada página responde con una verdad sencilla y un pasaje de la Biblia.
Cinco cosas lo distinguen:
list: Empieza donde empieza la Biblia. La primera pregunta es "¿Sabes quién es Dios?", y la primera respuesta es el versículo de Génesis 1:1, que dice que Dios creó los cielos y la tierra.
Describe a Dios con cinco palabras que un niño puede repetir: "Santo, Soberano, Amoroso, Fiel y Todopoderoso."
Explica a Jesús como un acto de amor. El libro dice que Dios mandó a su único Hijo a salvarnos y que Jesús regresó al cielo para preparar un hogar para todos los que lo reciben.
Cada verdad trae su versículo. Hay pasajes de Génesis, Apocalipsis, Juan, Jeremías, Efesios y Romanos, todos de la Reina-Valera Antigua.
Termina con una invitación a orar. Primero la autora comparte la oración que hizo por quienes lean el libro, y después deja una página para que el niño escriba la suya.

paras: La primera página abre con la pregunta del título, y la respuesta llega enseguida: Dios creó los cielos y la tierra y todo lo que habita ahí. El libro dice que no lo puedes ver y no lo puedes tocar, pero que "Él se deja sentir a través del trabajo que hace en tu vida." Luego aparecen las cinco palabras que lo describen y el versículo de Apocalipsis 1:8, "Yo soy el Alfa y la Omega".

stories.h2: ¿Sabes que Dios te conoce por nombre?
paras: En la mitad del libro la pregunta se hace personal. El texto contesta que Dios creó a cada niño "con mucho cariño y atención especial", que lo hizo "a propósito y con propósito" y que le dio talentos para usarlos con la gente que lo rodea. El versículo que acompaña la página es Jeremías 1:5.

stories.h2: ¿Sabes que puedes rezarle directamente a Dios?
paras: El libro termina con una invitación. La autora escribe: "Mire aquí cómo recé por ti." Después viene su oración, dirigida al Padre Celestial, por los niños que escuchen el mensaje. En la página siguiente se lee "Ahora te toca a ti. Puedes empezar algo así..." con una línea que empieza "Querido Papá Dios," y el resto en blanco, para que el niño termine con sus palabras.

why.title: Por qué existe este libro
paras: Lo que el libro mismo dice está a la vista. En la dedicatoria, la autora escribe: "Gracias por confiar en mí." Y en su oración por los lectores pide: "Te pido que el mensaje en este libro llegue a los oídos y corazones de todos los que lo escuchen."

faq.q: ¿De qué trata ¿Sabes Qué??
faq.a: Es un libro en español para niños de 4 a 8 años que, con preguntas sencillas y versículos de la Reina-Valera Antigua, presenta a Dios, a Cristo Jesús y al Espíritu Santo, y anima a cada niño a escribir su propia oración.

faq.q: ¿Dice el libro que Dios es amor?
faq.a: Con esas palabras exactas, no: la frase "Dios es amor" no aparece. Pero el libro describe a Dios como Amoroso, lo llama un Padre celestial "que te ama y quiere relación contigo", y explica que enviar a su único Hijo fue "un acto de amor". Es el mismo mensaje en palabras más sencillas.

faq.q: ¿Quién es Dios, según el libro?
faq.a: Es la primera pregunta del libro. La respuesta es que Dios es el creador de los cielos, la tierra y todo lo que habita ahí. No se puede ver ni tocar, pero se deja sentir por el trabajo que hace en la vida de cada niño.

faq.q: ¿Qué nombres o cualidades de Dios menciona?
faq.a: Cinco: Santo, Soberano, Amoroso, Fiel y Todopoderoso. También cita Apocalipsis 1:8, donde Dios dice que es "el que es y que era y que ha de venir, el Todopoderoso".

faq.q: ¿Qué dice el libro sobre Jesús?
faq.a: Responde a la pregunta "¿Sabes quién es Cristo Jesús?" con una idea central: su perdón fue un acto de amor. Dios mandó a su único Hijo a salvarnos, y Jesús regresó al cielo para preparar un hogar para todos los que lo reciben. El versículo es Juan 14:6.

faq.q: ¿Habla del Padre, el Hijo y el Espíritu Santo?
faq.a: Sí, de una forma sencilla. El libro dice que Jesús dejó su Espíritu Santo y que "Juntos, Dios, Jesús y El Espíritu Santo, son tres en uno." Explica también que por medio del Espíritu Santo tenemos acceso a Jesús y, a través de Él, acceso a Dios.

faq.q: ¿Enseña a hablar con Dios?
faq.a: Sí. La última pregunta del libro es "¿Sabes que puedes rezarle directamente a Dios?" La autora comparte su propia oración y deja una página con la frase inicial "Querido Papá Dios," para que cada niño termine la suya.

faq.q: ¿Para qué edad es y qué Biblia usa?
faq.a: Para niños de 4 a 8 años, como lectura en voz alta en español. Usa la Reina-Valera Antigua, con un pasaje junto a cada verdad. Se puede leer en una sentada.

book.meta: Get to the Point by Kevin White: the point of life is living in God's presence, where every guidance and provision you need is found today.
book.short: A pastor dismissed from the church he planted finds the point on a ten-day trip to India: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God.
book.about: You can be a Christian, even a pastor, and still totally miss the point. Kevin White prayed the sinner's prayer at ten, answered God's call into ministry as a teenager, served three churches and helped plant a church in Cary, North Carolina, working out of control, driven by fear of failure, until the church dismissed him in its third year. He had reached the top of the ladder only to realize it was leaning against the wrong wall. Two months later a ten-day mission trip to India showed him the point. Get to the Point makes one case from Scripture: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God. Not religion, not ministry, not even salvation itself. In ten chapters, using real-life stories and a metaphor of climbing Mount Everest, he shows how the point determines your why, your what and your how, and closes with a call to return to the intimacy of Eden. The foreword is by Captain O. A. Fish, founder of South Mountain Christian Camp.
who_for: Every person who has prayed the sinner's prayer, including the newly baptized
Pastors and ministry leaders who want their congregations to get to the point
Couples preparing for marriage and parents teaching their children
Students, business leaders and anyone struggling with addiction
Longtime believers who sense they have been settling for less

faq.q: What is Get to the Point about?
faq.a: It makes one case from Scripture: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God, and in His presence you will find every guidance and provision you will ever need, today.

faq.q: What does the book say is the purpose of life?
faq.a: Living moment by moment in the presence of God. The book says everything in the Christian faith serves this one purpose, and that the point determines your why, your what and your how.

faq.q: Is Get to the Point a book for pastors and church leaders?
faq.a: Yes among others. Kevin White wrote it as a pastor who was dismissed from a church he helped plant, and it is written for pastors who want to help their congregations get to the point, as well as for longtime believers, parents, couples and students.

faq.q: Why does the book say salvation is not the point?
faq.a: One chapter, Why salvation is not the point, argues that salvation serves the point of living in God's presence. The author writes that God could have given you a gift, but He filled you with the Giver instead.

faq.q: What happened in India?
faq.a: Two months after the church dismissed him, a ten-day mission trip to India, more than 8,000 miles away, was where Kevin White says he first saw the point, taught by the pastors and churches there to pursue God's presence.

book.bio: Kevin White is a pastor who gave his life to Jesus at age ten and answered God's call into Christian ministry during his senior year of high school. After college he served at three churches before helping to start a new church in Cary, North Carolina. When that church dismissed him in its third year, a ten-day mission trip to India became the turning point of his life, as the pastors and churches there taught him to passionately pursue the presence of God. He has called Cary home for thirty years.

sections.h2: For every believer who has prayed the sinner's prayer
paras: The author says it plainly: "Every person who prays the sinner's prayer needs this book." If you thought you had done everything you needed to do to be a Christian and still feel a gap, this book is written to meet you there.

sections.h2: For pastors and ministry leaders
paras: The introduction says that "Congregations need pastors who help them get to the point." The author wrote as a pastor who served three churches and who was dismissed from a church he helped start, and who then spent years learning what the point looks like in ministry.

sections.h2: For couples, parents and students
paras: "Before anyone gets married, they should be required to read this book." The author also writes that "Parents should lead their children through the principles in this book" and says that when his own children were small, he and his wife taught them how to get to the point.

sections.h2: For anyone struggling with addiction or settling for less
paras: "Anyone struggling with any addiction needs to read this book," the author writes. The book is not a recovery program, and it makes no medical claims. It is an invitation to live in a presence that, he says, fills a person with the Giver and not only the gifts.

audience.headline: You can be a Christian, even a pastor, and still totally miss the point.
audience.body: For every believer who has prayed the sinner's prayer, pastors and ministry leaders who want their congregations to get to the point, couples preparing for marriage, parents, students and anyone who senses they have been settling for less. Kevin White makes one case from Scripture across ten chapters: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God, and in His presence you will find every guidance and provision you will ever need, today. A note on subjects: the author tells of his own season of burnout and fear of failure and of being dismissed from a church. It is one pastor's testimony and a teaching book, not counseling or medical advice, and it is told without graphic detail. If a hard season is weighing on you, please talk with a trusted pastor, counselor or physician, and if you are in crisis, contact your local emergency services or a crisis line.

quote.text: Every guidance and provision you will ever need can be found right now, today, in the presence of God.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want the point of life
paras: A short book with a single idea, argued from Scripture and from the author's own story. He prayed the sinner's prayer at ten, answered a call into ministry as a teenager, served three churches and helped plant a new church, and then discovered, he says, that "I had reached the top of the ladder only to realize it was leaning up against the wrong wall."
Five things set it apart:
list: It says the point plainly. "God's whole point is giving you His presence." Not religion, not ministry, not even salvation by itself, but living with God moment by moment.

It names what the point is not. A chapter titled Salvation Is Not the Point argues that salvation serves the point, and the author writes that "God could have given you a gift, but He filled you with the Giver instead."
It follows the point through your why, your what and your how. Three chapters show how the point shapes your reasons, your work and your methods.
It uses real-life stories and a climbing metaphor. The author weaves in the challenge of climbing Mount Everest, and the idea of a ladder leaning against the wrong wall.
It is built to be taught. It speaks to children, pastors, couples, students and people struggling with addiction, and it comes with a foreword by the founder of a Christian camp.

paras: In the introduction, the author tells his own story in short steps, each one ending in the same line. He prayed the sinner's prayer at ten and was baptized. He became a husband, a minister, a father and a pastor of three churches. "I was a husband, father, Christian-church-planting pastor, but I was totally missing the point." In the third year of a new church he helped plant, he was dismissed, devastated and crushed. "Two months later, God flew me over 8,000 miles away to India." A short ten-day mission trip became a life-changing experience, and "for the first time in my life, while in India, I saw the point. It was clear as day!"

stories.h2: Climbing Everest and the wrong ladder
paras: The book uses the world's highest mountain as a picture. It describes the danger of the climb: "At 29,035 feet, Everest's summit has approximately one-third the air pressure that exists at sea level." It also tells how George Mallory answered the question of why people climb it: "Because it's there!" Then it turns to a ladder. "We climb ladders called careers, marriage, family, parenting only to find ourselves at the bottom of ladders called divorce, empty nesting, and retirement." Its answer: "Once you climb to the top of the ladder of God's presence, you won't need to climb any other ladder for the rest of your life."

In the chapter on how the point determines your what, the author describes learning to rest. For years he went into God's presence looking for an assignment, afraid that if he were not always busy he would be lazy. What he sensed instead was a call to simply be there. "God was teaching me that we are human 'Beings,' not human 'Doings.' It was a real struggle for me." He writes that it took him years "to stop fighting God for His gifts instead of receiving Him as the gift."

author.bio: Kevin White is a pastor who gave his life to Jesus at age ten and answered God's call into Christian ministry during his senior year of high school. After college he served at three churches before helping to start a new church in Cary, North Carolina. When that church dismissed him in its third year, a ten-day mission trip to India became the turning point of his life, as the pastors and churches there taught him to passionately pursue the presence of God. He is the founder and executive director of Global Hope India and has called Cary home for thirty years.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in his dedication: "That's the whole point!" He dedicates the book "to every pastor, teacher, worship leader, and believer around the world who faithfully pursues God's presence first, and then helps others live, moment by moment, in the presence of God."

He wrote it because, he says, he wishes it had been handed to him years ago: "Let me apologize in advance that it has taken someone this long to help you understand God's whole point and how to get to it."

faq.q: What is Get to the Point about?
faq.a: It makes one case from Scripture: the whole point of life is to live moment by moment in the presence of God, and in His presence you will find every guidance and provision you will ever need, today.

faq.q: What does the book say is the purpose of life?
faq.a: Living moment by moment in the presence of God. The author writes that "Engaging God's presence in you is the whole point of life," and that the point determines your why, your what and your how.

faq.q: Is Get to the Point a book for pastors and church leaders?
faq.a: Yes, among others. Kevin White wrote it as a pastor who was dismissed from a church he helped plant, and it is written for pastors who want to help their congregations get to the point, as well as for believers, parents, couples and students.

faq.q: Is it about intimacy with God?
faq.a: In its own words, it is about connection and presence. Chapter 1 says Adam and Eve "shared an intimate connection with God," and the conclusion says the author wants "Eden back today." It does not teach a technique for intimacy, it argues for a daily life in His presence.

faq.q: Does it teach a prayer life or listening to God?
faq.a: Yes, within the larger argument. He writes that "Prayer is an ongoing conversation we have with God while living moment by moment in His presence," and suggests talking to God a third of the time and listening the other two thirds.

faq.q: Why does the book say salvation is not the point?
faq.a: One chapter argues that salvation serves the point of living in God's presence. The author writes that God "could have given you a gift, but He filled you with the Giver instead."

faq.q: What happened in India?
faq.a: Two months after the church dismissed him, a ten-day mission trip to India, more than 8,000 miles away, was where Kevin White says he first saw the point, taught by the pastors and churches there to pursue God's presence.

faq.q: Is it a recovery program or counseling?
faq.a: No. It is a teaching book from one pastor's life and from Scripture. If you are struggling with addiction or your mental health, please also seek help from a trained professional, and contact a crisis line if you are in danger.

He and his team spent months collecting every verse in which God promises to give something, and GIFTS publishes that list, quoting the New Living Translation. White notes three discoveries: there are more verses about God giving land than anything else, the word YOU runs all through God's gifts, and the word ASK appears alongside them. stories.h2: Hundreds of millions of dollars of need
paras: The introduction tells how the author had just finished writing his fifth book and, with his company not yet a year old and living month to month, felt called to leave it in God's hands and go to India and Nepal. "We had no choice but to depend on the GIFTS of God daily for our very survival." In the hills of Northeast India and Nepal, leaders kept asking him to pray over needs too big for any person to fund: land, buildings, healing, food for widows, homes for orphans. "Any human soul would be totally crushed and devastated if it weren't for the revelation: The Father's going to GIVE it!" It was also there that God told him, "You're thinking too small."

In the chapter on the word YOU, the author asks why God's promises so often say it. "All throughout the Bible, you will see God using the word YOU along with the word GIFTS. God says: I will GIVE to YOU." He counts how often the word appears in the English Standard Version and the New King James Version, and he writes: "YOU means you. Don't accept some words but reject others." The chapter pairs it with a promise from Jeremiah 29:12: "when you pray, I will listen."

In the conclusion, the author writes that "every day is Christmas." Jesus "isn't a tiny baby in a manger but has been imparted into every believer through the Holy Spirit," and "Emmanuel means God with us, but some days, we live like God came and then left." For him the greatest gift is God Himself, and he asks readers to live each day with the expectancy of a child at Christmas: "discovering God's GIFTS in every direction you turn."

On mission he speaks multiple times a day in the hills of Northeast India and Nepal, praying with leaders over human need. GIFTS grew from God's instruction to him to write down everything His Word promises to give.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason comes from what he saw on the trip. "I'm convinced God took me over 8,000 miles away to India and Nepal to rub my nose in all He desires to GIVE."

He offers the book as an invitation to "think differently, pray differently, live differently and GIVE differently." And he wants readers to know where the gift ends: "The GIFT is experiencing God. It's knowing His Word, heart, will, and way."

faq.q: What is GIFTS about?
faq.a: A book by Kevin White that publishes every Bible verse where God promises to give, organized into land, life, family, increase, empowerment and everything, with chapters on You, Ask and Depend.

faq.q: Is it about God's blessings?
faq.a: It is about God's promises to give, which the Bible often calls blessings. The exact words "God's blessings" are not the book's frame, and it is not a collection of blessings or benedictions. It is a list of promised gifts with the author's teaching on each.

faq.q: Does the book show God's goodness?
faq.a: It shows God as a good Giver. The author builds on Jesus' words, "So if you sinful people know how to GIVE good GIFTS to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father GIVE good GIFTS to those who ask him." The book does not argue about goodness in the abstract. It lets the verses speak.

faq.q: What does it say about grace?
faq.a: It says a gift is not earned: "A genuine GIFT is undeserved, without any strings attached, and without any manipulation of return." It is not a study of grace as a topic, but the idea runs through the chapters.

faq.q: Does it teach that God will give us whatever we ask?
faq.a: No. It says "This book doesn't revolve around the notions of entitlement or attempting to control God," and that sometimes "the true GIFT lies in trusting God enough to ask, regardless of whether we receive."

faq.q: Does it cover God as Father and God's provision?
faq.a: Yes. The refrain is "The Father's going to GIVE it!" and the chapters, especially Increase, gather the verses where God promises provision, from rain and harvest to "everything you need."

faq.q: Does it cover the promise of land to Abraham?
faq.a: Land is the category with the most verses, the author says, and the chapter quotes the land promises to Abraham and his descendants and says the promise rests on faith. It is not a study of the covenant, it is a list of what God promised to give.

faq.q: How is it different from a devotional?
faq.a: It is organized as a list of Scripture promises by category, not as daily readings, with the author's comments on each category.

book.about: Every parent hopes to raise children who grow into kind, responsible, faithful adults, yet many of the simple habits that once shaped families are quietly disappearing. In Potter's Child, Stephanie Mathews offers ten habits parents can instill in their children, drawn from Scripture, her own life as a mother and the stories of people who have crossed her path. She prayed for years for a baby; when her twins finally arrived they came early, and the first months brought a NICU stay. Each habit is taught through personal testimony and true stories rather than a checklist, including the power of prayer, making your bed and getting the job done, and pitching in with chores at home. The book carries an original poem by Susan Ann Samuel opening each chapter, illustrations by Kalpana Paranjothy and a foreword by Barbara Hemphill. The habits are not only for children: many parents find they need to build the same ones in themselves. At its heart is one conviction: we are clay in the Potter's hands, and so are our children.

faq.q: What is Potter's Child about?
faq.a: It is a parenting book by Stephanie Mathews that offers ten habits parents can instill in their children, drawn from Scripture, her own life as a mother and true stories from pastors, physicians and parents.

faq.q: Does the book cover the habit of making your bed?
faq.a: Yes. Making your bed and getting the job done is one of the everyday habits the book teaches, alongside pitching in with chores at home and building character that lasts.

faq.q: Is Potter's Child about the power of prayer?
faq.a: Prayer is central. The book tells honest stories of faith, struggle and answered prayer, and explores the power of prayer and how God uses His children to bless one another.

faq.q: Is it only for parents of young children?
faq.a: No. It is for parents of babies, toddlers and teenagers, for grandparents and caregivers, and for any adult who wants better habits, since the same practices grow out of what we experience.

faq.q: Why is it called Potter's Child?
faq.a: The author believes we are clay in the Potter's hands, and so are our children. She invites parents to let God shape their homes, teach by example and remind their children every day whose child they are.

paras: In the first chapter, the author tells of a childhood prayer. "Most children often pray for things they can touch: toys, bicycles, games and shoes. When I was a child, I prayed for food." Money was very tight, and her mother had nothing to feed the children but green lentils at every meal. She remembers praying, "Lord, can we have something to eat? Not green lentils, please!" She told a senior student at a school Christian group that she was hungry, and the next day the student and her father arrived with fruit and vegetables from their garden, enough for two weeks, and then with more provisions. "I remember that day as if it happened yesterday because it was an answered prayer." Years later she found the student and thanked her, and the woman did not even remember it.

Chapter 2 asks whether it even matters that you made your bed this morning. The author's answer is that "making the bed in the morning sets the tone that begins the day in order." She is not talking about comfort. "This habit is rather about making the bed; the task itself." The chapter quotes Admiral William McRaven: "If you want to change the world, start off by making your bed." And it adds that "If you can't do the little things right, you will never do the big things right."

In the last chapter the author remembers being a child raised by a single mother and working to help pay the bills. "I was constantly daydreaming because that was the only thing I could afford to do." She dreamed of flying on a plane, of performing on stage, of owning a business and of being an author. "Would it amaze you if I said that all my dreams came true?" Some plans didn't work out the way she imagined, she says, but when they became reality "they turned out better than what I dreamed for myself."

author.bio: Stephanie Mathews is a mother, wife and small business owner who believes she is a Potter's Child, clay shaped by God's hands. After years of prayer for a baby, she and her husband welcomed premature twins. Her early years included dance classes at The Temple of Fine Arts in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and the Jesus Calls messages she began hearing at age nine. She took part in the StartUp Launch Program at UTD and has an event space in Rockwall, Texas. Potter's Child is her first book.

book.about: Say Yes to God is Michael J. Gaetke's true story of answering God's calling, a Christian memoir of mission work from Costa Rica to Kenya and the birth of Africa Servant Leader. Gaetke was a painfully shy boy who once froze in front of his class; a Sunday School teacher gave him 2 Timothy 1:7 and that verse anchored his life. He went on to build a business career and share his faith with employees, subcontractors and clients. Across twenty-two short chapters in five parts the book covers foundations of faith, mission adventures, why he sold his Porsche and what church planting taught him about multiplication, everyday ministry (his first day in prison, a gas station, a movie theatre, home groups), and reflections on family, stewardship and mentoring, with lessons from Moses, Mary, David and Paul. His principle: when God provides an opportunity, start with yes until God gives you a compelling no.

stories.h2: A feast at three in the morning
paras: The introduction takes you to a remote village in Papua New Guinea, reached by four-wheeler and then a three or four hour walk through the jungle. The children had never seen a white man and ran away screaming. His friend's father announced a feast, and the guests bunked on bamboo mats over a dirt floor until it was ready. "So, at three in the morning, we all woke up excited for the feast." As the honored guest, he had to eat first. What struck him was the welcome: "He just wanted to give his best, no hesitation." He adds, "It was an adventure I wouldn't have had if I hadn't said 'yes' to God."

stories.h2: A shy boy and a verse
paras: Chapter 1 tells of the author as a child, around seven or eight, "painfully shy and unsure of myself," who had to give an oral book report in front of the whole class. When his turn came, he "froze, and couldn't say a single word." The sense of failure stuck, until a Sunday School teacher shared a verse, 2 Timothy 1:7: "For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." That verse, he writes, "became my life anchor," and although he is still a fairly reserved person, "I am no longer shy at all."

stories.h2: Lord, send me to the gas station
paras: In Chapter 12, the author is stopping for a quick meal on his way home when he sees a van with a sign that reads "Need Gas." He feels a nudge to go and talk to the couple, even though he is in a hurry to beat the traffic. He listens, feels some skepticism, and buys them gas, telling them he does it in the name of Jesus. They answer: "we're believers too, and we just asked God to send someone." His lesson is "I was the answer to their prayer." It is about being open to saying yes "in those unplanned moments, which might seem small to us but are huge to someone else."

A painfully shy child, he committed his life to Jesus at a junior high camp at thirteen. He built a business career, sharing his faith with employees, subcontractors and clients. Over the decades he has served in missions from Papua New Guinea and Costa Rica to Kenya, where he has taught and spoken with Africa Servant Leader, and he has been involved in church planting and prison ministry.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's reason is in his letter to the reader. "My goal in writing this book is to lead you to a deep understanding: your life has significance." He says he wrote it "because of God's profound love for you and His desire for you to experience real life."
His invitation is the title: "buckle up, say 'yes' to adventure, and get ready for the ride of a lifetime."

faq.q: What is Say Yes to God about?
faq.a: Michael J. Gaetke's true story of answering God's calling: a Christian memoir of mission work from Costa Rica to Kenya and the birth of Africa Servant Leader, told in twenty-two short chapters.

faq.q: Is it a book about calling?
faq.a: Yes, in the sense that matters to most readers. It is about answering what God puts in your path, from the jungle to the gas station. The author does not write about a calling as a career test. He writes about saying yes to opportunities and keeping the yes "until God gives you a compelling 'no.'"

faq.q: Is Say Yes to God a Christian memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It is a warm, humble Christian memoir about how saying yes to God carried an ordinary businessman into a life of service in his own city and around the world.

faq.q: What adventures are in the book?
faq.a: The book opens in the jungle of Papua New Guinea at a three-in-the-morning feast, and includes mission work in Costa Rica and Kenya, his first day in prison, church planting, and ministry in a gas station and a movie theatre.

faq.q: What does the book say about missions?
faq.a: That missions can be far or near. The author writes that he has served in Latin America, Papua New Guinea and Kenya, and that "mission work isn't always about crossing oceans; sometimes, it's about crossing the street."

faq.q: What is Africa Servant Leader?
faq.a: The ministry whose birth the book tells in Chapter 9. After a first trip to Kenya, the author and his friends founded a nonprofit to teach servant leadership there, and he has taught and spoken with Africa Servant Leader, including at a graduation dinner for people who completed its course.

faq.q: What does "start with yes" mean?
faq.a: The author's principle: when God provides an opportunity, start with yes until God gives you a compelling no. He says it is not about being someone special: "I'm no one special, but I serve a special God!"

faq.q: Is it only for people who travel?
faq.a: No. Some of the best stories are close to home. "You can be on adventures in faraway and exotic places, but sometimes your great adventures are right where you live."

book.short: Pastor and missions leader Kevin White shows how one word from God can redirect your life, through ten one-word chapters from ONE to WORD that begin at God's call in Deuteronomy 30 to choose life.
book.about: On a 1998 trip to India, after ten years in full-time ministry and eighty- and ninety-hour work weeks, Kevin White worshiped with believers in thatch-roof huts who had no bulletins, budgets or Bibles but an undeniable sense of God's presence. On the flight home he committed to pursue God's presence every day, and one word, PRESENCE, rewrote his philosophy of ministry. More words followed: COURAGE, CATCH, FILL. The book is built from ten words, ONE, DISASTER, PROSPERITY, COLLISION, VISION, VALUE, WHY, NOISE, EVERYONE and WORD, each chapter building on the last like colors on a paint-by-number canvas. It begins in Deuteronomy 30, where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and pleads with them to choose life. Readers learn to notice and act on single words from God, to ask Him for their own word, to tell the words that lead to disaster from the words that lead to prosperity, and to help others find theirs.
who_for: Believers who want to hear God clearly and act on a single word from Him
Pastors, church planters and ministry leaders who want God's direction for family, work and church
Readers who want to slow down and savor Scripture one word at a time
