faq.q: What is What's Your Word? about?
faq.a: It is a book by pastor and missions leader Kevin White on how one word from God can redirect a life. Ten one-word chapters, from ONE to WORD, begin at Deuteronomy 30 and teach readers to notice, ask for and act on their own word.

faq.q: What does choose life mean in this book?
faq.a: The book starts where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and asks them to choose life. The author shows that we choose our path one word at a time.

faq.q: Is this a book about prosperity?
faq.a: Two of the ten word chapters are DISASTER and PROSPERITY, framed by Deuteronomy 30. The book sets the words that lead to disaster against the words that lead to prosperity and says God pleads with us to choose life.

faq.q: What was the author's own word?
faq.a: On his first trip to India in 1998 the word was PRESENCE: he committed to pursue God's presence every day. Later words were COURAGE, CATCH and FILL.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Every believer who wants to hear God clearly, whether or not they already seek a word from God each year, and readers in family, business, church and nonprofit life.

book.bio: Kevin White has served in full-time Christian ministry as a pastor, entrepreneur and church planter and holds a degree in theology. A life-changing trip to India in 1998 led him to pursue God's presence every day. He is the founder and executive director of Global Hope India, which empowers pastors in India through short-term missions, and he has traveled to India over fifty times, taking 1,000 people on short-term mission trips. He is the author of Audacious Generosity and Get to the Point, and in November 2021 he launched Spirit Media to reinvent Christian publishing.

sections.h2: For believers who want to hear God clearly
paras: The author says that using thousands of words but never hearing God speak one specific word over your life "is a tragedy." He writes that God "has prepared a very specific word for your life," and he wants you to be "comfortable asking God for His word for your life."

sections.h2: For pastors, church planters and ministry leaders
paras: The author had served as a pastor for ten years before his trip to India. He writes that "The expectation I put on myself to do great things for God nearly killed me," and he offers this book as what he learned afterward: take action on a single word from God, and let Him carry the momentum.

sections.h2: For readers who want to savor Scripture
paras: "I know from personal experience that it is possible to rush through God's word and miss the importance of single words." He asks you to slow down and taste, as he had to learn to do at the table: "Taste and see that the Lord is good."

sections.h2: For anyone choosing a path
paras: The book is also for people at a turning point in family, work, church or a nonprofit. The author says the book will show you "how to choose God's path of prosperity for your life," and that "You choose your path."

audience.headline: God gives you a choice, and you answer with one word.
audience.body: For believers who want to hear God clearly and act on a single word from Him, pastors, church planters and ministry leaders who want God's direction for family, work and church, and readers who want to slow down and savor Scripture one word at a time. Kevin White starts in Deuteronomy 30, where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and builds ten chapters, from ONE to WORD, on the power of a single word. A note on subjects: the chapter on DISASTER speaks plainly about violence, including a news story of a fatal shooting and a suicide, and about suicide, gun violence and the toll of the pandemic. It is told without graphic detail. The book is a faith teaching from one pastor's experience, not counseling, medical advice or financial advice. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide or self-harm, please contact local emergency services or a crisis line right away, and talk with a physician or licensed professional.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to hear God's word for their life
paras: A book built on ten words, each chapter adding to the last, like colors on a paint-by-number canvas. The author is a pastor, church planter and missions leader who says one word from God rewrote his philosophy of ministry.
Five things set it apart:
list: It begins with a choice, and that choice is the frame for every chapter. "Choose life" is where Deuteronomy 30 leads, and the book comes back to it again and again.

It starts with the author's own word. On a flight home from India in 1998, after years of working sixty, eighty, even ninety hours a week, he committed to pursue God's presence every day. One word, PRESENCE, "rewrote my complete philosophy of ministry."
It teaches you to notice words in Scripture. "What's Your Word? will help you notice, appreciate, and activate single words."
It gives you ten words in order. ONE, DISASTER, PROSPERITY, COLLISION, VISION, VALUE, WHY, NOISE, EVERYONE and WORD, each chapter building on the one before.
It is for every setting. The author says you can use it "in your life, family, business, church, and nonprofit."

paras: Chapter 1 begins with a peppermint stick. When the author was in third grade, his teacher gave everyone one, and he asked for another. She took the one back, broke it in half and handed it to him. "Now you have two," she said. "I was disappointed because I knew I still had only ONE." The point, he says, is that in Deuteronomy 30 God gives His people one choice: "life or death." "You must pick ONE." And you answer with one word. "God isn't looking for a thick book back from you, a paragraph, or a sentence."

The introduction describes the author's first trip to India in 1998. He had been a pastor for ten years, a church planter who "knew all the church growth strategies," and his work week had grown to ninety hours. In India he saw churches in thatch roof huts "without bulletins, budgets, or Bibles" and "an undeniable sense of God's presence." On the plane home, "I committed to passionately pursue the presence of God every day for the rest of my life." God, he says, focused his attention on one word. "PRESENCE."

In the chapter on NOISE, the author tells how his first book came back with an unexpected invoice because the manuscript was 75,000 words and the package he had paid for allowed 50,000. Halfway through a book on clear messaging, he felt sick to his stomach. "In seven days, I trimmed the manuscript down from 75,000 words to 48,000 words." If it didn't help to clearly make his points, it had to go. "I eliminated the NOISE. The pit in my stomach was gone." His editor voided the invoice and agreed the book was so much better. He applies the lesson to listening to God: "Being bombarded with so many words that we can't hear even one single word from God for our lives is a contradiction."

faq.q: What is What's Your Word? about?
faq.a: A book by pastor and missions leader Kevin White on how one word from God can redirect a life. Ten one-word chapters, from ONE to WORD, begin at Deuteronomy 30 and teach readers to notice, ask for and act on their own word.

faq.q: What does choose life mean in this book?
faq.a: The book starts where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and asks them to choose life. The author writes that "We choose which path we take by which word we act on."

faq.q: What is the presence of God in this book?
faq.a: It is the author's own first word, from his 1998 trip to India. He writes that his word became PRESENCE and that he committed to pursue God's presence every day. The word is the book's opening story, and it connects to his earlier book, Get to the Point.

faq.q: Is it a book about prosperity?
faq.a: Two of the ten word chapters are DISASTER and PROSPERITY, framed by Deuteronomy 30. The author sets words that lead to disaster against words that lead to prosperity, and he says God pleads with us to choose life. It is not a study of prosperity in the Bible, and it does not promise wealth. He names what prosperity meant to him: "living on a budget, avoiding debt, having high quality relationships, saving and investing, or being outrageously generous."

faq.q: Is it about prayer for guidance?
faq.a: It teaches you to ask God for a word and to act on it, and the author writes that "God is responsible for the momentum" while "You are responsible to act on it." It is not a collection of prayers.

faq.q: Does it teach how to hear God's voice?
faq.a: In the sense that matters here: it teaches you to notice the single word God speaks over you and to take action on it. The book says "I encourage you to place the burden of identifying the word on God." It is not a technical manual on hearing God's voice.

faq.q: Is it about obeying God?
faq.a: Yes. The last chapter says you can choose your word and then "You choose whether to obey or not." Having knowledge of God's WORD without taking one single WORD from God, he writes, is "a contradiction to the very WORD of God."

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Every believer who wants to hear God clearly, whether or not they already ask God for a word each year, and readers in family, business, church and nonprofit life.

book.short: De un pueblo de Grecia a los supermercados de Estados Unidos: un cuento infantil basado en una historia real que enseña que la fe, la familia, el trabajo duro y la esperanza pueden sostener un gran sueño hasta hacerlo realidad.
book.about: De niña, en un pequeño pueblo de Grecia, a Voula le encanta cocinar, hornear e inventar recetas nuevas. Sueña con ser chef. Cuando otros se ríen y le dicen que su sueño es imposible, se promete seguir creyendo. Voula se muda con su familia a Estados Unidos en busca de un futuro mejor: no habla el idioma, no puede leer el nuevo alfabeto y la rechazan una y otra vez. Tiene que criar sola a sus tres hijos. Cuando una enfermedad grave la deja en coma, su familia se queda a su lado, orando y confiando en Dios. Voula se recupera y, con su familia, empieza a llevar su salsa tzatziki especial a los supermercados. Es un cuento infantil ilustrado, basado en una historia real, para leer en voz alta en familia, como cuento para dormir, en el aula, en bibliotecas e iglesias.

faq.q: ¿De qué trata El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula?
faq.a: Es un cuento infantil ilustrado, basado en una historia real, sobre una niña de un pequeño pueblo de Grecia que sueña con ser chef. Voula se muda a Estados Unidos, enfrenta puertas cerradas, cría sola a sus tres hijos y sigue creyendo hasta que su salsa tzatziki llega a los supermercados.

faq.q: ¿Es una historia real?
faq.a: Sí. El libro está basado en la historia real de la YiaYia Voula, la abuela griega del autor, Tyler Stavlas, quien creció ayudándola a preparar su famoso tzatziki.

faq.q: ¿Para qué edades es este libro?
faq.a: Para niños de 5 a 8 años, según la hoja de datos del libro.

faq.q: ¿Sirve como cuento infantil para dormir o para leer en voz alta?
faq.a: Sí. La descripción lo presenta como ideal para leer en voz alta en familia, como cuento para dormir, en el aula, en bibliotecas e iglesias.

faq.q: ¿Es un libro infantil en español sobre fe, inmigración y perseverancia?
faq.a: Sí. Trata de la perseverancia, la herencia griega, la inmigración, la fe cristiana, la familia, el emprendimiento y la esperanza, y es la edición en español del libro en inglés YiaYia Voula's Big Dream.

book.bio: Tyler Stavlas creció en la cocina con su YiaYia, su abuela griega, ayudándola a preparar su famoso tzatziki mientras escuchaba las historias de las dificultades que enfrentó y de cómo nunca se rindió. Escribió este libro para compartir su mensaje con los niños de todas partes: sueña en grande y no te rindas nunca. Hoy es director de producto de YiaYia Voula's Foods y fundó, con un amigo, Squeegee Clean NC. Da charlas sobre perseverancia, emprendimiento y liderazgo de servicio, y fundó Hunger for Change, una organización sin fines de lucro.

sections.h2: Para familias hispanohablantes que buscan cuentos infantiles con valores
paras: Si busca un libro en español que hable de esfuerzo, de familia y de fe sin dejar de ser un cuento, este lo hace. Es corto, tiene una heroína con nombre y apellido de familia, y cada página avanza un paso en su vida.

sections.h2: Para abuelos y nietos
paras: El libro nace en una cocina, entre un nieto y su abuela. Si usted es abuelo o abuela, puede leerlo y luego contarle a su nieto cómo fueron sus propios comienzos. La pregunta del final sirve para eso: ¿cuál es tu sueño?

sections.h2: Para maestros y bibliotecas
paras: Es una lectura breve para el aula, con una historia clara, un personaje que se levanta después de cada no y una pregunta para conversar. Según la nota del autor, se dona un ejemplar de este libro a cada biblioteca pública de su condado.

sections.h2: Para niños que tienen un sueño y miedo de que se rían
paras: La primera dificultad de Voula no es el idioma ni el dinero. Es que otros se ríen de ella siendo niña. El libro muestra qué hace: llora, se aleja, respira hondo y decide seguir. Es una escena corta que un niño reconoce de inmediato.

audience.headline: Una niña de un pueblo pequeño de Grecia sueña con ser chef, algunos se ríen de ella, y ella decide seguir creyendo.
audience.body: Para niños de 5 a 8 años, para las familias hispanohablantes que leen juntas en voz alta y para los abuelos que quieren contar de dónde vienen. Tyler Stavlas cuenta la historia real de su abuela griega, YiaYia Voula: una cocinera que llega a Estados Unidos sin hablar el idioma, que oye "no" en cada puerta, que cría sola a sus tres hijos y que confía en Dios hasta ver su tzatziki en los supermercados. Una nota sobre los temas: es un cuento ilustrado, breve y con final esperanzador. En él la protagonista pasa por la pobreza, por noches sin un lugar donde dormir, por tres trabajos a la vez y por una enfermedad grave que la deja en coma. El texto lo cuenta con sencillez, y su familia ora a su lado. Si un niño a su cargo ha vivido una pérdida o una enfermedad en casa, conviene leerlo juntos y dejarlo hacer preguntas.

what_makes.title: Qué hace especial este libro para niños que sueñan en grande
paras: Es la historia de una persona real, contada por su nieto. Desde la primera página, un niño sabe que Voula existió y que su sueño de ser chef se cumplió. Lo que cuenta el libro es todo lo que pasó entre una cosa y la otra.
Cinco cosas lo distinguen:
list: Es una historia real. El subtítulo lo dice: una historia real de no rendirse nunca. La primera página explica cómo se pronuncia YiaYia Voula (YA-ya VÚ-la) y que el nombre significa abuela Voula.

Muestra el "no" sin esconderlo. Cuando Voula pide trabajo en Estados Unidos, el libro dice que lo intentó "una y otra vez" y que en cada trabajo le decían que no, hasta que un hotel la contrata como chef.

Pone la fe en los momentos más difíciles. Voula ora al mudarse y la familia sigue orando mientras ella está enferma. El libro no presenta la fe como un adorno al final, sino como lo que sostiene a la familia.
Está escrito para leerse en voz alta. Las frases son cortas, y casi cada página cierra con una acción: ella respira hondo, estudia, prueba, sonríe, sigue.

Termina con dos preguntas para el niño: "¿Cuál es tu sueño?" y "¿Qué lograrás si nunca te rindes?". Después de ellas, el libro cuenta qué fue de la marca de la familia, YiaYia Voula's Foods, que según el libro nació en 2024 y hoy está en más de 300 tiendas.

details.Título: El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula
details.Subtítulo: Una historia real de no rendirse nunca

paras: Poco después del comienzo, algunos oyen a Voula decir que será chef y se ríen: ¿cómo va a ser una gran chef una niña pobre de un pueblo pequeño? A Voula le corren las lágrimas por la cara. Entonces se aleja, respira hondo y toma una decisión. Es la decisión que sostiene el resto del libro y la que el niño recordará.

stories.h2: Tres trabajos y un techo prestado
paras: Ya en Estados Unidos, Voula se queda sola a cargo de sus tres hijos. Acepta tres trabajos: en una pescadería muy fría, de mesera y de chef. El libro dice que su fe en Dios le daba fuerzas. Y dice algo más: "Algunas noches, Voula y sus hijos no tenían dónde dormir." Pero corazones generosos les abrieron sus puertas, y poco a poco la esperanza volvió a encontrarlos.

stories.h2: De la cama del hospital al supermercado
paras: Cuando Voula enferma gravemente, la familia no se aparta de su lado. Ahí viene la pregunta que el libro deja flotando: "¿Se recuperaría Voula? ¿Llegaría a ver su sueño hecho realidad?" Ella abre los ojos, los médicos quedan asombrados y la familia da gracias a Dios. Después empiezan a llevar su tzatziki a las tiendas. Unas dicen que no hay espacio. En una, el dueño lo prueba y exclama que esa salsa tiene que estar en todas sus tiendas.

author.bio: Tyler Stavlas creció en la cocina con su YiaYia, su abuela griega, ayudándola a preparar su famoso tzatziki y escuchando las historias de las dificultades que enfrentó y de cómo nunca se rindió. Hoy es director de producto de YiaYia Voula's Foods. Fundó Hunger for Change, una organización sin fines de lucro que, según el libro, ha donado 750 libras de tzatziki sin vender a bancos de alimentos locales. Da charlas sobre perseverancia, emprendimiento y liderazgo de servicio.

why.title: Por qué existe este libro
paras: La página sobre el autor lo dice con sus propias palabras: él "escribió este libro para compartir su mensaje con los niños de todas partes: sueña en grande y no te rindas nunca".

El libro cierra con el mismo mensaje, dicho de otra forma. "El mayor regalo de YiaYia Voula no fueron solo sus recetas: fue mostrarle al mundo que, aunque la vida sea difícil, puedes confiar en Dios, seguir intentándolo y nunca renunciar a tus sueños."

faq.q: ¿De qué trata El Gran Sueño de la YiaYia Voula?
faq.a: Es un cuento infantil ilustrado, basado en una historia real, sobre una niña de un pequeño pueblo de Grecia que sueña con ser chef. Voula se muda a Estados Unidos, enfrenta puertas cerradas, cría sola a sus tres hijos y sigue creyendo hasta que su salsa tzatziki llega a los supermercados.

faq.q: ¿Es uno de esos cuentos infantiles que son reales o inventados?
faq.a: Es real. Según el libro, cuenta la historia de la abuela griega del autor. La expresión cuento infantil es nuestra descripción: el texto de las páginas no la usa, y lo que se lee es una historia contada en tercera persona, en frases cortas.

faq.q: ¿Sirve como cuento infantil para dormir?
faq.a: Sí, para leer en voz alta en familia. Es corto y termina bien, con una pregunta tranquila para el niño. Pero tiene una escena de enfermedad grave y coma, así que algunos padres lo preferirán de día o junto a una conversación. La palabra dormir aparece una sola vez en el texto, y no es para describir el libro.

faq.q: ¿Es un libro infantil en español o una traducción?
faq.a: Es la edición en español de YiaYia Voula's Big Dream: A True Story of Never Giving Up. La traducción es de Spirit Media Publishing, según la página de datos del libro.

faq.q: ¿Es una historia de inmigrantes?
faq.a: Cuenta cómo la familia de Voula deja Grecia para mudarse a Estados Unidos con la esperanza de un hogar nuevo. La palabra inmigrante no aparece, pero el libro dice que no hablaba el idioma, que no podía leer el nuevo alfabeto y que cada día traía un nuevo desafío.

faq.q: ¿Enseña a superar obstáculos?
faq.a: Sí, mediante la historia y no con una lista de consejos. Voula supera el rechazo, la falta de dinero, el cansancio de tres trabajos y una enfermedad grave. La frase superar obstáculos no aparece en el libro, y su lección más clara es la que está en la última página.

faq.q: ¿Para qué edades es este libro?
faq.a: Para niños de 5 a 8 años, según los datos del libro. Un niño menor puede disfrutarlo en voz alta, y un lector de ocho años puede leerlo solo.

faq.q: ¿Habla de Dios?
faq.a: Sí. Voula ora al mudarse a Estados Unidos, su fe le da fuerzas durante los tres trabajos, y su familia ora y confía en Dios mientras ella está enferma. Es una historia cristiana contada sin sermones.

book.meta: Raised in a Barn is Van Eure's memoir of the Angus Barn in Raleigh: the family story and the 12 Commandments of hospitality her team works by.
book.short: Angus Barn leader Van Eure shares the funny, heartfelt stories and 12 Commandments behind one of the highest-grossing independent restaurants in the United States.
book.about: When a guest gets stuck in a bathroom stall, Van Eure tries to slide under the door to help, and gets stuck herself. That story opens Raised in a Barn, a warm, funny and candid memoir from the woman who has run the Angus Barn in Raleigh, North Carolina, for more than forty years. The Angus Barn opened in 1960, founded by Van's father and his partner Charles Winston, two former college football players with no restaurant training. Van tells the story of the Barn's founding, of the father she finally came to know and love, and of how she came to lead the family business. She then lays out the 12 Commandments every member of her team has worked by for over twenty years, resting on three values: Integrity, Teamwork and Excellence. The book has a foreword by Ken Blanchard and a scrapbook of photos.

sections.h2: For restaurant owners and managers
paras: If you run a place where people eat, you will recognize the nights the book describes: everything goes right, or everything falls apart in thirty seconds. Van says plainly that you will never reach perfection in this business, and that what counts is what you do next. Each commandment is a habit you can bring to a pre-shift meeting.

sections.h2: For business and team leaders in any field
paras: The stories happen in a steakhouse, and the lessons travel. Ask the person closest to the problem. Put "we" before "me." Keep learning. Take care of your people. The foreword calls the best leaders servant leaders, and the book gives examples from the kitchen, the front desk and the parking lot.

sections.h2: For readers who love a family memoir
paras: The first chapters are a family story: a founding in 1960, a grandfather who put his house up as collateral, a father who coached little league like it was the NFL and a daughter who finally got to know him. It is funny, and it is also tender.

sections.h2: For anyone in a job that serves others
paras: You do not need a dining room, a title or a uniform. Van writes that you just need the awareness to notice when someone needs help and the willingness to step in. That fits a nurse, a teacher, a pastor, a hotel clerk or a volunteer.

audience.headline: The woman who has led the Angus Barn since 1988 opens her memoir stuck under a bathroom stall door, and then shows how the restaurant is run.
audience.body: For restaurant owners and managers, business and team leaders in any field, anyone who serves people for a living, and readers who love a funny, honest family memoir with a Southern voice. Van Eure tells how two former college football players with no restaurant training opened a steakhouse on Highway 70 in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1960, and how the 12 Commandments her team has worked by for over twenty-five years grew out of real people and real mistakes. Ken Blanchard wrote the foreword. A note on subjects: the book is warm and funny, and it is written for adults. It uses some strong language, including a few swear words, and the opening story is a body-humor scene in a restroom. It also touches on a father and daughter who struggled to know each other, on the death of a parent, and on mental illness research. It is a memoir and a leadership book, not a how-to for starting a restaurant.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who serve people
paras: The book opens with a woman stuck in a restaurant restroom and the owner, Van, who tries to help and gets stuck herself. A server named Debbie arrives and slides under the door like it is no big deal. That story sets the tone for everything that follows: hospitality is not polish, it is what you do when things go wrong.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a memoir and a leadership book at once. The first three chapters tell the family story: the founding, a speech her father gave in 1986, and how she came to lead the Barn. Chapters 4 through 15 take one commandment at a time.
Every commandment comes with a story. The 20-Foot Rule is a seafood station and a cook named Raymond. The recovery chapter starts with a five-pound lobster that did not arrive.
It is built on three values: Integrity, Teamwork and Excellence. The book says these are woven into the commandments, the stories and the whole culture of the Barn.
It has real numbers. One location, more than five hundred people, over 350,000 guests every year, a wine cellar of more than 28,000 bottles, and the Wine Spectator Grand Award every year since 1989.
It ends with the Barn's own mission and with the people who carry it forward, with a scrapbook of family and team photos at the back.

paras: A guest with a hip replacement cannot get off the toilet in a restroom stall. Her granddaughter finds Van, who thinks she can slide under the door and help. She cannot. Now two people are stuck. Van calls for Debbie, a server who is "teeny," who slides under the door, helps the woman up, and then helps Van get free. The lesson she takes from it is not about restrooms:
"Sometimes you think you can fit, and sometimes you absolutely cannot."

In Chapter 7, Van is apologizing to a private group of twenty because the seafood did not come out with the rest of the entrees. The menu had grown over the years, but one person still handled all the seafood. She sits down with the sauté cook, the line cooks and the servers. They think they are in trouble.
"Nobody is in trouble. I need your help."

Raymond, one of the cooks, answers with an idea: a seafood station at each grill. It cost $60,000 and fixed the problem. The rule is not a measurement. It means asking the people who work closest to the problem. The chapter adds a story about consultant Tom Peters, who walked down four flights of stairs and asked one person why people did not stay.

stories.h2: The lobster that did not arrive
paras: Chapter 11 tells of a couple who had come to the Barn for thirty years to celebrate, always ordering a five-pound lobster a week ahead. One year the host got the date wrong. The kitchen plated five one-pound lobsters, and a chef explained exactly what happened. They were still unhappy, so Van learned they were leaving for Jamaica the next day. When they came back, the Barn met them at the airport and brought them straight to the restaurant, where a chef cooked the five-pound lobster. The book states the principle:
"What you do in the next thirty seconds is where character lives."

author.bio: Van Eure has led the Angus Barn in Raleigh since her father's death in 1988, and she began working there at the age of seven. After a mountain-climbing trip to Kenya, she stayed for five years teaching school before returning home. Under her leadership the Barn has become one of the highest-grossing independent restaurants in the United States, and the book says its turnover rate of 16.5 percent leads some to joke that "it's easier to get a job with the FBI." Her honors include the National Restaurant Association's Industry Legends Award in 2019, and she chairs Walk for Hope, which has helped raise more than $150 million for mental health research. Raised in a Barn is her first book.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The seed was planted years ago. In A Word of Thanks, Van writes that one of her managers, Jefferson Napier, "wrote a whole manuscript about our 12 Commandments" twenty-five years earlier, believing a book about the way they do things would help other businesses. She did not take it further then. Now she writes:
"I do see the value in sharing these basic principles."
The prologue says what she wants the reader to take from it:
"Most of what I know didn't come from a book. It came from moments like this."

faq.q: What is Raised in a Barn about?
faq.a: It is a memoir by Van Eure, who has led the Angus Barn restaurant in Raleigh, North Carolina, since 1988. She tells the story of the Barn's founding in 1960, the father she finally came to know and love, how she came to lead the family business, and the 12 Commandments her team works by.

faq.q: What is the Angus Barn?
faq.a: The Angus Barn opened in 1960 on Highway 70 in Raleigh and still operates from that one location. The book says it employs more than five hundred people, serves over 350,000 guests every year and has received the Wine Spectator Grand Award every year since 1989. It was founded by Van's father and his partner, Charles Winston, who had no restaurant training.

faq.q: What are the 12 Commandments of the Angus Barn?
faq.a: They are, in order: You Are Who You Hire; Serve Your Team; We Before Me; The 20-Foot Rule; Just OK Is Not OK; The Customer Is Always the Paying Customer; Serving Is a Privilege; It's Not the Mistake, It's the Recovery; Never Stop Learning; Be There; Keep the Main Thing the Main Thing; and Reach Out & Lift Up. Each has its own chapter, from 4 to 15.

faq.q: Is it one of the good memoir books for people in business?
faq.a: Yes. It is a personal story with a business lesson on nearly every page, and the author says plainly that these are "lessons carved out of real experience." The word memoir appears on the cover, and the stories come from family, staff and guests.

faq.q: Is it one of the hospitality books worth reading for restaurant owners?
faq.a: It is written by a restaurant leader for people who serve customers. Hospitality is the central idea, and the book defines it as what shows up when things go wrong. It is a book of stories and principles, not a start-up guide.

faq.q: Does it cover North Carolina history?
faq.a: Some of it. The opening chapters describe Raleigh and Highway 70 when it was a two-way country road, and Van's grandfather Thad Eure Sr. served as North Carolina's Secretary of State for fifty-three years. It is a family and restaurant story first, not a history of the state.

faq.q: Does the book cover customer service and servant leadership?
faq.a: Yes. Serve Your Team, Serving Is a Privilege and The Customer Is Always the Paying Customer each have a chapter. Ken Blanchard, who wrote the foreword, writes that the best leaders are servant leaders.

faq.q: Does the book contain strong language?
faq.a: A little. A few swear words appear in the stories, starting with the bathroom rescue, and the tone is conversational and humorous. Readers who prefer none should know that before they begin.

book.short: An ice age bedtime story: on the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy named Silas wakes in a prehistoric land and must find his way home with a little mouse and a gentle woolly mammoth. Ends with real woolly mammoth facts.
book.about: It is the night before Silas starts kindergarten, and he is excited but a little nervous. After pancakes, a bath, teeth and prayers with his mom, he drifts off to a story and, aw-da-sudden, finds himself in a land he does not know. He follows a little mouse he names Whiskers until he is lost, cold and hungry. In the morning the hill begins to shake: he has been sleeping on a real woolly mammoth. Woolly knows the land well and carries Silas on his head across a deep river. Kenneth W. sections.h2: For children about to start kindergarten
paras: If your child is counting down to the first day, this gives the nerves a story. Silas is brave in the end, but he is scared on the way, and he is lost for most of the book. The ending says he was not nervous anymore, and that he was excited for his new adventure.

sections.h2: For parents and grandparents who read at bedtime
paras: The book is built for the end of the day. It begins with pancakes and a bath, moves into prayers and a story, and finishes with a morning. The sentences are short, the pages turn quickly and the sound words, such as aw-da-sudden, are fun to say out loud.

sections.h2: For kids who love woolly mammoths
paras: The mammoth is not a side character. He has a name, a voice and a sense of humor, and he knows the land. At the back of the book, the facts page tells a young reader how tall mammoths stood, what the tusks were used for, and where scientists have found them frozen in ice and mud.

sections.h2: For families who want a gentle story about making friends
paras: Silas worries about friends at the start and finds two before breakfast. The book does not lecture. It shows a boy who follows a mouse, trusts a mammoth, and discovers that new friends can turn up in unexpected places.

audience.headline: On the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy falls asleep, wakes up in the Ice Age, and rides home on a woolly mammoth.
audience.body: For children ages 4 to 7 who are about to start school or worried about making new friends, and for the parents and grandparents who read to them at bedtime. Kenneth W. Pullin sends Silas from a dinner of pancakes in Niceville to a land of gray boulders, cave people, a little mouse named Whiskers and a gentle giant named Woolly, then back to a morning that is not quite what he expects. A note on subjects: this is a gentle bedtime adventure. Silas gets lost, cold and hungry, the sun starts to set, and a hill shakes and rises under him before he finds out it is a mammoth. A deep river has to be crossed. Everything ends warmly, with a hug, a dance and a surprise in a bookbag.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who are nervous about a first day
paras: Silas is excited about school, but he is also "a little nervous," and the book says why: he wonders if it will be hard to make new friends. Then the story gives that worry somewhere to go. By morning he is excited about kindergarten, and he has made a friend who is eleven feet tall.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts with a real bedtime. Dinner is pancakes, then a bath, teeth, prayers with his mom, and a story. The adventure begins as his eyes close.
It names the worry out loud. A child hears that being excited and being nervous can happen on the same night.
The hero is a mammoth. Woolly is big, strong and kind. He carries Silas across a deep river and bounces him back up his head whenever he slides.
The mouse stays with him. Whiskers curls up beside Silas when he is scared, and the book finishes with a question about him.
It ends with real mammoth facts. After The End, a full page tells how tall they stood, how much they weighed, how long their tusks grew and how scientists know how old they were.

paras: Silas wakes up alone. Whiskers is gone, and he feels alone and sad. Then the hill begins to shake. It rises so high he almost falls off, and he holds tight to some brush. When the hill starts to move forward with big back-and-forth motions, "like a boat on the ocean," he realizes the truth: he is on top of a real woolly mammoth. He screams so loud that Woolly stops moving, and Silas slides down his head to the ground.

Woolly knows where to go, but the river is deep, so Silas has to ride on his head. Whiskers squeaks and joins them. Woolly asks if Silas can swim, and Silas says he has a pool in his backyard where he practices all the time. The water is calm at first, then the current grows stronger. Woolly is so big that it does not bother him, and Whiskers stays right beside Silas the whole way.

Silas wakes up in his own bed, eats breakfast and hugs his mom and dad. As he heads out the door, something moves inside his bookbag. Out pops Whiskers. Then comes the last question of the book, left open for the child:
"Or was it really a dream?"

paras: The idea started with small things a child said. The dedication remembers a little girl running into a room to ask:

faq.q: What is Silas and Woolly the Mammoth about?
faq.a: It is a woolly mammoth bedtime story by Kenneth W. Pullin. On the night before kindergarten, a nervous boy named Silas falls asleep, wakes in a prehistoric land and finds his way home with a little mouse named Whiskers and a gentle woolly mammoth named Woolly. It ends with real woolly mammoth facts.

faq.q: Does it have real woolly mammoth facts?
faq.a: Yes. After The End, a full page called The Woolly Mammoth says they stood up to eleven feet tall and weighed over 6 tons, had two layers of fur, and were more closely related to Asian elephants than to African elephants. It also says remains have been found frozen in ice and mud in Siberia. The phrase woolly mammoth book is our description, and it fits a story with a facts page at the back.

faq.q: Is it a good bedtime story for kids?
faq.a: It is framed as one: Silas eats dinner, takes a bath, says his prayers and falls asleep while his mom reads. The adventure is his dream, and he wakes to his mom's voice. The word bedtime is not printed in the book, and the bedtime routine is what makes the framing.

faq.q: Is it a good read aloud for kindergarten?
faq.a: It is a short read-aloud with a kindergarten morning at the center. The word kindergarten appears twice, on the night before the first day and in the closing pages, when Silas says he is excited for his new adventure. It has 42 pages, short sentences and a question at the end for a class to talk about.

faq.q: Is it one of the books for 4 year olds?
faq.a: It is written for ages 4 to 7. Younger listeners will follow it by the pictures and the funny sound of aw-da-sudden, and early readers can try the short lines on their own.

faq.q: Is the book about starting school?
faq.a: It is about the night before. The school day itself is only the last page. What the book gives a child is a way to talk about the worry, with a boy who thinks he may not make friends and ends up with two.

faq.q: Is there prayer in it?
faq.a: Yes, briefly. Silas says his prayers before bed, and he says them with his mom. The story is not a Bible story, and it is a bedtime book that begins the way many family bedtimes do.

faq.q: Who wrote it?
faq.a: Kenneth W. Pullin, a lifelong Virginian who writes poems for the milestones in his children's lives. This story was inspired by his grandson Silas.

sections.h2: For young readers who love fairies and fantasy
paras: If your child likes tiny creatures with big feelings, this book is full of them. A fire fairy can make sparks with a snap of his fingers and hear fire crackle and breathe. A snail named Quickie speaks very slowly and gives very good advice. A tall, thin library grows out of the side of a pine tree. The Nymphs of Moonlight have hair the color of moonlight.

sections.h2: For families who read aloud together
paras: The chapters are short enough for a night at a time, and each one ends on a turn: a noise, an arrow, a prayer, a plan. The dialogue is simple and the story moves, so it is easy to read out loud. A family can read a chapter and then use the Discovery Questions for that chapter to talk about it.

sections.h2: For homeschool families and Sunday school teachers
paras: The Bible stories in the book are the ones children often hear in class: Jericho, the furnace and David. The fairies read them in a library and then act on them. The Discovery Questions point back to the Scripture, ask what children think, and end with a prompt such as when they were brave even though they were scared.

sections.h2: For children who get anxious
paras: When Dickens feels anxious, he has already tried reading, and it does not help. Quickie tells him to talk to God about it. The book does not promise that worry will vanish. It shows a child praying, listening and finding peace, and then doing the next thing.

audience.headline: When small elves carry off every parent, a timid fire fairy and his friends turn to prayer and Bible stories to find the courage to bring their families home.
audience.body: For young readers who love fairies and fantasy, and for the families, homeschool groups and Sunday school teachers who read aloud together. Jenna Kris sends Ember, Rose Petal and Raindrop from the land of Whimsy through Shadow Valley and the Hills of Moonlight to the mushroom libraries of the Questing Woods, where a fairy named Dickens helps them read about Jericho, the fiery furnace and David. A note on subjects: this is a gentle fantasy with some real fear in it. A dark valley with growls in the cracks, an ambush with flying arrows, parents carried away, a fire that spreads in a market, and a king who clings to his throne. The families are reunited at the end. The book presents prayer and trust in God as what gives its characters courage.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for children who feel afraid
paras: It begins with a family trip and ends with the story of why you can be brave when you are scared. In between, a fairy who freezes behind a tree becomes the one who runs toward the fire.
Five things set it apart:
list: The hero is the timid one. Ember hides when his family is taken. His hands go cold and spark-less. He is not told to be brave. He finds out what courage looks like.
Friends hold on. When the families are gone, Rose Petal takes one of Ember's hands and Raindrop takes the other, and the three of them "held on tight and didn't let go."
Prayer is part of the plot. Dickens feels anxious about his friends, prays, and is told to go to the Hills of Moonlight. Ember prays the night before the rescue.
Three Bible stories carry the plan. The fairies read about the Battle of Jericho, King Nebuchadnezzar with the fiery furnace, and King David, and they use what they learn.
It has a gentle structure for reading together. Fourteen short chapters, Discovery Questions grouped by chapter, and a glossary of fairy words at the back.

paras: Far away in the Questing Woods, a young fairy named Dickens cannot shake an anxious feeling about his friends. He asks Quickie what to do. Quickie says to talk to God. Dickens flies to the roof of a mushroom and prays:
"Dear God, I feel anxious and scared, and I don't know why."

He sits and listens. Nothing comes except a peace he did not have before. That night God tells him to go to the Hills of Moonlight, so he packs a bag, tells Quickie goodbye and flies out into the night.

stories.h2: The libraries of the Questing Woods
paras: In Chapter 6, the four fairies reach the Questing Woods and Quickie sends them to the war and battle library, number three. It is a tall, thin mushroom sticking out of the side of a pine tree, with a flat blue roof and a door carved with shields, swords and horses. They look for the Battle of Jericho, King Nebuchadnezzar and King David, and the first thing Ember says about Jericho is:
"A wall? How do you battle a wall?"
The next chapters are the answers: Joshua and the people march and obey, three men trust God in a furnace, and a shepherd boy faces a giant.

In Chapter 12, Ember stands in the Elf Kingdom market, bigger than he has ever been. His job is to distract the crowd. He juggles fireballs, then one wobbles and sails into a vendor's booth. The canvas catches and the fire spreads. His first instinct is to run.
"Ember didn't think. He ran toward the fire, not away from it."

He calls the flames back into the center of the square, away from an elf mother and her children, and puts them out with a clap of his hands. The book says what he knows about fire fairies: "Fire never hurts a fire fairy."

author.bio: Jenna Kris is a Christian fantasy author from Central Virginia who writes wholesome adventure stories filled with faith, courage and wonder. Inspired by her love of storytelling, she brings imaginative worlds to life through heartfelt characters and meaningful lessons. She enjoys baking gluten-free treats, gardening, crocheting and singing in her church choir. The book's author note calls her the author of The Fairies' Quest series. Her other book from Spirit Media Publishing is The Fairies Quest, and several characters, including Rose Petal, Raindrop, Dickens, Quickie and Indigo the blue bird, appear in both.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The dedication says it first:
"This book is dedicated to the Lord. May this book bring Him honor and glory."
The ending says what the author hopes a young reader carries away, after Ember thinks back over the Bible stories he has read:
"four little fairies got their families back because they listened to God and followed where He led, even when they were scared."

faq.q: What is The Fairies and the Elf King about?
faq.a: It is a Christian fantasy chapter book and family read-aloud by Jenna Kris, in fourteen chapters. A fire fairy named Ember and his friends, Rose Petal and Raindrop, are left alone when small elves carry off every parent. With help from a praying fairy named Dickens, they turn to Bible stories to find the courage to bring their families home.

faq.q: Is it a good book for bedtime stories?
faq.a: It is written in fourteen short chapters, so a family can read one a night. The word bedtime does not appear in the book, and the description fits how many families read it. There is some fear in the first half, and the ending is peaceful, with the families going home.

faq.q: Are there fairy books for kids with a Christian message?
faq.a: This is one. The main characters are fairies, and the faith is part of the plot: prayer, listening to God, and Bible stories as guides. The book is a fantasy first, and it does not use Scripture as a sermon.

faq.q: Is this a Christian fantasy book?
faq.a: Yes. The book is set in a made-up world of fairies, elves and Nymphs, and its Bible content is told inside the story. The Discovery Questions at the back include references such as Joshua 6, Daniel 3 and 1 Samuel 16:7.

faq.q: Is it one of the chapter books for 7 year olds?
faq.a: It is a 90-page chapter book with fourteen short chapters, for young readers who are ready for chapters, and younger children will enjoy it read aloud.

faq.q: Is the fiery furnace in the book?
faq.a: Yes. In Chapter 7, Of Kings and Statues, the fairies read about King Nebuchadnezzar's gold statue and the three men who would not bow. Ember thinks of that story again the night before the rescue and again when the elf king's golden statue is left standing in the empty square.

faq.q: Is it connected to The Fairies Quest?
faq.a: Some characters appear in both books, and the author note calls her the author of The Fairies' Quest series. Each book tells its own story.

faq.q: Where does the story take place?
faq.a: In the world of Fantasy, in the land of Whimsy and beyond: Shadow Valley, the Hills of Moonlight, the Questing Woods, Moonlit Ridge and the Elf Kingdom.

book.about: Many followers of Jesus spend more than two thousand hours a year at work, yet it is easy to compartmentalize faith. The Forgotten Witness is an invitation to reconnect professional life with spiritual calling. Justin Creasman writes as a working professional, not a pastor, drawing on his own years in the marketplace. Across twelve chapters and an epilogue, each built around one theme, the book explores what it means to practice the way of Jesus on the job: endurance, surrender, rhythm, boldness, community, workmanship, prayer, Scripture, service, witness, solitude and crafting a rule of life. sections.h2: For working Christians in any job
paras: If you have felt that your faith lives on Sunday and your career lives the rest of the week, this book names that split and offers small steps to close it. The preface pictures a face across a coffee counter, a coworker at the next desk, a law enforcement officer and a small business partner as the congregation you already have.

sections.h2: For business owners and marketplace leaders
paras: The book is written by someone who has managed people. It asks what you do when the trash is overflowing and you are hungry, how you treat people with less authority, and whether your team can tell what you believe from how you work. Two readers with marketplace leadership roles contributed advance praise.

sections.h2: For small groups and working lunch groups
paras: Each chapter ends with questions for discussion and a practice to try before you meet again. The author has led prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands at work, and the book is written with that kind of group in mind.

sections.h2: For readers who want to share their faith without being pushy
paras: The book keeps returning to consistency over volume. The epilogue says a Known Witness is not a louder Christian but a consistent one. Evangelism here means a prayer before a meeting, the truth told when a lie would be easier, and a trash bag changed when no one is watching.

audience.headline: Most of us spend 2,080 hours a year at work. This book asks whether the person three feet away knows you follow Jesus.
audience.body: For working Christians in any job: at a desk, behind a counter, on a shop floor, in a classroom or running a small business. Justin Creasman writes as a working professional, not a pastor, with twelve chapters and an epilogue on endurance, surrender, rhythm, boldness, community, workmanship, prayer, Scripture, service, witness, solitude and a rule of life, each with Reflection questions and a Reach Practice. A note on subjects: the book is a Christian living guide for adults. One chapter gives a general overview of religious protections under United States employment law, and it says plainly that this is general information and encouragement, not legal advice. The author also names stories from his own work without naming people or companies.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want to live their faith at work
paras: It starts with a plain question, "Do you feel purposeful in your career?", and it keeps its feet on the ground. The author says up front that this is not a book about perfect Christians at work. It is about a faith that shows up in the small things.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is written by a working professional. Justin Creasman has spent his career in the marketplace, starting prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands at work.
It gives each chapter two tools. At the end you find questions for Reflection and a Reach Practice, an action to try that week.

It talks about the law without pretending to be a lawyer. The chapter on laws and policies explains Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 in general terms, names its limits, and tells the reader to consult an attorney for their own situation.
It is honest that not everyone has the same freedom. The author's note acknowledges readers in places where speaking about faith costs far more.
It ends with a clear picture of the goal: moving from a Forgotten Witness, present and faithful but unknown, to a Known Witness of Jesus.

stories.h2: A semester at a fast-food restaurant
paras: In Chapter 1, the author tells how he entered college in 2007 meaning to become a neurosurgeon. Two years in, he burned out. He took a semester away to work at a fast-food restaurant, and he now calls that one of the best decisions of his life. It is the book's first lesson about endurance, and it comes with a line that fits any season:
"Your failures and miscalculations are building blocks for your future successes."
In Chapter 6, a shift has run long, the leftover food in the break room is calling, and the trash in the manufacturing area is overflowing. As a manager he could delegate. Instead he serves.
"I replaced the trash with a new bag and discarded the old one."
The food tastes the same fifteen minutes later, and another manager who saw it takes the same road next time. The chapter ties it to Mark 10:45.

stories.h2: What am I actually allowed to do here?
paras: Chapter 4 turns to a practical question that sits under every workplace witness:
"what am I actually allowed to do here?"

The author describes Title VII in general terms, names its limits, and stops to say it protects him in ways it will not protect every reader. What carries across every border, he writes, is how you work and how you treat people.

author.bio: Justin Creasman is a marketplace leader who has spent his career building formational communities in the workplace. Born and raised in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, he holds a bachelor's degree in biology from North Carolina Central University and is pursuing graduate studies with Antioch School. At work he has started prayer groups, Bible studies and discipleship bands, and he helped plant City Movement Church in the Raleigh-Durham area. His website is justincreasman.com.

faq.q: What is The Forgotten Witness about?
faq.a: It is a Christian living guide to faith at work. Justin Creasman, a working professional and not a pastor, invites readers to reconnect professional life with spiritual calling, to see the workplace as a mission field and to make room for the Holy Spirit to guide, convict and strengthen, across twelve chapters and an epilogue.

faq.q: What does the book say about the Holy Spirit?
faq.a: It treats the Holy Spirit as the guide of a believer's workday. The book asks readers to let the Holy Spirit examine their hearts, to listen for the Spirit's leading, and to speak up when the Spirit prompts. The term appears about thirty times across the book.

faq.q: Is it one of the good Christian living books for working people?
faq.a: It is written for people who spend most of their week at work. Its chapters are practices, such as prayer, Scripture, service and solitude, not theology lectures, and each ends with Reflection and a Reach Practice.

faq.q: Is it a Christian leadership book?
faq.a: It is a faith-at-work guide that includes leadership. The author writes as a manager who stopped to change a trash bag and as someone who started groups at work, and several stories come from his own time as a manager.

faq.q: What is marketplace ministry, and does the book teach it?
faq.a: Marketplace ministry is living out your calling inside a job, not only at church. The book calls it vocational ministry and says the workplace can be a mission field. Two readers who lead in the marketplace wrote the advance praise.

faq.q: Is it an evangelism book?
faq.a: It is about being a witness, not about giving a sales pitch. It says consistency, workmanship and compassion speak before you open your mouth. Evangelism appears a few times in the book, and the practices are quiet and daily.

faq.q: What does the book say about faith at work and the law?
faq.a: One chapter offers a general overview of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the religious protections it provides in the United States. It is general information and not legal advice, and it tells readers to consult an attorney licensed where they work.

faq.q: Can a small group use it?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter closes with Reflection questions and a Reach Practice, which makes the book suited to personal study, a working lunch group or a small band of believers.

faq.q: What is the Ultimate Book Marketing Guide about?
faq.a: It is a 120-page guide by Kevin White that teaches authors how to market a book, covering your brand, email list, launch team, web page, social media, the largest online bookstore, paid ads, reviews, awards, book clubs, podcasts and influencers.

faq.q: Is it a good book on book marketing for beginners?
faq.a: It is written for beginners and for authors with a book already out. The chapters are short, each one is built around a single tactic, and the introduction explains why most books go unfound. It is a practical overview, not a technical manual for every platform.

faq.q: Is it for self-published authors?
faq.a: Yes. The book is written for independent authors and for authors who have used a publisher. It lists the many tasks of publishing and selling a book and says one reason Spirit Media was created was to have a team that could help authors through them.

faq.q: Does it cover the largest online bookstore?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 9 says that bookstore is the number one seller of books in the world, and it names four strategies: a strong listing, fulfillment, protecting your work and paid ads. It also says the listing either sells or fails.

faq.q: Is it a Christian marketing book?
faq.a: It has a Christian perspective throughout, and Scripture supports its argument for taking a message to the nations. The tactics themselves, such as email, reviews, awards and podcasts, apply to any author.

faq.q: Can it help me get reviews, awards and podcast interviews?
faq.a: Chapters 11, 12 and 14 cover each of those. Chapter 11 explains why editorial and customer reviews matter and how a launch team can help, Chapter 12 offers a list of book award sites, and Chapter 14 shows how to prepare a portfolio, an offer and a vision to get booked as a podcast guest.

faq.q: Does the book guarantee my sales?
faq.a: The subtitle uses the word guaranteed, and the book prints its guarantee terms near the front. No book can promise a result for every author, so read the terms and follow the steps you can.

sections.h2: For authors with a book that is not selling
paras: If your book has been out for months with few sales, the first chapter is for you. It says a book is not set in stone and explains the changes that made a difference for one author: a new title built around what readers search for, a new description and bio, a table of contents and a fresh layout.

sections.h2: For authors who have not published yet
paras: The book says the best time for an author to take responsibility for marketing is while writing. If you are still writing, use the early chapters to plan your brand, your email list and your launch team before the release date.

sections.h2: For Christian and independent authors
paras: The guide is written for authors who feel a message from God for the nations. It reminds you that Psalm 96:3 says to publish His glorious deeds among the nations, and it argues for publishing in every format everywhere. It is also useful if your message is not religious, because the tactics are practical.

sections.h2: For authors who dislike marketing
paras: The conclusion speaks to authors who hate marketing and says plainly that some authors refuse to do it. It offers a choice: follow the steps yourself, or let a publisher partner with you. You decide which fits your book.

audience.headline: A publisher's 120-page playbook for the author whose book is published but not selling, with fifteen short chapters from the first launch team to the first podcast interview.
audience.body: For independent and Christian authors who have put a book on the market and are waiting for readers to find it, and for authors who have not published yet and want to plan their marketing before they do. Kevin White, CEO of Spirit Media, draws on the lessons his team learned marketing his own books and those of Spirit Media authors. He treats marketing as part of the writing calling, and the book is full of steps you can act on. A note on the book: it is a practical guide with a Christian perspective, and Scripture appears throughout. It is also written by a publishing company, and its conclusion invites authors to partner with Spirit Media. Many of the statistics in the book come from third-party sources named in the text and listed in its reference pages.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for authors who want their book to be found
paras: The book opens with a hard fact: it says most independent authors' books sell fewer than 250 copies, and it names a cause: they were put on the market but never marketed. Here is what sets the guide apart:
list: It starts before you publish. Chapter 1 says to begin marketing while you are still writing, and it also tells authors with a published book that a makeover is still possible.
It is built from real makeovers. The opening chapter walks through how a book was retitled, redescribed and relaid out to become easier to find.

It covers the whole map. Fifteen chapters run from your brand and email list to launch teams, a web page, social media, the world's largest online bookstore, paid ads, reviews, awards, book clubs, podcasts and influencers.
It is generous. One chapter treats giving books away as a marketing strategy, with the author's own numbers.
It is short enough to use. At 120 pages in a large 8.5 x 11 inch format, with callouts and numbered steps, it is meant to be worked through with a pen.

stories.h2: A book retitled around its reader
paras: In Chapter 1, an author with four decades as a minister and marriage counselor, who had published with a well-known Christian publisher in 2019, asks the team to look at a book that was not selling. They found three reasons: it was put on the market but never marketed, it was not published with marketing in mind, and the cover did a poor job of showing what was inside. They retitled it Escaping Anxiety, wrote a new description and author bio around the words readers search for, added a table of contents and gave it a fresh layout. The team's summary of the lesson:
"You need to do whatever it takes for your book to be found."

Chapter 3 tells how the author decided to give away thousands of copies in order to sell millions. In June 2021 he arranged a bulk print of 2,000 paperbacks and cut the cost from over eight dollars a copy to under three. He reports that more than $150,000 was donated to a missions charity by people who had received one or both of his books as thank-you gifts, and he draws one conclusion:
"One of the best marketing strategies in the world is generosity."

stories.h2: The surfer who is not ready
paras: In the introduction, the book compares publishing to surfing. The best surfers know that anyone wanting the next big wave must be ready, and that without preparation it ends in a wipeout. The book carries the picture into Chapter 6, where it says that authors who sell more than 250 books have carefully implemented smart strategies and that the first step is a launch team of people who volunteer to help promote the book.

He says one reason he created Spirit Media was to have a team that could help authors work through the many tasks of publishing and selling, and that he wants more authors to take their message to the nations. The conclusion closes on a promise he takes from his own experience:
"Where God guides He provides."

faq.q: What is the Ultimate Book Marketing Guide about?
faq.a: It is a 120-page guide by Kevin White that teaches authors how to market a book, covering your brand, email list, launch team, web page, social media, the largest online bookstore, paid ads, reviews, awards, book clubs, podcasts and influencers.

faq.q: Is it a good book on book marketing for beginners?
faq.a: It is written for beginners and for authors with a book already out. The chapters are short, each one is built around a single tactic, and the introduction explains why most books go unfound. It is a practical overview, not a technical manual for every platform.

faq.q: Is it for self-published authors?
faq.a: Yes. The book is written for independent authors and for authors who have used a publisher. It lists the many tasks of publishing and selling a book and says one reason Spirit Media was created was to have a team that could help authors through them.

faq.q: Does it cover the largest online bookstore?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 9 says that bookstore is the number one seller of books in the world, and it names four strategies: a strong listing, fulfillment, protecting your work and paid ads. It also says the listing either sells or fails.

faq.q: Is it a Christian marketing book?
faq.a: It has a Christian perspective throughout, and Scripture supports its argument for taking a message to the nations. The tactics themselves, such as email, reviews, awards and podcasts, apply to any author.

faq.q: Can it help me get reviews, awards and podcast interviews?
faq.a: Chapters 11, 12 and 14 cover each of those. Chapter 11 explains why editorial and customer reviews matter and how a launch team can help, Chapter 12 offers a list of book award sites, and Chapter 14 shows how to prepare a portfolio, an offer and a vision to get booked as a podcast guest.

faq.q: Does the book guarantee my sales?
faq.a: The subtitle uses the word guaranteed, and the book prints its guarantee terms near the front. No book can promise a result for every author, so read the terms and follow the steps you can.

audience.headline: A Christian Bible study workbook for believers who have been forgiven and still feel stuck, from a licensed counselor who joins God's Word with what research says about the mind and the body.
audience.body: For anyone who has come to God, received His forgiveness and still asks why they feel depressed, why they return to the things that hurt them, or whether the blood of Christ is enough for what they have done. Kami Tahyi, MS, LPCC, writes from the counseling office and the church pew. Mended is six short sessions of plain teaching, Scripture to write out and honest questions to answer, so you do the work of healing and not only the reading.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want healing they can work through
paras: Many books on emotional healing are read once and shelved. This one is designed to be written in, talked over in a small group and returned to. Here is what sets it apart:
list: It is a working book. Most sessions ask you to write out a verse, list your own thoughts or describe a time you felt something.

It joins faith and research. The author cites Paul Ekman's six basic emotions, the Centers for Disease Control research on adverse childhood experiences, and teachers such as David Seamands, Larry Crabb and Bessel van der Kolk, and she keeps each tied to Scripture.
It names the church's part. Session Two says the church can supply protective factors for people who were wounded, including caring adults, a sense of purpose and social connection.
It treats feelings as information. She says that feelings are not wrong, that we should avoid telling anyone not to feel a certain way, and that our thoughts shape what we feel.
It is built for groups. The back of the book has leader ideas, a set of group rules, and a questionnaire and a morning routine to use alongside the sessions.

paras: In Session Three, the author tells of a huge glass dome built in the desert in the early 1980s, with purified air and water, to see whether people, plants and animals could thrive. Everything did well except the trees, which fell over as they grew. Scientists realized the one thing they had forgotten was wind. The wind, she writes, makes roots grow deeper, and she asks the reader to share about a time when a struggle helped them grow stronger roots.
In Session Two, the author says many people she has worked with know that God has forgiven them and still cannot forgive themselves. She calls that a theology we create and asks one direct question:
"Is the blood of Christ enough for your sins?"

In Session Five the author draws on a film about happiness that she says she has watched with clients 75 times or more. Its first principle is that happiness is not based on circumstances. She notes that the researchers do not share her faith but have some good things to say, and she pairs the principle with Paul's lines on contentment from Philippians 4.

author.bio: Kami Tahyi, MS, LPCC, is a licensed counselor. After painful life experiences, she found a church home at a church plant's first service on Easter Sunday 2009. In the years since, she has attended college, become a licensed counselor and worked as a counselor at a women's residential treatment facility. She writes that the more she studies, the more she knows God's Word has all the answers, and that her education, license and position let her bring together God's natural healing and what research has uncovered.

paras: This is the Special Edition for First Responders of a book about time. The words inside are the same as in the Work Staff edition, and the book itself is general. list: It is short enough for a break room. At 60 pages in a 4 x 6 inch size, it fits a duty bag or a pocket, and each chapter is a few pages.

paras: In the first chapter the author points to Isaiah 38, where God turned the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz backward ten degrees because Hezekiah asked. He notes that there are several theories about how it happened, and warns that attempting to explain it can lead some to doubt God. He puts it simply, that faith requires no explanation, and then asks the reader whether they have faith that God can help with their time, even in supernatural ways.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
"My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success."
It is short on purpose, so that a reader finishes it, answers the questions and starts to make changes.

intro: The book begins by setting the facts of time next to the God who made it:
excerpt: Every movement of the second hand on the clock brings us closer to eternity.
The top priority in our time management to-do list must be to give Him time each day.
Are our schedules so tight that we cannot stop for a divine appointment?
Unlike wasted money that may be replaceable, we only have one shot at time.
Helping people by giving them your time is the best gift you can give.

paras: In the first chapter the author points to Isaiah 38, where God turned the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz backward ten degrees because Hezekiah asked. He notes that there are several theories about how it happened, and warns that attempting to explain it can lead some to doubt God. He puts it simply, that faith requires no explanation, and then asks the reader whether they have faith that God can help with their time, even in supernatural ways.

In Gifts of Time, the author looks at Jesus stopping on the way to Jerusalem to bless children, and at Cornelius, who did not check his schedule or put off sending for Peter. He says God speaks for one of two reasons, to make us a blessing to someone or to give us a blessing, and he wonders whether our schedules are so tight that we would miss it.
In Proper Investment of Time, he asks whether you are investing your time in the right people, and gives three steps. The first is to acknowledge that time is limited:
"Acknowledge that not only your money and energy, but also your time is a finite resource."

The second is to become aware of where it goes, since, as he puts it, your calendar will reveal the truth. The third is to change what needs to change, including activities that are unproductive or unhealthy.

author.bio: Daniel W. Evans is a Christian author who says that he has traveled through the states as an evangelist and listened to many pastors talk about church growth. In Your Time he writes from that experience and from his home church in Durham, North Carolina, where he counted how many members give their time as volunteers and found the figure to be 36 percent. He uses Scripture and personal observation to urge readers to put God first and to steward every hour well. The back of the book describes two other offerings from him: a one-day process in five steps, and A Commitment to Unleash Your Leader Potential, a program for the leader in each of us.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author's stated hope is simple. He wants you to see that your time is precious, that no one can replace it, and that God belongs at the top of the list. He puts it as a prayer:
"My prayer is that this booklet will help you recognize and realize that you are a potential success."
It is short on purpose, so that a reader finishes it, answers the questions and starts to make changes.

faq.q: What is the Special Edition for Work Staff?
faq.a: It is Your Time: The Greatest Gift You Receive and Give, by Daniel W. Evans, with a cover and edition name made for staff at work. The text inside is the same as in the Special Edition for First Responders.

faq.q: Is the content about the workplace?
faq.a: Only in part. The book is a general Christian look at time, priorities and giving, with a few pages on employees, leaders and business owners. The edition name tells you who the cover was prepared for.

faq.q: What is the book about?
faq.a: Time as a gift from God that we cannot control, the order of our priorities, giving time to others and investing it well.

faq.q: Which Bible translations does it use?
faq.a: The copyright page lists the NIV and the Amplified Bible, and the text also cites the AMPC. The author capitalizes He, His and Him when referring to God, Jesus and the Holy Spirit.

faq.q: How long is it?
faq.a: It is a 60-page, 4 x 6 inch paperback, a booklet that can be read in an evening.

faq.q: Does it have questions to answer?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter ends with a Take a Moment to Focus question and space to write, such as Is God included in your daily routines of managing your schedules?

faq.q: Does it include a prayer?
faq.a: Yes. Setting Your Time Straight invites you to pray a printed prayer aloud, asking God's forgiveness for wasted time and help to invest it in Him and in others.

faq.q: What is Pure and Simple?
faq.a: It is a 74-page book of 31 stories about worship by children and teenagers ages 6 to 16, each with a reflection and a question for people who plan worship.

faq.q: Is it a children's book?
faq.a: It looks like one, and children can read it, but the introduction says it is not. It is written by children for the benefit of those who design and lead worship.

faq.q: Who wrote the stories?
faq.a: Young people ages 6 to 16 wrote and drew them as part of the "Listen to the Kids!" storytelling project. They are printed in the children's own handwriting, spelling and drawings.

faq.q: What does each story follow?
faq.a: A story map with three points: a possibility, a hurdle and a discovery. The reflection and question come after.

faq.q: Which kinds of churches is it for?
faq.a: The book does not say which churches the children attend. Their stories mention spirituals, the Bible, singing, silent prayer, kneeling, dancing, a children's play on Pilgrim's Progress and a church camp, and each reflection asks leaders to adapt what they take from it.

faq.q: Can a small group or a worship team use it?
faq.a: Yes. The introduction says the questions are written to launch a conversation about how a service, or worship outside of church, might look.

sections.h2: For children's ministry leaders, parents and grandparents
paras: The stories show what children actually notice in a service. If you have wondered why a child fidgets, dances, goes quiet or asks about a word in a song, there is likely a story here that sounds like them.

sections.h2: For small groups and church staff
paras: Each story and reflection is short enough to read one at a time. The reflections can open a discussion about distraction, belonging, music, prayer or the Bible, and the introduction says the stories do not dismantle time-tested patterns of worship but inspire additional practices that seek to revitalize it.

audience.headline: Thirty-one young worshipers say what gets in the way of meeting God, and what helped them find Him anyway.
audience.body: For pastors, worship leaders, parents and anyone who plans or sits through a service. Pure and Simple: Advice on Worship from Young People gathers the handwritten stories of children and teenagers, ages 6 to 16, each paired with a short reflection and one question to bring back to your own church. As the introduction puts it, "This may look like a children's book, but it is not."

what_makes.title: What makes this book for people who want worship that welcomes every age
paras: Most books about worship are written by adults for adults. This one lets the children speak first. Here is what sets it apart:
list: The stories are in the young people's own words and drawings. Each one is a handwritten, illustrated storyboard that follows three points: a possibility, a hurdle and a discovery.

The hurdles are real and familiar. Boredom, distraction, a noisy home, sore feet, a voice that feels too small and kids who give funny looks all show up, and so do the ways the young storytellers found to press on.
Every story has a reflection and a question. A short note draws out what the story teaches, and each ends with a question for the people who design worship to take back to their own congregation.

It covers a wide range of ages. The storytellers are 6 to 16 years old, and their stories reach from a six-year-old who felt happy singing with the music to a sixteen-year-old who chose to bow down when the songs pushed feelings.
It makes no demands on you. The introduction says the stories are not strategies for radical practices but keys that can open doors, when we are willing to look at our habits with fresh eyes.

stories.h2: A lantern going up to God
paras: A ten-year-old thinks of prayers as lanterns rising to God. She says that YouTube and other media are addicting and keep her from worshiping, and that she feels God's comforting presence when she prays. The reflection compares her lanterns to incense in ancient worship, and notes that returning to prayer breaks through whatever stands in the way.

A sixteen-year-old goes into worship hoping to praise God for His glory and faithfulness. The songs seem to push him toward his feelings, so he ignores them and chooses to bow down in reverence. The reflection says worship includes the whole person, and that choosing to worship can set us free from our worries.
A twelve-year-old hoped to sing to the Lord but did not like the sound of their own voice.
The reflection says that God receives worship from any voice that speaks or sings His praise, and that there is more to worship than singing songs.
