sections.h2: For readers who have moved a lot and wonder where they belong
paras: The author moved six times in a year as a child. She says that for a long time she looked into other people's windows and fell into unhealthy relationships, searching for home. If that sounds like you, her story will feel familiar.

sections.h2: For people who have lost a home, a country or someone they love
paras: She writes about ruins, shelling and people fighting over a loaf of bread, and about the grief that follows. She asks hard questions of God and does not hurry the answer. She is clear that she is one of millions who lost a physical home in 2022.

sections.h2: For readers who think in pictures and prayer
paras: The book is made of visions, colors and rooms, and it asks you to imagine along with her. It may suit someone who prays with their eyes closed, or who keeps a journal, or who simply wants a slow book with room to think.

sections.h2: For small groups, counselors and coaches
paras: Each chapter closes with questions that can be answered alone or together. The author is herself a coach who helps people find joy in their work and life, and she invites readers to send their stories to her website.

audience.headline: A spiritual memoir told as a walk through the rooms of a heavenly house, asking where home really is when you have lost the one you had.
audience.body: For readers who have been searching for a place to belong. Aleksa Aishpur grew up in Ukraine in the lawless years after the Soviet Union fell apart, moved from house to house as a child, and did not know what it was to call a place home until she was thirty. Home pairs the visions she believes came from God with Scripture and with questions for you to answer, and it asks whether home might be something you carry inside.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who feel they have no place of their own
paras: Most books about belonging tell you how to find a house or a community. This one starts from the other direction. It is short, quiet and visual, and it invites you to write the ending yourself. Here is what sets it apart:
list: It is told as a house with rooms. The author is led through a castle of light, and each room, from Gifts and Foundation to War, Past, Storm, Seasons, Mirror, Inheritance and Changes, shows her something about herself and God.

It comes out of real loss. She writes about growing up without a father, about delivering bread to people near the fighting in eastern Ukraine, and about fleeing on the first day of the full-scale war in 2022.
It ties nearly every vision to the Bible. Most chapters have a Bible Scriptures section, so the reader can test what she saw against the Word.
It asks you to answer. Every room ends with four to six questions, and one chapter, Yours, asks you to close your eyes and find your own room.
It is honest about what she did not understand. She says she nearly left out the last room, because it took years before it made sense to her.

blocks.text: The book opens with a friendly greeting from the author:

paras: Hi, it's nice to meet you!

blocks.text: She tells you plainly what she was looking for as a girl and as a young woman:

paras: I would not know what it was like to call a place home until the age of thirty.

blocks.text: Her answer comes in the Introduction, and the rest of the book unpacks it:

paras: HOME is not a physical place and not people around me, but HOME is me, myself.

blocks.text: In the room called Storm, she walks on water with Jesus as the sea rises, lies down in the waves without fear, and draws a lesson about panic:

paras: Calm down, wait for the storm to end, and then make a decision.

blocks.text: And the last page ends with an invitation:

paras: This eternal house, your HOME, is already inside you.

paras: On the second floor, the author finds a hall covered in rubies, with red sofas, chandeliers and a carpet that runs the length of the hall. She falls asleep on a velvet sofa, and when she wakes she sees from the window that she is inside a castle, high on a mountain above the clouds. She reads the red as the power of the blood of Jesus, and she searches the Bible and finds rubies in Isaiah 54 and in the city of Revelation.

In the second room, the author finds a small black-and-white room with a thick book of every war in history. She writes about delivering bread near the front line in 2014, and about two men fighting over a loaf. She writes that she hates war, that hatred rose in her heart in that room, and that she felt God with her, understanding all of it.
The last room is absolute darkness. She screamed into it to measure the space, and learned that it was a small room with a floor, walls and a ceiling:
"What I don't see doesn't mean danger."
It took her years to understand this room. She decides, in the end, that when we are close to God His light can blind us for a while, and that only later do we see how close He was.

author.bio: Aleksa Aishpur is from Kyiv, Ukraine. She holds a bachelor's degree from the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, co-founded a crowdfunding platform in Ukraine, and co-founded a church. As a teenager she volunteered with young people in prison, children with cancer and people with disabilities, and in 2022 she worked on humanitarian efforts across the United States, Ukraine and Romania. She works as a coach in personal development, business and career, and says that she wants to help people find joy in their work and in their lives. She began writing Home in 2017.

paras: The author says she began writing Home in 2017, after war began in eastern Ukraine, and that the pain around her raised the question of where our home is when a house can be destroyed. She hopes each reader will find their own rooms, and she writes that the book has no ending, so that those who read it can create their own.
